Dot = observed win percentage · 50% = an even split

Each judgment selects one overall winner, considering New, Useful, and Surprising jointly. We average the win percentages against the three opponents, giving each opponent equal weight. For example, 40%, 60%, and 80% against the three opponents gives a 60% overall score. This describes the judges’ preferences for these papers, not absolute creativity. Equal scores share a rank.

The ranking describes the sampled pairs; the ranking across all eligible pairs remains uncertain.

Sampling uncertainty: what these scores can tell us

We increased the sample after the initial results were observed. These exploratory reference ranges use a calculation intended for a sample size chosen in advance. No confidence guarantee is claimed for this extended run. They do not measure judge disagreement, correctness, or future system performance. Wide ranges leave the ranking across all eligible pairs uncertain; overlapping ranges do not mean the systems are equal.

Statistical method and assumptions

The calculation treats the response to every possible paper pair as fixed, with only the sampled pairs changing. Keeping model settings fixed does not guarantee the same reply on another call. These bounds exclude variation between repeated calls, changes in the provider’s model, agreement with human experts, and future papers. The full-pool order remains uncertain. See Bardenet and Maillard, Concentration inequalities for sampling without replacement.

Exploratory fixed-size Serfling reference ranges with Bonferroni correction, intersected with deterministic unsampled-mass bounds.

The target of 10 paper pairs per matchup was chosen after observing the initial 6-pair-per-matchup results. The displayed ranges use the nominal 95% fixed-size calculation as an exploratory reference. They have no 95% coverage guarantee for this post hoc extension and are not sequentially valid. Calculations condition on the frozen released-paper pools and fixed judge/order instrument. Each pair averages four overall creativity votes; agent summaries weight opponents equally. Variance estimates and standard errors are fixed-size descriptive references for this extension. These ranges do not quantify uncertainty about future systems, future papers, or judge reliability.

How the comparison works

The lists of eligible released papers are saved before sampling. The separately labeled human–AI co-discovery paper is excluded. Distinct paper pairs are sampled uniformly within each scientist matchup. Each judge chooses one overall creativity winner, considering New, Useful, and Surprising jointly, in both paper orders. Each complete paper pair contributes four overall votes. Votes are averaged within the paper pair, then paper pairs within a matchup. Each opponent matchup receives equal weight.

New, Useful, and Surprising

These concepts are considered jointly in one overall creativity judgment. They are not scored separately; the judge explains the relevant tradeoffs.

New
How clearly the judge can connect the paper’s least familiar contribution to earlier research. A weaker connection can suggest novelty; the judge’s memory cannot verify it.
Useful
Whether the paper explains how its approach works and provides evidence for its claimed benefit.
Surprising
How far the paper’s central approach departs from the obvious approach to its question.

Conceptual foundations: Runco and Jaeger (2012), The Standard Definition of Creativity, discusses originality and effectiveness. Acar, Burnett, and Cabra (2017), Ingredients of Creativity: Originality and More, examines surprise alongside originality and value. These support the broad concepts. They do not validate CREST’s specific definitions or its model judging method. Why one joint judgment?

What this comparison leaves uncertain

  • Topics, release dates, underlying AI models, computing resources, and which papers each team chose to release differ across the paper collections.
  • Judges read extracted PDF text; visual plots and experimental claims were not independently verified.
  • The results concern these released papers and these judges. Small collections sharply limit what can be inferred about future papers.

  • This compares fixed released public-paper pools, not future-system capability or a controlled benchmark.
  • Topic, date, model backbone, compute, and publication-selection differences confound causal interpretation.
  • PDF text extraction excludes visual plot inspection and may omit equations, tables, or other content.
  • Only two judges and two answer orders define the fixed instrument; their errors and rubric validity are not quantified by sampling bands.
  • Only complete four-judgment paper-pair blocks contribute scores. Partial completion may be selective; primary ranks require the entire plan.
  • Opponent matchups receive equal weight, regardless of released collection sizes or sampled pair counts. Each verdict is one overall creativity choice guided jointly by New, Useful, and Surprising.
  • Small eligible pools, including Agentic v3's two autonomous papers when present, sharply limit representativeness.
  • Known costs cover successful result records only; missing provider billing or failed attempts may add unrecorded charges.
  • The target of 10 paper pairs per matchup was chosen after observing the initial 6-pair-per-matchup results. The displayed ranges use the nominal 95% fixed-size calculation as an exploratory reference. They have no 95% coverage guarantee for this post hoc extension and are not sequentially valid.
  • 60 prior judging attempts were excluded from rankings; their known cost $13.873186 and 0 unknown-cost attempts remain included in total accounting. Earlier extraction pass and separate-criterion judging were excluded; final ranking uses fresh overall judgments only.

How Much of a Learned Evolution Strategy Is the Algorithm It Was Anchored To? vs. ENHANCING RESILIENCE: ROBUST LOW-DIMENSIONAL DIFFUSION MODELS AGAINST INPUT PERTURBATIONS · 4 saved judgments

gemini gemini-4-argon

A: How Much of a Learned Evolution Strategy Is the Algorithm It Was Anchored To? (Sakana Agentic Scientist (v3))

B: ENHANCING RESILIENCE: ROBUST LOW-DIMENSIONAL DIFFUSION MODELS AGAINST INPUT PERTURBATIONS (Sakana AI Scientist (v1))

Preferred: How Much of a Learned Evolution Strategy Is the Algorithm It Was Anchored To?

Evaluated relative to their respective fields and tasks, Manuscript A demonstrates substantially stronger overall creative quality than Manuscript B across New, Useful, and Surprising. For New, breaking Manuscript A into its constituent building blocks yields: (1) separable diagonal CMA-ES with cumulative step-size adaptation (A pages 2–5), (2) permutation-equivariant Deep Sets population encoders and coordinate-shared MLPs (A pages 3–4), (3) zero-initialized bounded multiplicative residual gates g(v) = exp(ln 2 · tanh(3v)) on CMA-ES updates that allow exact source-level recovery of the classical algorithm via an identity gate g ≡ 1 (A pages 1–2, 4), and (4) success-rate-gated antithetic mirrored sampling paired with a pair-consistent evolution-path normalization µ_eff^path = (∑_pairs(w_a - w_b)^2 + ∑_unpaired w_i^2)^(-1) to preserve neutral step-size variance when learned recombination weights differ across mirrored pairs (A page 5). A's least placeable building blocks—the pair-consistent path normalization for asymmetrically weighted mirrored pairs and the exact subtractive identity-gate attribution parameterization—cannot be pinned to a single prior paper; they can only be placed more broadly within the evolution-strategy adaptation subfield literature (e.g., Hansen, 2016) and the meta-black-box optimization subfield literature (e.g., Lange et al., 2023). In contrast, Manuscript B breaks down into: (1) standard Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) with sinusoidal embeddings (B pages 3–5), (2) Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) adversarial training with tuned perturbation magnitude ε = 0.005 and mixed clean/perturbed batches (B pages 4–6), and (3) scaling MLP hidden dimension and layer count on 2D toy datasets (B pages 5–6). Even B's least placeable block—applying FGSM perturbations x_0^perturbed = x_0 + ε · sign(∇_{x_0} L(x_0)) during 2D DDPM training—is directly placeable in two specific foundational works: Goodfellow et al. (2014) for FGSM adversarial training and Ho et al. (2020) for DDPM training, with MLP scaling being textbook common knowledge. For Surprising, the obvious approach to A's task (meta-evolving a black-box evolution strategy on low-dimensional analytic functions for zero-shot transfer to a 704-dimensional reinforcement learning control task) is to parameterize the update rule with a neural network, show that the transferred optimizer beats an external CMA-ES baseline on the target task, and claim successful transfer; the obvious approach to B's task (improving diffusion model robustness against input perturbations) is to augment training with FGSM adversarial examples, tune ε, and increase network capacity. B follows that obvious direction directly without any unexpected conceptual twist (B pages 4–6). These largely belong to established CMA-ES, residual-learning, and set-network approaches. Its least specifically placeable operative rule is the success-dependent mirroring probability: I can locate this only broadly in adaptive/mirrored evolution-strategy literature, not identify an earlier identical formulation. B’s hardest-to-place claim is instead that very low dimensionality intrinsically amplifies perturbation damage; I cannot identify an established source for that premise. That potentially unusual claim should be distinguished from its familiar interventions, rather than denying it novelty simply because it is unsupported. Neither manuscript earns novelty merely from assembling its ingredients. For A’s stated attribution task, the obvious approach is a learned-off ablation; for B’s robustness task, it is adversarial augmentation followed by perturbation-strength and capacity sweeps. Its more unexpected central move is showing that apparent transfer success becomes a budget-dependent head start whose advantage reverses on final solution quality (A pages 6–8). B largely follows the expected intervention sequence, without deriving a mechanism specifically addressing its proposed low-dimensional vulnerability. A makes its attribution mechanism concrete: pinning every multiplicative gate to one removes learned modulation while retaining the same classical core and fixed machinery. The reported anytime scores—1.191 for the full method and 1.107 for the identity control—and the positive paired increment on all eight seeds support a local, implementation-specific learned contribution. The control’s 220.7-higher final return also establishes a practically important distinction between faster progress and a better endpoint (A pages 6–7). These conclusions remain limited by configuration selection on the evaluation seeds, one meta-training run, one transfer environment, and separately retrained auxiliary ablations (A page 10); they do not establish universal transfer failure or isolate every component causally. B supplies a reasonably actionable augmentation recipe, but its evidence does not establish the advertised clean-preserving robustness. Its perturbed evaluation compares generated samples against perturbed reference data, which does not directly measure the output-consistency objective stated earlier (B pages 4 and 6). The baseline lacks perturbed metrics, every reported perturbed KL divergence is infinite, and average clean KL rises from 0.418 to 0.965 in the final configuration (B page 7). Lower perturbed Frechet distance among modified configurations is useful partial evidence, but cannot resolve those gaps. Thus, despite B’s harder-to-source dimensionality premise, A more successfully converts a substantive, somewhat unexpected finding into a controlled and usable scientific conclusion. That connection between mechanism, evidence, and revised interpretation supports the overall choice.

B's claimed payoff follows directly from its controlled attribution: query-conditioned MaxSim selection lifts exact-match accuracy from the 0.52 query-blind merge ceiling to 0.91 alone and to 0.98 with the two chunk-level supporting components, without adding trainable parameters or altering the training loss (B pages 5–7, Table 1). Under Surprising, for A's task of improving transformer training efficiency via context window adjustment, the obvious approach is a sequence-length curriculum or heuristic window schedule during training; A's abstract (A page 1) stays entirely within that expected direction and offers no unexpected central move on A pages 1–2. For B's task of overcoming multi-fact interference when internalizing long contexts into LoRA weights (B pages 1–3), the obvious approach is to increase the hypernetwork's read-out and output-head capacity or add auxiliary training losses that supervise key–value binding and penalize distractors; B departs sharply and centrally from this expectation both by turning head redesigns (0.32 exact match) and auxiliary binding losses (0.46 exact match) into falsifiable negative controls that fail to breach the 0.52 query-blind ceiling (B pages 2–6), and by repurposing ColBERT-style token-level retrieval not to fetch text into a prompt, but as a parameter-free merge-time router over generated weight adapters (B pages 3–4, 8–9). As a tradeoff, B's empirical scope is bounded to a synthetic single-query multi-needle benchmark, inherits the chunk-separability ceiling of a frozen encoder, and experiences run-to-run training collapse variance that requires restart and magnitude-prior mitigation (B pages 4–5, 7–8), whereas A frames a general language-modeling efficiency task (A page 1); however, B's transparent handling of these limitations and its complete, rigorous execution overwhelmingly outweigh A's unsubstantiated outline.

A consists of context-window adaptation, conditioning on sequence length and model capacity, and a promised training-efficiency payoff (A page 1). Its least placeable building block is the capacity-dependent adjustment rule: I can locate the general direction in adaptive-attention and sequence-length-curriculum research, but no actual rule is supplied to distinguish it from those approaches. That underspecification is not evidence of novelty. B’s blocks include generated low-rank adapters, adapter composition, token-level MaxSim scoring, and relevance-aware span placement (B pages 3–4). Major primitives have identifiable antecedents in LoRA and ColBERT. Its least placeable claim is the specific experimental diagnosis that query-blind composition, rather than generation or supervision, dominates this system’s retrieval failures. I cannot name a prior work establishing that particular result; I can place it only broadly in adapter-interference and routing research. The unusual assembly of familiar primitives contributes to unexpectedness, not automatically to newness. For A’s efficiency task, the obvious approach is to tune or schedule context length; its proposal follows that direction without specifying a distinctive control mechanism. For B’s multi-fact retrieval task, an obvious approach is to strengthen the adapter generator or its binding supervision. B instead moves the decision to query-time weight composition: retrieval scores select an adapter rather than retrieve text into the prompt (B pages 3–4). Query-conditioned routing is familiar, so this is not a wholly unexpected principle, but relocating it to composition is a central and meaningful departure. The decisive difference is whether that departure produces a supported payoff. A asserts successful experiments, but provides no adjustment algorithm, timing measurements, accuracy results, or efficiency–quality comparison; the method and results on A page 1 remain placeholders, and A page 2 supplies no usable experimental evidence. Important qualifications remain: configurations are evaluated once, implementation details are incomplete, and the evidence concerns one synthetic task with training instability (B pages 4–5 and 8). Failed alternative heads and losses also do not prove that query-blind composition is intrinsically incapable of preserving queryable bindings. Nevertheless, B’s bounded empirical diagnosis and operational redirection offer substantially stronger creative quality than A’s unworked efficiency proposal, without needing to accept B’s broader impossibility claims.

This is supported but narrow evidence: configuration selection reused evaluation seeds, only one transfer environment was tested, and several auxiliary ablations confound mechanism removal with separate meta-training runs (B page 10). For A’s task, the obvious approach is cardinality-first column ordering followed by row clustering; its subset-specific permutations and singleton recycling depart meaningfully from that direction. The stronger departure is the experimentally supported conclusion that a successful learned optimizer mostly inherits its above-reference margin, while its remaining learned benefit changes with budget and reverses on final quality (B pages 6–9). Despite A’s credible engineering contribution and B’s familiar ingredients, B turns its central design into a more securely demonstrated, counterintuitive scientific finding. On page 7 and in Table 1, B explicitly states that its 26.2560 score trails AdaEvolve (26.30) and EvoX (30.52), yet in Section 5 (B page 9) it falsely claims that 26.2560 outperforms both OpenEvolve and AdaEvolve. Additionally, Figure 3's caption claims up to a 1.55x improvement over Round-robin (B page 8) despite Round-robin scoring 0.00 throughout the text and Table 1 (B pages 1, 2, 7), and baseline runtimes are never empirically tabulated. Regarding Surprising, for Paper A's task of transferring a meta-evolved evolution strategy from low-dimensional analytic functions to high-dimensional control, the obvious approach would be to benchmark the learned optimizer against classical CMA-ES and an unanchored neural baseline, highlight the 1.191 vs. 1.000 headline win and 2.42x speedup, and claim successful zero-shot transfer. Paper A departs centrally from this expected direction by designing its architecture to deconstruct and refute the naive reading of its own headline improvement (A pages 1, 4, 6–8), proving that most of the gain is scaffolding and that the learned modulation trades early speed for worse final return. For Paper B's task of minimizing a maximum fractional ratio W_j / (M - S_j) across capacity-constrained bins, the obvious combinatorial optimization approach is parametric binary search over the target ratio K to linearize the capacity check, paired with First-Fit/Best-Fit Decreasing and move/swap local search. While applying this clean deterministic formulation to LLM placement departs practically from heavyweight MILP or evolutionary baselines in serving literature (B pages 2–3), algorithmically it follows the expected textbook direction for fractional bin packing. Weighing the tradeoffs, Paper B delivers a fast, training-free solver that directly improves static placement scores in milliseconds (B pages 6–8), whereas Paper A requires expensive outer meta-evolution and uncovers a negative result on asymptotic transfer where its learned gates ultimately underperform its unlearned anchor on final return (A pages 6–8, 10). However, Paper A's exact subtractable design, rigorous diagnostic execution, and central departure from headline-driven reporting far outweigh Paper B's textbook algorithmic assembly and internal reporting inconsistencies.

Its least-placeable mechanism is the success-conditioned mirroring rule (A page 5): I can locate that only within mirrored evolution-strategy research, not a specific earlier formulation. B uses an SLO-weighted pressure proxy, fixed-target fractional-constraint conversion, standard packing heuristics, and move/swap refinement. Its constraint conversion is standard quasiconvex feasibility-bisection reasoning, as treated in Boyd and Vandenberghe’s Convex Optimization; its least-placeable block is the particular weighted-request-rate/remaining-memory proxy (B page 4), which I can place only within LLM-serving placement research. Thus, the least-placeable elements of both reach only subfield-level identification; neither paper earns novelty simply from assembling familiar components. For A’s stated attribution task, the obvious approach is a matched learned-component ablation; for B’s placement task, it is memory-aware greedy packing or integer programming. A makes its ablation exact through identity-valued gates, then takes the central conclusion somewhere less expected: learning improves accumulated early performance while worsening the final solution. That reversal is more consequential than merely estimating a learned contribution (A pages 4 and 7). B’s conversion of fractional pressure into target-dependent item weights is an effective simplification, but its subsequent bisection, packing, and local refinement follow a conventional optimization direction (B pages 5–6). A’s mechanism is sufficiently worked out to support its narrow payoff. Pinning every gate to one preserves the surrounding machinery, producing scores of 1.107 without learning and 1.191 with learning; the paired learned increment is positive on all eight evaluation seeds, while the unlearned anchor finishes 220.7 return higher (A pages 6–7). This supports attribution and metric sensitivity, not universal optimizer superiority. Configuration selection on those evaluation seeds, one meta-training run per configuration, and a single transfer environment restrict generalization; separately trained ablations also confound several secondary mechanism claims (A page 10). B correctly derives W + KS ≤ KM and reports a refinement improvement from 26.2332 to 26.2560 (B pages 5 and 8). However, greedy initialization cannot generally guarantee a feasible packing, and heuristic packing failure cannot certify infeasibility for bisection. Consequently, neither guaranteed placement success nor mathematical optimality follows from the described algorithm. The reported 0.021-second runtime lacks sufficient workload and timing detail to establish the claimed comparative efficiency, and no serving measurements demonstrate prevention of SLO violations (B pages 6–7). Its conclusion also claims superiority over AdaEvolve despite its own table reporting a lower score (B pages 7 and 9). A therefore provides the stronger creative payoff: a precisely operationalized experiment revealing a meaningful limitation of learned optimization, rather than a familiar heuristic pipeline whose broader assurances need repair.

In contrast, B makes a central, unexpected departure from standard practice in meta-optimization. Rather than stopping at its strong positive headline result—where the learned strategy beats the pinned CMA-ES reference 1.191 to 1.000 across 8/8 seeds (B page 1, 6)—B constructs the optimizer so that forcing all gates to 1 recovers the exact classical core + sampling scaffolding on the same code path, and uses this null control to dismantle the naive reading of its own win (B page 1–2, 6–8). Showing that 55.8% of the apparent transfer margin comes from the unlearned scaffolding (1.107), that the learned contribution shrinks from 86.5% at generation 1,000 to 44.2% at generation 2,000, and that the learned modulation actually reverses sign on final return (finishing 220.7 lower than the identity-gate anchor despite halving log-regret during in-distribution meta-training, B page 7–8) turns a routine benchmark win into a rigorous methodological critique. For Useful, there is a clear tradeoff between A's narrow engineering compliance on a competitive benchmark and B's thorough mechanistic and diagnostic execution, which strongly favors B. A's central mechanism (Algorithm 1, A page 6) is explicitly worked out and meets the strict 16 MB (15,896,434 bytes) and 10-minute constraints while edging out the parent baseline from 1.0611 to 1.0600 val_bpb (A page 1, 7). However, as A candidly notes, the payoff is tiny (0.00108 BPB) and borderline statistically significant across seeds (p ≈ 0.13, A page 8–9), the diagonal initialization is indistinguishable from full Cholesky initialization (+0.00012 BPB, Table 2, A page 7–8), and there is an unresolved mechanical tension in Table 2 where the unweighted SVD parent recipe achieves 1.0611 in Table 1 yet is reported as crashing at step 4886 inside the ALS ablation due to 'un-scaling the decomposed right factor'—an operation that an unweighted SVD does not require (A page 7–8). Conversely, B's mechanisms—both the anchored residual optimizer with pair-consistent path normalization (B page 3–5) and the decompositional transfer audit (B page 5–6)—are completely worked out and rigorously validated. B's pair-consistent normalization is proved essential (+0.294 paired delta across 8/8 seeds, preventing step-size freeze at generation 500, B page 8–9), the learned residual is statistically supported (+0.083 ± 0.016 paired over the anchor on 8/8 seeds, B page 6–7), and B meticulously audits its own single-meta-run weight confounds and horizon sensitivities (B page 10). Thus, B is more New, far more Surprising in its central direction, and more convincingly Useful relative to its stated research task.

A’s central blocks are curvature-weighted low-rank error correction and alternating discrete quantization with continuous SVD updates (A pages 4–6). Even its least routine core block, sensitivity-weighted residual decomposition, has a close named precedent in LQ-LoRA; alternating quantization and low-rank fitting also appears in LoftQ. B likewise relies substantially on established blocks: separable CMA-ES, identity-initialized residual gates, permutation-equivariant conditioning, and antithetic sampling (B pages 4–5). Its pair-aware correction to evolution-path normalization is the block I can place least specifically: the underlying variance calculation is elementary, but I can locate its particular algorithmic application only in mirrored-sampling evolution-strategy literature, not a specific prior formulation. Neither manuscript deserves novelty credit merely for assembling familiar components. Both proposals are operationally developed, but their supported payoffs differ. A supplies an implementable weighted-factorization algorithm and reports a 15,896,434-byte artifact with 1.0600 BPB. Its no-ALS ablation supports the usefulness of iterative refinement. However, the comparison with an estimated parent-baseline score is modest and statistically unresolved at the reported p≈0.13, while the failed unweighted-initialization run does not establish that curvature alignment is mathematically necessary for stability (A pages 7–8). In particular, an evaluation crash is not a diagnosis of the asserted conditioning mechanism. B’s recoverable identity-gate control directly addresses its attribution task: turning learning off leaves the same classical core and fixed machinery, making the conditional learned contribution measurable. The reported +0.083 paired anytime-score increment across all eight evaluation seeds, alongside the anchor’s 220.7 higher mean final return, supports a concrete distinction between faster progress and better eventual solutions (B pages 6–9). This is not evidence of general transfer failure: there is only one control environment, one meta-training run per configuration, development selection used the evaluation protocol, and several auxiliary ablations also change the learned weights (B page 10). Those limitations restrict generalization, but do not erase the central same-code identity-control comparison. For A’s compression task, the obvious approach is sensitivity-aware quantization with residual reconstruction; weighting the SVD and alternating its updates develops that expected direction. For B’s attribution task, the obvious approach is baseline and component-ablation comparisons. Exact identity recovery is a particularly effective implementation of that approach, not intrinsically a surprising invention. The stronger departure is the central finding that the learned optimizer’s apparent success changes interpretation with budget and reverses under final-solution quality: learning supplies a head start while its nonlearned anchor ultimately finishes better (B pages 7–8). Thus B’s advantage is not simply greater experimental detail or more candid prose. Its worked-out control turns familiar optimization machinery into a supported, consequential explanation of what the learned component actually contributes. That explanatory payoff and substantive directional reversal outweigh A’s useful but less securely attributed refinement.

Its least placeable substantive block is the diagnosis that composition-time interference, rather than adapter-generation capacity, dominates the studied retrieval failure; I can place that only broadly in adapter-composition and binding research, not in a specific earlier result. B combines dictionary encoding, trie partitioning, incremental frequency updates, and bounded lookahead. Its least placeable block is the particular frequency-times-squared-string-length priority, which I can place only broadly in heuristic trie/data-layout optimization, not identify as an established formula (B pages 4–5). Neither receives novelty credit merely for assembling familiar components. For A’s task, the obvious approach is to improve the adapters’ representation of multiple bindings through capacity, supervision, or better merging; for B’s task, it is to put repetitive columns first and sort rows to share prefixes. Query-conditioned retrieval itself is familiar, but relocating it to adapter composition changes the proposed explanation of failure. B’s branch-specific column choices and adaptive lookahead meaningfully elaborate the expected sorting/trie direction rather than substantially redirecting it. Frozen-encoder MaxSim selects the relevant adapter, and the reported component comparison moves exact-match accuracy from 0.52 to 0.91 with selection alone, then to 0.98 with span placement and aligned chunking (A page 6). This demonstrates a useful remedy in the tested setting, though single evaluations, training collapses, and one synthetic benchmark do not establish the claimed structural impossibility of successful query-blind composition; unsuccessful head and loss variants cannot rule out all such alternatives (A pages 4, 7–8). B supplies more explicit implementation details, including integer-coded counting and subtraction-based updates, and reports workable prefix sharing on real tables (B pages 4–6). However, its headline comparison mixes normalized scores, raw hit rates, and runtime improvements, so comparative payoff is unresolved. Its own lazy-greedy ablation exceeds the proposed lookahead method, while the asserted theoretical robustness guarantee is not demonstrated (B pages 6–7). No end-to-end serving-speed evidence closes that gap. Thus A’s narrower but directly supported intervention, coupled with its central diagnostic redirection, outweighs B’s practical implementation strengths and more conventional algorithmic refinement.

Conversely, A's tradeoff is that its evaluation is restricted to a synthetic multi-needle benchmark on a single frozen ~2B model and requires mitigation for run-to-run training collapses (A pages 4–5, 7–8). Nevertheless, A's mechanism is thoroughly worked out and delivers a decisive, well-attributed payoff: across 30 valid trained configurations under a controlled 3-hour GPU budget, parameter-free query-conditioned MaxSim selection alone lifts exact-match accuracy from the 0.52 query-blind ceiling to 0.91, and combining relevance-profile atom placement (0.93) with delimiter-aligned cuts reaches 0.98 across 128 to 65,536 tokens (A pages 4–7, Table 1, Figures 2–4). A's diagnostic falsification of competing hypotheses and massive empirical payoff on its stated task, combined with its surprising cross-domain routing insight, outweigh B's real-world dataset scope and make A the clear overall winner.

A builds from hypernetwork-generated adapters, low-rank composition, MaxSim retrieval, and relevance-aware chunking; B builds from cardinality-based column ordering, string-length weighting, and lexicographic row grouping. A’s adapter-generation and matching primitives have identifiable antecedents in HINT and ColBERT, so their unusual assembly should not itself receive New credit. Its least-placeable substantive claim is the diagnosis that composition, rather than encoding or supervision, governs the observed multi-needle failure; I can relate that only to neural binding/interference literature, not identify a specific earlier statement of this result. B’s least-placeable block is its precise mean-squared-string-length divided by unique-ratio score (B pages 4–5); I can place it only broadly within database-layout and prefix-compression heuristics, not in a particular prior formulation. Neither exact block therefore has a specific antecedent I can confidently name. For A’s task, the obvious approach would be to strengthen the adapter generator, improve binding supervision, or refine query-blind merging. Its central departure is instead to postpone selection until the query arrives and use retrieval scores to choose weight-space contributions—not retrieve text into the prompt (A pages 3–4). Query-conditioned retrieval is familiar, but moving that decision to adapter composition is a meaningful change of direction. For B’s task, the obvious approach is to put repetitive columns first and sort rows to cluster shared prefixes. Length-weighting that ordering follows the stated objective relatively directly; discovering that static ordering suffices instead of dynamic recursion is a useful but smaller departure (B pages 5 and 8). A also provides more direct evidence connecting its intervention to its stated payoff. Frozen-encoder MaxSim routing reportedly raises exact match from 0.52 to 0.91, with relevance placement and delimiter-aligned cuts reaching 0.98; the unsuccessful head and loss variants provide relevant comparison mechanisms (A pages 4–7). These results support a practical repair on the tested substrate, not the stronger claim that query-blind composition necessarily discards information: a query-aware decoder could in principle retrieve from weights containing multiple facts. Single evaluations, training collapses, and the fixed model and budget further limit the causal generalization (A pages 4 and 7–8). B’s algorithm is more explicitly specified and readily implementable. Its reported 0.946-second runtime and score improvements over cardinality sorting and dynamic ordering support usefulness as a layout heuristic (B pages 5–6 and 8). However, the larger serving payoff is not established. Matching adjacent row prefixes permits ordinary KV reuse for suitably framed separate requests, not automatically for successive rows within one serialized table, where preceding attention context differs; B pages 3–5 leave that distinction unresolved. Squared character-prefix overlap is also a proxy, with no demonstrated token-level cache, latency, or memory savings. Thus, despite B’s clear implementation and A’s overextended bottleneck interpretation, A’s more consequential directional shift is backed by a direct intervention-and-ablation result on its actual retrieval task. That supports the stronger overall creative contribution.

For B's task of fixing multi-fact retrieval in context-to-LoRA hypernetworks, the obvious approach is to increase the capacity of the hypernetwork's read-out and output heads or add training-time auxiliary losses that supervise multi-fact binding and penalize distractor interference. B departs dramatically from this expected direction: it implements both obvious approaches as formal negative-control families to prove they fail to cross a 0.52 query-blind ceiling (plateauing at 0.32 and 0.46, B pages 2-6), and instead reframes weight-space context internalization as a merge-time routing problem. By assembling an information-retrieval primitive (ColBERT MaxSim) directly into the hypernetwork's frozen encoder space to select which chunk's weight adapter dominates at composition time—with zero new parameters and no retraining (B pages 1-4)—B achieves a much stronger conceptual departure. Regarding Useful, A's central mechanism—static column ordering by length-weighted cardinality followed by lexicographical row sorting (A pages 4-5)—is worked out and executes in 0.946 seconds across five real-world datasets (A pages 5-6). A combines cardinality-based column prioritization, lexicographic row grouping, and a mean-squared-string-length/unique-ratio score (A pages 4–5). The first two are established database layout and prefix-compression techniques; for the exact score, its least placeable block, I can identify only that subfield, not a specific prior formulation. B combines hypernetwork-generated adapters, MaxSim retrieval, query-dependent routing, and relevance-guided span placement (B pages 3–4). Generated adapters and MaxSim are specifically traceable to HINT and ColBERT. Its least placeable block is relevance-guided adapter-span (“atom”) placement, which I can locate only broadly in retrieval-guided representation selection, not a particular prior algorithm. Neither manuscript therefore warrants novelty credit simply for assembling familiar components, and B’s use of retrieval is not itself a new primitive. The stronger distinction is how the mechanisms support their intended payoff. A gives an actionable, inexpensive sorting heuristic and reports a combined score of 0.6984 versus GGR’s 0.692, with a 0.946-second runtime; its ablations also support choosing static over more elaborate ordering under its scoring rule (A pages 6 and 8). However, the connection to actual KV-cache savings needs repair. Equal prefixes of adjacent rows do not automatically yield reusable KV states when those rows appear after different histories within one serialized table. A does not clearly specify the independent row-prompt arrangement needed to justify that reuse, nor demonstrate end-to-end serving benefits from its squared-character objective (A pages 3–6). Its evidence supports a layout-proxy improvement more securely than the claimed drop-in inference improvement. B’s mechanism is coherent: score chunks against the query using frozen token features, then let the relevant chunk’s adapter dominate composition. The reported increase from 0.52 to 0.91 with selection alone, followed by 0.98 with span placement and boundary alignment, directly measures success on its stated retrieval task (B page 6). Comparisons against head redesign and auxiliary supervision strengthen the practical diagnosis. Nevertheless, these are best-configuration results on one synthetic benchmark, with run collapses and limited implementation detail; they do not establish a universal query-blind ceiling. A query-blind adapter can in principle preserve multiple bindings for a decoder that subsequently receives the query. B’s evidence supports a bottleneck in the tested system and budget, not its strongest structural-impossibility language (B pages 3–4 and 7–8). For A, the obvious approach is low-cardinality-first ordering and grouping similar rows; weighting string lengths and dropping dynamic refinement develop that expected direction. For B, the obvious approach within context-to-LoRA is improving generated representations or binding supervision, while conventional retrieval would fetch relevant text. Moving query-dependent selection into weight composition is a more consequential departure, although query-aware routing is familiar in principle. B wins because this central reframing has substantially stronger task-level support, not because its benchmark is larger or its constituent techniques are unprecedented. Its narrow synthetic scope and incomplete causal claims temper, but do not erase, that advantage over A’s modest proxy gain and unresolved cache-reuse assumption.

Evaluated relative to their respective fields and tasks, Manuscript A demonstrates substantially stronger overall creative quality than Manuscript B when considering New, Useful, and Surprising jointly. Regarding New, we break each manuscript into its constituent building blocks and examine the least placeable block independently of how the blocks are combined. Manuscript A relies on: (1) chunked context-to-LoRA hypernetwork generation and rank-axis adapter concatenation (A page 1, page 3), which is standard material in the hypernetwork PEFT and adapter-merging literature such as HINT (Ivison et al., 2023) and LoRAHub (Huang et al., 2023); (2) token-level maximum cosine similarity (MaxSim) late-interaction scoring (A page 3, page 4), which appears in a specific named work, ColBERT (Khattab et al., 2021; Santhanam et al., 2022b); (3) delimiter-aligned chunk cutting (A page 4), which is standard material in retrieval-augmented generation preprocessing; and (4) using a frozen encoder's token-level relevance profile to center the span ("atom") from which a hypernetwork constructs a weight-space adapter (A page 4, page 6). While every general component in A has roots in dense retrieval or PEFT, A's least placeable block—relevance-peak atom placement for hypernetwork-emitted weight updates—can only be placed at the level of the broader subfields of span-based dense retrieval (e.g., Ma et al., 2022) and hypernetwork parameter generation rather than a specific prior formulation. Manuscript B relies on: (1) VoxelNet and image backbones projected into a Bird's Eye View (BEV) grid with a CenterPoint detection head (B page 4, page 6, page 7), which is standard material in multi-modal 3D detection (Zhou & Tuzel, 2017; Yin et al., 2020); (2) MLP-based 2D Cartesian coordinate positional encodings (B page 5), which is standard material across BEV vision transformers; (3) Euclidean distance transforms and binary masks over rasterized HD map channels (B page 5), which is standard material in map-aware autonomous driving perception; and (4) a sigmoid-gated convex combination of two feature embeddings added to a BEV feature map (B page 5, page 6). Even B's least placeable block—gated additive fusion of rasterized HD map embeddings and Cartesian coordinate embeddings in BEV—is a standard formulation appearing across numerous works in multimodal BEV perception and gated multimodal units. Regarding Surprising, for Manuscript A's task of resolving multi-fact retrieval failures in long-context hypernetwork-generated LoRA adapters, the obvious approach is to increase the hypernetwork's read-out/output-head capacity to represent multiple key–value bindings or add auxiliary training losses that supervise multi-target separation (A page 2, page 3). For Manuscript B's task of leveraging HD semantic maps to improve 3D bounding box geometry in BEV object detection, the obvious approach is to encode rasterized HD map channels alongside spatial coordinates and fuse them into the BEV feature map prior to the detection head (B page 2, page 5). Manuscript A makes a sharp, central departure from its obvious direction: it demonstrates that modifying the generator architecture and training objective both fail because query-blind adapter merging inherently induces weight-space superposition of co-resident facts, and it instead reframes weight-space context internalization as an inference-time routing problem solved by repurposing ColBERT-style token-level MaxSim inside the hypernetwork's frozen encoder to select which chunk's adapter dominates the merge (A page 2, page 4, page 7). By contrast, Manuscript B follows the expected direction for map-aware BEV fusion almost directly, and its only unexpected twist—that raw binary map masks marginally outperform Euclidean distance transforms by +0.0002 (B page 1, page 9)—is an incidental preprocessing ablation detail rather than a central conceptual departure. Regarding Useful, Manuscript A's central proposal is a parameter-free, training-free query-conditioned merge-time router using late-interaction MaxSim over the frozen encoder's token states, paired with relevance-profile atom placement and delimiter-aligned chunk boundaries (A page 4). The mechanism is fully worked out and validated through a falsifiable experimental design across 30 valid trained models under a fixed 3-hour single-GPU budget across context lengths from 128 to 65,536 tokens (A page 4, page 6, page 8). Its claimed payoff follows decisively: while read-out/head redesigns plateau at 0.32 exact-match accuracy, auxiliary training losses plateau at 0.46, and the strongest query-blind merge reaches a ceiling of 0.52, adding query-conditioned MaxSim selection alone lifts accuracy to 0.91, and adding atom placement and delimiter-aligned cuts reaches 0.98 (A page 6 Table 1, page 7 Figure 3), with training-collapse variance transparently separated from the accuracy ceiling (A page 7, page 8 Figure 4). Manuscript B's central proposal is Hybrid Semantic-Cartesian Positional Encodings (HSC-PE), which passes BEV Cartesian coordinates and HD map Euclidean distance fields through MLPs and fuses them via a learned sigmoid gate before a CenterPoint head (B page 5, page 6, page 7 Algorithm 1). While B's pipeline is coherent enough to run and clear a competition threshold (0.1763 aggregate score, B page 8 Table 1), its claimed payoffs suffer from internal contradictions and missing evidence. Specifically, B's Figure 4 caption asserts that the Euclidean distance transform is "a transformation demonstrated by the ablation study to be critical for optimal performance" (B page 6), which directly contradicts Table 2 and the text showing that removing the distance transform in favor of raw binary masks actually improves the score to 0.1766 (B page 9, page 10). Moreover, removing the entire semantic map encoding only reduces mAP by a marginal 0.0017 (0.1763 to 0.1746 in Table 2, B page 9), and although B motivates its entire method as optimizing strict 3D IoU alignment (Eq. 1, B page 4) to fix yaw and dimension errors, it actually trains with standard CenterPoint focal and L1 losses (B page 6) and explicitly admits that it lacks any breakdown of high-IoU, yaw, or dimension metrics to verify that geometric alignment improved, alongside a missing verification artifact (`verified_scores.json`, B page 9, page 10). Even accounting for the tradeoff that A is evaluated on a synthetic benchmark whereas B tackles a multi-sensor real-world driving dataset, A's surprising cross-domain routing assembly and rigorously demonstrated diagnostic payoff make it far more creative overall.

A offers the stronger creative contribution through a more consequential diagnostic intervention, although neither paper introduces fundamentally unfamiliar computational primitives. A’s building blocks are hypernetwork-generated adapters, adapter composition, ColBERT-style MaxSim retrieval, relevance-guided span placement, and boundary-preserving chunking (A pages 2–4). Its least-placeable substantive claim is that composition, rather than generator design or supervision, governs the observed multi-fact failure; I can situate that in weight-space memory and interference research, but cannot name a prior work establishing this particular diagnosis. B’s blocks are BEV fusion, coordinate embeddings, Euclidean distance fields, complementary sigmoid gating, and center-based detection (B pages 4–7). Map-assisted detection already has a specific precedent in HDNET: Exploiting HD Maps for 3D Object Detection, while the mixing operation is standard gated feature fusion. B’s least-placeable finding—that raw masks suffice without engineered distance fields—fits learned-representation-versus-feature-engineering research, but I cannot identify a specific prior demonstration of its result. Neither manuscript deserves novelty credit merely for assembling familiar blocks. For A’s task, the obvious approaches are stronger binding supervision, greater adapter capacity, or retrieving relevant text; for B’s task, the obvious approach is to fuse map information into sensor-derived BEV features and regress boxes. Query conditioning is itself natural for retrieval, but A makes a meaningful directional departure by using retrieval to select weight updates rather than prompt content, and by testing this against upstream redesigns. B’s use of map information as gated positional encoding is a more modest departure from conventional feature fusion; the raw-mask finding reverses its preprocessing hypothesis but is secondary to the central architecture. A also connects that departure more convincingly to a demonstrated payoff. Frozen-encoder MaxSim selects the relevant chunk adapter, raising reported accuracy from 0.52 to 0.91; relevance placement and aligned chunking subsequently reach 0.98 (A pages 4 and 6). These interventions support a useful remedy on the stated synthetic task. They do not establish A’s stronger structural claim that query-blind composition necessarily prevents retrieval: the downstream model still receives the query, and budget-limited negative controls cannot exclude better representations or training. Single-run evaluations and incomplete merge specifications further limit the attribution (A pages 3–5). B specifies its gating equations more explicitly and tests an actual sensor-perception task, but its supported payoff is narrower than its geometric explanation. Removing semantic encoding changes the aggregate result only from 0.1763 to 0.1746, without uncertainty estimates or isolated yaw/dimension evidence (B page 9). Moreover, its stated mAP formula is TP/(TP+FP+FN), not average precision, so the evaluation definition needs repair (B page 7). Map-misalignment robustness is also untested. Thus A’s bounded but directly demonstrated routing intervention provides a stronger connection between an unexpected research direction and an effective mechanism than B’s largely conventional fusion proposal and incompletely isolated geometric benefits.

Paper B decomposes into: (1) chunked context-to-LoRA hypernetwork generation and rank-axis adapter concatenation (B pages 1, 3), placeable in hypernetwork adapter and model-merging works such as HINT (Ivison et al., 2023) and LoRAHub (Huang et al., 2023); (2) token-level maximum cosine similarity (MaxSim) scoring (B pages 3-4), placeable specifically in ColBERT and ColBERTv2 (Khattab et al., 2021; Santhanam et al., 2022b); and (3) relevance-profile atom placement that centers a hypernetwork chunk summary span on a token-level relevance peak alongside delimiter-aligned chunk cuts to prevent weight-space key-value superposition (B page 4). B's least placeable block—locating the hypernetwork adapter's generation atom via a token-level relevance peak within the frozen early-exit encoder—cannot be placed in a single prior paper and is only placeable broadly within the context-compression and dense retrieval subfield literatures. Regarding Surprising, for Paper A's task of improving 3D object detection with HD maps, the obvious approach would be to rasterize HD map layers, encode them alongside spatial coordinates into BEV features, and fuse them into the detection backbone. Paper A follows this expected direction directly (A pages 4-7); its only unexpected element is an incidental empirical ablation finding that raw binary map masks slightly outperform its proposed Euclidean distance transform by +0.0002 mAP (A page 9). For Paper B's task of resolving multi-fact retrieval failures in context-to-LoRA hypernetworks, the obvious approach would be to increase the hypernetwork's read-out/output head capacity or add auxiliary training losses that supervise key-value binding and penalize distractor interference. Paper B departs centrally from this expected direction: it proves through negative controls that both obvious approaches fail to cross a 0.52 accuracy ceiling caused by weight-space superposition (B pages 2-6), and instead recombines token-level late interaction (MaxSim) from text retrieval with hypernetwork weight composition, turning the hypernetwork's frozen encoder into a parameter-free, training-free merge-time router over generated LoRA adapters (B pages 3-4). Regarding Useful, Paper A's central mechanism—dynamically gating MLP-encoded Cartesian coordinates and EDT-processed HD map masks into the BEV feature map (A pages 5-7)—is worked out algorithmically, but its claimed payoff of resolving strict 3D volumetric yaw and dimension alignment is weakly supported and internally inconsistent. Specifically, removing the entire semantic map encoding only reduces mAP by 0.0017 (0.1763 to 0.1746, A page 9, Table 2), and A's Figure 4 caption claims that the EDT operation is 'demonstrated by the ablation study to be critical for optimal performance' (A page 6) when Table 2 and the text actually show that dropping EDT for raw binary masks improves performance to 0.1766, rendering EDT 'over-engineered and unnecessary' (A page 9). Conversely, Paper B's mechanism is thoroughly worked out and its payoff is rigorously demonstrated: across 30 valid configurations under a fixed 3-hour single-GPU budget and a 2B frozen base model on contexts from 128 to 65,536 tokens, B isolates the exact failure mode against two negative-control families (head redesign at 0.32 and auxiliary losses at 0.46) and a strong query-blind merge baseline (0.52), showing that query-conditioned MaxSim routing alone lifts exact-match accuracy from 0.52 to 0.91 without retraining or new parameters, and reaches 0.98 when combined with relevance-profile atom placement and delimiter-aligned chunk cuts (B pages 4-8, Table 1, Figures 2-4). Weighing the tradeoffs, Paper A evaluates on a realistic, multi-sensor autonomous driving benchmark (Lyft Level 5, A page 7) whereas Paper B relies on a synthetic multi-needle benchmark with templated single-fact queries and exhibits occasional training-run collapses that require restart stabilization (B pages 3, 4, 7-8). Source specificity therefore does not establish a decisive novelty difference, and I do not count either unusual assembly as ingredient-level novelty. Gating map and Cartesian embeddings develops that expected direction; the reversal favoring raw masks is less expected but incidental and numerically marginal. For B’s task, obvious approaches include improving binding capacity or retrieving the relevant chunk using the query. Retrieval itself is unsurprising; the more consequential departure is applying its address to weight-update composition rather than supplying retrieved text or redesigning the generator (B pages 3–4). B also connects that departure more directly to its demonstrated payoff. Its operationally described MaxSim router selects the adapter associated with the queried fact, and the component comparison reports 0.52 to 0.91 from selection alone, followed by 0.98 with span placement and aligned chunking (B page 6). Moreover, A page 7 labels TP/(TP+FP+FN) as mAP, although average precision requires precision–recall integration, leaving the metric specification in need of correction without necessarily invalidating the reported scores. B’s evidence is nevertheless narrower than its strongest rhetoric: one evaluation per configuration, training collapses and one synthetic setting limit causal generalization (B pages 4–8). Failure of the tested heads and losses cannot prove a universal query-blind ceiling, especially because the decoder still receives the query. Its implementation details and uncertainty reporting also need improvement. Even with those qualifications, B’s supported local routing result makes its central conceptual redirection more convincing than A’s largely inferred geometric-refinement payoff.

A builds on incremental BPE, DFS interval validation, flat SIMD search, atomic fast paths, and a centroid-tree fallback (A pages 4–6). The layout and branchless-search ingredients are recognizable in cache-aware search work such as Khuong and Morin’s Array Layouts for Comparison-Based Searching. Its least placeable block is the empirical finding that almost all relevant suffix trees fit within eight candidates (A page 8); I cannot locate that particular result more narrowly than empirical BPE algorithm engineering. B builds on separable CMA-ES, population-equivariant and coordinate-shared networks, identity-centered multiplicative residuals, and mirrored sampling (B pages 4–5). These are familiar optimizer and residual-learning ingredients. Its least placeable claim is the particular budget- and metric-dependent decomposition of transferred performance into scaffolding and learning (B pages 6–8), which I can place only in learned-optimizer evaluation literature, not a specific earlier result. Neither manuscript earns novelty merely from assembling familiar components. A offers a worked, actionable optimization: flatten candidate trees, gather historical timestamps, test intervals in parallel, and select the deepest valid candidate while retaining the original fallback. Reported reference-token agreement and a 1.123× geometric-mean improvement over incremental BPE support a practical throughput payoff (A page 7). Its component ablation is especially informative: flattening produces 1.128×, whereas adding SIMD raises that to 1.138× on the ablation subset (A page 9). Thus the contribution is substantially a data-layout improvement, not the much larger algorithmic advance suggested by comparisons with heap BPE. ARM performance and broader serving savings are not demonstrated by the supplied experiments. B’s useful mechanism is experimental identification rather than simply a better optimizer: forcing every residual gate to one removes learned influence while preserving the nonlearned implementation. This supports a meaningful comparison between the full strategy’s 1.191 score and the identity anchor’s 1.107, with a positive paired learning increment on all eight evaluation seeds (B pages 4–6). The mean terminal-return reversal—3488.5 versus 3709.2—then shows that the learning increment buys earlier progress rather than uniformly better optimization (B pages 7–9). This conclusion remains narrow: one transfer environment, one meta-training run, configuration selection on the evaluation seeds, and missing paired terminal-return statistics limit generalization; several secondary ablations also confound mechanism changes with retraining (B page 10). For A’s task, the obvious approach is cache-conscious and vectorized acceleration of incremental searches; replacing search with exhaustive parallel validation of unexpectedly tiny candidate sets is a useful but fairly direct departure. For B’s attribution task, the obvious approach is an unlearned baseline or module ablation, so the identity control alone is not especially surprising. The more consequential departure is the supported finding that successful in-distribution learning and improved transferred anytime performance coexist with inferior final solutions and a large nonlearned contribution. A supplies a credible engineering payoff and a distinctive structural observation, but B’s exact intervention turns a performance claim into a qualitatively different, operationally useful conclusion about when learning helps. That substantive diagnostic contribution, rather than its critical presentation, makes B the stronger overall creative work.

Neither manuscript’s unusual assembly alone establishes New, and B’s canonical-form terminology does not make its underlying rotation mathematics new. For A’s stated attribution task, the obvious approach is a matched learned-versus-disabled ablation; for B’s efficient reasoning-stabilization task, it is a structured recurrent controller or a cheaper continuous-time solver. B combines separable CMA-ES, identity-initialized residual gates, permutation-equivariant pooling, antithetic sampling, and controlled ablation. Its least readily placeable mapping is the mirrored-pair weight correction to evolution-path normalization (B page 5); I can place that in mirrored-evolution-strategy literature but cannot confidently name an exact prior formulation. Thus neither gains a decisive originality advantage merely from assembling familiar components. For A’s small-sample LSVI task, the obvious approach would be regularized or structured Fisher solves with variance reduction; replacing the estimated Gram matrix with analytical polynomial orthogonality is a meaningful directional departure. For B’s attribution task, the obvious approach would be a no-learning ablation, so that control alone is not surprising. B goes further through its central finding: the learned contribution changes with budget and reverses between anytime performance and final solution quality, rather than behaving like a fixed improvement over its backbone (B pages 6–8). The decisive difference is how securely these departures deliver their intended payoff. A works out a valid whitening identity under its assumptions and reports substantial Gaussian-benchmark improvements and informative variance ablations (A pages 5, 8–9). But its advertised non-Gaussian extension assumes that sufficient statistics and finite Askey polynomial features span the same space. Ordinary Gamma statistics include log(x), and Beta statistics include log(x) and log(1−x), so the proposed polynomial change of basis does not generally exist for those families. This is a load-bearing failure in the claimed mechanism, not merely missing experimental breadth. A page 5 also acknowledges quadratic mapping cost unless additional structure exists, limiting the unconditional linear-cost claim; its Poisson results show control variates worsening KL dramatically rather than universally stabilizing updates (A page 15). B’s narrower payoff is better supported. Pinning every multiplicative gate to one makes the learned parameters irrelevant while preserving the remaining implementation, providing an operationally exact null for its attribution question (B pages 4–5). The reported comparison isolates a +0.083 paired anytime increment, while the anchor finishes 220.7 return higher on average (B pages 6–9). This establishes a useful distinction between learning an early-progress advantage and improving the eventual solution. One meta-training run, development on the evaluation seeds, one transfer environment, and the absence of paired final-return evidence limit generalization; separately retrained secondary ablations also cannot cleanly identify every component’s effect (B pages 7 and 10). Nevertheless, the central identity-gate comparison survives those secondary confounds. B therefore offers the stronger overall creative contribution: a modestly original but workable experimental construction that reveals an unexpected limitation, rather than a more ambitious analytical extension whose principal generality requires repair.

For New, breaking Paper B into its constituent building blocks shows that each block comes from an existing named paper or standard material across several works: (1) the time-inhomogeneous Neural Merton Jump Diffusion backbone and its truncated per-step Poisson-Gaussian mixture density are taken directly from Neural MJD (Gao et al., 2025; B pages 1, 3-4); (2) computing the L1 Bayes-optimal point forecast by finding the root of a 1D mixture CDF F_mix(x) = 0.5 via Newton-Raphson iterations and mapping it through exp(.) via monotone quantile preservation (B page 4) is standard material across statistical decision theory and numerical analysis textbooks; (3) generating K candidates via midpoint inverse-CDF stratified sampling at q_k = (k - 0.5)/K (B page 4) is standard variance-reduction material in Monte Carlo textbooks (e.g., Glasserman's Monte Carlo Methods in Financial Engineering); (4) penalizing the deviation between the analytical 1-step Merton jump-diffusion variance sigma_tau^2 + lambda_tau(nu_tau^2 + gamma_tau^2) and empirical historical return variance (B page 5) is standard moment-matching / variance targeting in financial econometrics (e.g., GARCH variance targeting and neural SDE volatility regularization); and (5) resetting an Euler-Maruyama rollout to a closed-form conditional mean (B page 5) is a basic numerical reset. Even B's least placeable block—regularizing predicted neural jump-diffusion variance parameters against context return variance (B page 5)—is standard material in financial econometrics and neural SDE literature. By contrast, breaking Paper A into its building blocks yields: (1) context-to-LoRA hypernetwork generation and rank-concatenation merging (placeable in HINT by Ivison et al., 2023 and LoRA merging works such as LoraHub by Huang et al., 2023; A pages 1-3); (2) token-level late-interaction MaxSim scoring (placeable in ColBERT by Khattab et al., 2021 and ColBERTv2 by Santhanam et al., 2022b; A pages 2-4); (3) delimiter-aligned chunking (standard in retrieval-augmented generation chunking literature; A page 4); and (4) relevance-profile atom placement—repositioning the internal sub-span ('atom') inside a hypernetwork's frozen early-exit encoder onto a token-level query-relevance peak before emitting the merged adapter—alongside localizing multi-needle context-to-LoRA failure to query-blind rank-concatenation superposition (A pages 2-4, 6). A's least placeable block (relevance-profile atom placement for hypernetwork weight emission and late-interaction routing over hypernetwork-generated chunk adapters) cannot be named to a specific prior work and is placeable only at the broader subfield level of hypernetwork context internalization and dynamic adapter routing. For Surprising, the obvious approach to Paper A's task—improving multi-needle retrieval in a context-to-LoRA hypernetwork—is to increase the capacity and inductive bias of the hypernetwork's read-out/output heads or to add auxiliary training losses that supervise key-value binding and penalize distractor digits; for Paper B's task—improving MAE point forecasts, Best-of-K sample coverage, and long-horizon stability in Neural MJD—once one notes that the model already outputs an analytical 1-step Poisson-Gaussian mixture (B pages 1, 4), the obvious approach is to replace noisy Monte Carlo sampling with standard analytical properties of that predicted mixture (its median for L1 loss, stratified quantiles for coverage, and variance regularization). Paper B follows that expected statistical refinement directly (B pages 2, 4-5). Paper A departs much further and more centrally: it turns the obvious architectural and training-loss approaches into falsifiable negative controls, proves they hit a hard superposition ceiling at <= 0.52 because query-blind adapter merging structurally superposes co-resident facts (A pages 2-4, 6-7), and instead repurposes a token-level information-retrieval primitive (ColBERT MaxSim) as a parameter-free merge-time router over generated weight adapters (A pages 3-4, 8-9). For Useful, there is an important tradeoff between the two manuscripts. Paper B works out its mechanisms with explicit equations (Eqs. 1-10, B pages 3-5) and demonstrates empirical improvements on both real-world S&P 500 equities and synthetic jump-diffusion data (+16.1% Mean MAE, +40.2% Best-of-K minMAE, and a 2.2x sampling speedup over same-environment Neural MJD; B pages 6-7, Tables 1-4). However, several of B's mathematical and empirical claims have substantive flaws: (i) in multi-step rollouts (tau = 1, ..., T_f), B chains step-wise conditional medians (B page 4, lines 198-200) and applies the identical quantile stratum q_k across every step (B page 4, Eq. 7), which assumes comonotonic paths and ignores that the sum of step-wise medians of asymmetric jump mixtures is not the multi-step marginal median; (ii) the 'Spectral Energy-Variance Conservation Loss' (B page 5, Eqs. 8-9) performs no spectral or frequency-domain analysis, slightly degrades or leaves flat all metrics at T_f = 7 (B page 7, Table 3), and actually worsens Mean MSE by 36% at T_f = 14 (from 1503.0 to 2045.6 in Table 5, B page 12) before helping at T_f = 28 (B pages 8-9, 12); and (iii) Proposition 1's Euler-Maruyama with Restart solver (B page 5; Appendix B, page 11) bounds weak error trivially by overwriting the stochastic trajectory state with the deterministic closed-form mean E[S_tau | C] at every integer boundary. Conversely, Paper A's central mechanism—using frozen-encoder MaxSim scores to select the dominant chunk adapter at merge time, paired with relevance-profile atom placement and delimiter-aligned chunk cuts (A pages 3-4)—is backed by a tightly controlled 30-configuration attribution study (A pages 4-8, Table 1, Figures 2-4) where all three query-blind families plateau at 0.32, 0.46, and 0.52, while MaxSim merge-time routing alone jumps from 0.52 to 0.91 and the two chunk-level components reach 0.98 exact match across 128 to 65,536 tokens (A pages 5-7). Paper A's limitations under Useful are that its method is presented entirely in prose without mathematical equations (leaving unspecified the exact merge-weighting formula and how query-dependent relevance-profile atom placement on A page 4 reconciles with pre-query adapter emission on A page 1) and that its evidence is restricted to one synthetic single-target benchmark (candidly noted on A pages 5, 8). Even accounting for B's fuller mathematical notation and real-world financial evaluation, B's multi-step mathematical approximations and mixed horizon results temper its advantage in implementation detail, whereas A's diagnostic reframing, harder-to-place adapter-routing mechanisms, and decisive falsifiable attribution from 0.52 to 0.98 give A the edge.

Its hardest-to-place block is the horizon-independent weak-error claim for mean-reset trajectories; I can place that only broadly in numerical SDE analysis, not an established theorem. Thus neither manuscript earns New credit merely for assembling familiar components, and B’s unusual theoretical proposal remains distinct from whether it is correct. For A’s task, obvious approaches include improving adapter capacity or binding supervision, or retrieving relevant text for the prompt; for B’s tractable-mixture forecasting task, obvious approaches include loss-appropriate mixture statistics and variance-reduced sampling. A’s central departure is to put retrieval inside weight composition, changing when the system decides which information to express rather than enlarging its information generator. Query-based routing is familiar, so this is not a wholly unexpected invention, but it is a substantive redirection. B largely develops the expected analytical direction; its less-expected mean-reset restart is ancillary to its three headline contributions. A also supplies a relatively direct mechanism test: query-conditioned selection alone raises reported exact match from 0.52 to 0.91, with relevance placement and delimiter alignment bringing it to 0.98 (A page 6). These interventions explain how the improvement arises rather than merely asserting a payoff. However, family-best comparisons, training collapses, and one synthetic task cannot establish that query-blind composition necessarily destroys bindings or that no better head or loss could succeed (A pages 4, 7–8). The supported result is a strong local routing benefit, not a structural impossibility theorem. B provides valuable fixed-checkpoint ablations and across-seed estimator comparisons, supporting practical gains from replacing Monte Carlo selection and improving candidate coverage (B pages 6–7). Its one-step median inversion is sound in principle. Nevertheless, repeatedly using each candidate’s same quantile across time does not establish faithful joint Merton-path sampling, so oracle coverage gains have a narrower meaning than distributional fidelity (B page 4). More seriously, resetting stochastic states to their means removes variance; it cannot generally preserve convergence to the original process for nonlinear observables, invalidating the claimed general weak-error argument (B pages 5 and 11). The variance penalty also helps at 28 days but worsens the reported 14-day results (B page 12), limiting the stability claim. B’s operational improvements remain useful, but its theoretical guarantees need repair. Overall, A’s more unexpected relocation of the decision mechanism, coupled with its clearly demonstrated local payoff, outweighs its limited scope and overextended bottleneck interpretation.

B makes the stronger overall creative contribution, although its conclusion should be restricted to the tested system and budget. A’s building blocks are the Merton Poisson–Gaussian mixture, loss-optimal point estimation, Newton CDF inversion, stratified inverse-transform sampling, variance matching, and mean-reset simulation (A pages 4–5). Most are standard formulations in statistical decision theory and stochastic simulation. Its least-placeable claim is the horizon-independent weak-error guarantee for mean-reset simulation: I can locate its general setting in numerical-SDE stabilization, but cannot name a specific prior theorem establishing that guarantee. B builds from hypernetwork-generated adapters, low-rank composition, MaxSim retrieval, query-conditioned routing, and relevance-aware chunk placement (B pages 3–4). HINT and ColBERT specifically locate its adapter-generation and retrieval primitives. Its least-placeable substantive claim is the diagnosis that composition, rather than encoding capacity, governs this particular multi-fact failure; I can place that only broadly in associative-memory binding and interference research, not in a specific prior result. Thus neither manuscript deserves novelty credit merely for assembling familiar components, and the specificity of identifiable precedents does not establish a decisive novelty advantage by itself. For A’s inference-improvement task, the obvious approach is to exploit the available mixture distribution with loss-matched estimators and variance-reduced sampling. Its central methods largely follow that direction, although replacing stochastic trajectory generation with deterministic quantiles is a useful implementation choice. For B’s context-internalization task, the obvious approach is to improve storage capacity, binding supervision, or adapter merging; query-based text retrieval is also familiar. B’s more unexpected central move is to relocate retrieval into the composition of generated weights, leaving the generator and training objective unchanged. The surprise lies in where selection happens and the resulting bottleneck diagnosis, not in inventing query relevance scoring. A provides meaningful operational evidence: matched-model experiments on financial and synthetic sequences, estimator swaps, component ablations, and horizon tests support practical forecasting improvements (A pages 6–7 and 12). However, several stronger payoffs do not follow from its mathematics. Reusing the same quantile rank at successive steps creates rank-coupled increments, rather than exact sampling of the original jump-diffusion trajectory distribution (A page 4). More seriously, resetting stochastic states to their expectations removes variance; it cannot generally yield the claimed vanishing weak error for nonlinear observables merely by refining the integration step (A pages 5 and 11). These problems limit the interpretation of its oracle-path improvements and theoretical stability guarantee without erasing the reported empirical gains. B’s mechanism is coherent and its component ladder directly addresses its stated diagnostic task: query-conditioned selection alone raises reported exact match from 0.52 to 0.91, with relevance placement and aligned boundaries bringing it to 0.98 (B page 6). Nevertheless, pooled best-configuration results, incomplete routing specifications, and insufficient repeated-seed evidence weaken reproducibility and causal certainty. Its negative controls cannot prove that query-blind composition inherently discards the needed information: the decoder still receives the query, so better learned representations could potentially retain accessible bindings. B also explicitly limits evaluation to synthetic, single-target retrieval and acknowledges training collapse (B pages 7–8). On balance, its supported, narrower finding—that merge-time addressing resolves the observed failure—is a more consequential and unexpected mechanism-level insight than A’s mostly conventional inference refinements, whose broader exactness claims require repair.
