The decisive distinction is how well each manuscript connects its conceptual departure to its demonstrated payoff. A builds from hypernetwork-generated low-rank adapters, adapter composition, MaxSim retrieval, and relevance-aware chunking (A pages 3–4). MaxSim is specifically placeable in ColBERT; A’s least-placeable claim is the empirical localization of interference to composition in this particular weight-space memory system. I can connect that claim only to the adapter-interference literature, not name an earlier demonstration. B builds from directional finite differences, spatial-Gram repulsion, fidelity penalties, and manifold Langevin updates (B pages 4–5). Manifold Langevin is specifically established in Girolami and Calderhead’s work; B’s least-placeable block is probing velocity sensitivity along the normalized conditional-minus-unconditional guidance direction. I can place that only broadly in score-geometry/Jacobian-regularization research, not an exact prior formulation. Neither receives novelty credit merely for assembling familiar components. For A’s task, the obvious approach would be improving key–value binding through adapter capacity, supervision, or interference-aware merging. Its central departure is postponing selection until the query arrives and routing generated weights rather than retrieving prompt text. Query-based selection is familiar in retrieval, so this is a meaningful relocation rather than an entirely unexpected principle. For B’s task, the obvious approach would be reducing or annealing guidance, repelling denoising trajectories, or optimizing initial seeds. B extends the last direction by coupling batch layout repulsion to norm-constrained initialization; this is a substantive extension, but initialization-time intervention itself is already established. A provides a relatively direct connection between its intervention and success: query-conditioned selection raises exact match from 0.52 to 0.91, while relevance placement and boundary alignment reach 0.98 (A page 6). These component comparisons support routing as an effective fix for the stated retrieval task. Important qualifications remain: implementation details and replicated uncertainty are missing, configurations are evaluated once, and training collapse occurs (A pages 4–5, 7). Moreover, the decoder still receives the query, so failed capacity and loss variants cannot establish that query-blind composition is fundamentally incapable of retrieval. A demonstrates a practical bottleneck under its budget, not a universal impossibility. B supplies more explicit update equations and meaningful evidence across architectures, including diversity gains and experiments identifying norm restoration as a stabilizer (B pages 7, 9–10). However, its distinctive explanatory claims are less secure. Its own ablations show that ordinary post-hoc rescaling performs similarly to tangent dynamics, while the proposed fidelity hinge is dormant by default and ineffective when activated; the replacement CLIP objective only partially recovers lost quality (B pages 9, 16). The directional Jacobian norm derived on B page 14 is not a Rayleigh quotient and does not distinguish contraction from expansion, weakening the claimed basin-escape explanation. Fidelity is also a genuine tradeoff rather than uniformly preserved, as the DiT precision and feature-distance results show (B page 18). Finally, the approximately 3% overhead claim on B page 10 is unreconciled with the 63.7% default overhead reported on B page 15. Overall, A’s narrower but more directly supported reframing outweighs B’s inventive geometric formulation and broader demonstrations. The choice rests on the alignment between A’s central conceptual move and its supported local payoff, not on benchmark scale or the raw magnitude of incomparable metrics.

For New, Manuscript A breaks down into four main building blocks at diffusion initialization time (t=T): (1) a Directional Score Curvature Potential (U_sharp) that probes finite-difference velocity changes strictly along the normalized classifier-free guidance (CFG) vector d_c (A page 4, 14); (2) Batch Cross-Attention Spatial Gram Dispersal (L_repulse), which minimizes pairwise Frobenius cosine similarity of mid-block spatial Query Gram matrices across a batch of noise seeds at t=T (A page 4–5); (3) a Hinge-Gated Text-Fidelity Anchor (L_fid) and its active CLIP-x0 cosine replacement on Tweedie clean estimates (A page 5); and (4) Spherical Tangent Langevin Dynamics on the Gaussian hypersphere S^{D-1}(sqrt(D)) via tangent projection and radial retraction (A page 5, 14). While spherical Langevin dynamics and CLIP-x0 guidance are standard formulations in named works (e.g., Girolami & Calderhead, 2011; Bansal et al., 2023), A's least placeable building blocks—probing directional score curvature specifically along the CFG difference vector d_c at t=T and repelling batchwise spatial Query Gram matrices at pure noise—cannot be placed in a single prior paper, sitting instead in the broader subfield literature of training-free diffusion seed optimization and cross-attention layout control (adjacent to SAIL, Jeon et al., 2024; DivIn, Li et al., 2026; and InitNO, Guo et al., 2024; A page 2–3). Manuscript B breaks down into: (1) chunked context-to-LoRA hypernetwork generation and rank-concatenation merging (B page 1, 3); (2) negative-control hypernetwork read-out/head modifications and auxiliary binding/margin losses (B page 3–4); (3) query-conditioned token-level late-interaction (MaxSim) scoring over frozen encoder token representations to select which chunk's adapter dominates the merge (B page 2, 4); and (4) relevance-profile atom placement and delimiter-aligned chunk cutting (B page 4, 6). B's core routing block is directly placeable in specific named works—ColBERT and ColBERTv2 (Khattab et al., 2021; Santhanam et al., 2022b; B page 2, 4)—while its chunk-boundary and windowing heuristics belong to standard retrieval chunking and the hypernetwork adapter subfield (e.g., HINT, Ivison et al., 2023; B page 2). Thus, A relies on less specifically placeable mathematical building blocks than B. For Surprising, the obvious approach to A's task of mitigating CFG mode collapse without retraining is either intervening along the reverse denoising trajectory t in [T-1, 0] via step-wise particle guidance or running unconstrained Euclidean optimization on pixel-level Tweedie L2 differences at t=T (A page 1–3); for B's task of fixing multi-needle retrieval in context-to-LoRA hypernetworks, the obvious approach is increasing the capacity of the hypernetwork's read-out/output head or adding training-time auxiliary binding losses to separate co-resident facts (B page 1–4). B makes a sharp, central conceptual departure by using those two intuitive directions as falsifiable negative controls—showing both hit a 0.52 exact-match superposition ceiling—and reframing long-context weight internalization as a merge-time routing problem solved without retraining via late-interaction addressing (B page 2, 5–7). A departs from standard trajectory interventions and scalar pixel-space potentials by operating strictly at t=T on the sqrt(D)-hypersphere using directional CFG curvature and compact 64x64 cross-attention Query Grams, uncovering the unexpected mechanistic result that raw t=T Query Grams yield higher full-system diversity than full-resolution Tweedie x0 Grams because Tweedie clean estimates at pure noise are noise-dominated and low-rank (A page 5, 15). For Useful, the tradeoff decisively favors A. Although A's ablations reveal that two of its four headline components simplify in practice—the default cross-attention hinge anchor (tau_fid = -0.22) is completely dormant (L_fid = 0) and fails when forced active, requiring replacement by the direct L_{CLIP-x0} anchor under aggressive dispersal (A page 5, 8, 15–16), and simple post-hoc radial rescaling matches full tangent-space projection across step counts K (A page 9–10, 19)—A is thoroughly worked out with explicit equations (A page 3–5, 14), complete hyperparameters (A page 20), and transparent ablations. Its claimed payoff is rigorously supported across UNet (SD v1.4) and Diffusion Transformer (DiT-XL/2, PixArt-alpha) backbones, real-world diversity benchmarks (GeoDE, DollarStreet), and compositional suites (GenEval, T2I-CompBench), both standalone and stacked with trajectory guidance (A page 6–9, 17–18). Weighing all three qualities together, B's surprising diagnostic framing cannot overcome its directly placeable ColBERT primitive and its mathematically underspecified, internally strained mechanism, whereas A combines less placeable t=T geometric and spectral potentials with surprising insights into noise-stage feature representations and a fully worked-out, broadly validated system.

Manuscript B relies on two building blocks: maintaining an exponential moving average (EMA) of token attention weights across training iterations, R(x_i) = alpha * R(x_i) + (1 - alpha) * attn_weight(x_i), and multiplying pre-softmax attention scores by those historical weights via A' = softmax(A * R) (B page 3). Its least placeable block—tracking a cross-iteration running average of attention weights per token index in a dictionary to multiplicatively scale dense pre-softmax logits—is a minor variant of standard material found across attention-biasing and EMA-based token-importance tracking literatures (such as heavy-hitter tracking in KV-cache eviction and dynamic token pruning). Regarding directional departure, for A's task of low-latency MoE expert replication and placement, the obvious approach is running a sequential greedy bin-packing loop (such as largest-processing-time-first) or a relaxed linear program; A makes a central, productive departure by transforming hierarchical two-key sorting and sequential bin-packing into branchless CPU tensor indexing via its composite scalar projection and zigzag scatter matrix (A pages 4-6). A’s central building blocks are diffusion denoising, an auxiliary transition-probability predictor, and a transition loss. The diffusion backbone is specifically recognizable from Ho et al.’s DDPM; its least placeable block—the learned mode-transition component—can be located only broadly in learned-transition and mixture-model literature because its actual operation is unspecified (A pages 2–3). B’s blocks are sensitivity-aware quantization, weighted low-rank approximation, and alternating discrete/continuous refinement (B pages 4–6). Its alternating residual-quantization/factor-fitting block has a specific antecedent in LoftQ, while weighted low-rank quantization-error correction appears in LQER. B therefore has identifiable precedents, and its particular assembly should not itself receive novelty credit. A is less specifically placeable, but the text provides little substance with which to distinguish an original mechanism from a generic proposal. The decisive difference is whether the proposals work well enough to support their intended payoff. A says it learns transition probabilities using reconstruction and transition losses, but supplies neither a transition rule nor definitions of those losses (A page 3). It also leaves unexplained how Inception-based evaluation is applied to its 2D data, reports no IS values, and provides no direct measurement of transitions. Its claim of improved FID on every dataset is contradicted by the Moons entry, which worsens from 0.6161 to 0.6192 (A page 3). B, by contrast, specifies an actionable mechanism: weight the quantization residual, obtain and unscale truncated-SVD factors, re-quantize the weights after subtracting the correction, and recompute the correction using Cholesky weighting (B pages 5–6). Its reported three-seed performance and artifact size support feasibility in its stated setting, while the no-refinement ablation provides some evidence that alternating updates help (B pages 7–8). These results support only a narrow payoff: comparison scores are estimated, ablations are single-seed, the reported p≈0.13 does not establish conventional statistical significance, and elapsed-time compliance is asserted without measured timings. The failed unweighted control also does not establish that curvature weighting is strictly necessary for stability. For A’s task, the obvious approach is to use diffusion noise and sampler or schedule adjustments to move between modes; adding an explicit learned transition component changes that direction modestly, without revealing an unexpected operational principle. For B’s task, the obvious approach is sensitivity-aware quantization followed by a one-shot low-rank repair; making rounding and repair repeatedly adapt to each other is a concrete but still modest departure from that sequential pipeline. Neither manuscript is radically surprising. B’s advantage is that its directional choice produces an inspectable, coupled mechanism with limited supporting evidence, whereas A’s less specifically placeable proposal does not establish how mode transitions occur or whether they improve. That difference outweighs B’s recognizable antecedents and uncertain performance margin.

The claimed payoff follows and meets all task constraints: on the FineWeb validation set, A achieves a 3-seed average val_bpb of 1.0600 within a 15,896,434-byte artifact (<16 MB) and <10-minute training budget (A page 6-7, Table 1). Crucially, A's ablations (A page 7-8, Table 2) prove that the mechanism works as claimed: removing ALS degrades val_bpb by +0.00069, the fast diagonal initialization matches full Cholesky initialization (1.05999 vs. 1.06011), and attempting ALS with an unweighted SVD initialization crashes completely at step 4886 due to ill-conditioned factors. Conversely, Manuscript B's central proposal—adding a mode transition mechanism and loss with a transition rate of 0.8 to a diffusion model (B page 2-3)—is merely asserted and in need of fundamental repair. Section 4 (B page 2-3) contains zero equations, architectural specifications, or definitions explaining how modes or transition probabilities are defined or supervised. Furthermore, B's empirical evidence is defective: it contains unresolved placeholders ('Figure ??' on B page 3; 'Figure 1: PLEASE FILL IN CAPTION HERE' on B page 4), repeatedly claims to evaluate and improve Inception Score (IS) (B page 1, 3, 4) while omitting IS entirely from all tables (B page 3-4), and falsely claims on B page 3 that its model achieves lower FID than the baseline on all datasets, when Table 2 (B page 3) shows the proposed model actually performs worse on Moons (0.6192 vs. 0.6161) and differs by only thousandths on the remaining datasets. For Surprising, the obvious approach to A's extreme compression task would be applying uniform or mixed-precision GPTQ or standard single-pass unweighted SVD on the quantization error matrix (A page 2-3); A departs centrally from this by coupling a damped diagonal Hessian warm-start with an iterative Cholesky-weighted ALS refinement loop, revealing the non-obvious dynamic that unweighted SVD causes alternating optimization to diverge whereas a cheap diagonal curvature scaling suffices to stabilize it (A page 5, 7-8). For B's task of improving mode coverage in diffusion models, the obvious approach is modifying the diffusion transition kernel or adding an auxiliary transition objective; B merely states that it adds a mode transition loss without specifying any mechanism that departs from existing explicit-transition diffusion frameworks (B page 2-3). Weighing the tradeoffs, Manuscript A candidly acknowledges that its novel algorithmic contribution is a targeted ~40-line refinement on top of a heavily engineered inherited architecture, and that its overall 0.00108 BPB gain over the parent baseline is modest (roughly 1.1 pooled standard deviations, p ≈ 0.13 across 3 seeds, A page 8-9). However, a concrete, mathematically complete, and empirically validated algorithmic refinement that solves a critical numerical stability bottleneck under extreme compression constraints far outweighs Manuscript B's unsubstantiated assertions, missing mechanism definitions, and self-contradictory results.

A offers the stronger overall creative contribution, although it is a targeted refinement rather than a fundamentally new compression principle. Its least routine mathematical block—Hessian-weighted rank truncation—is nevertheless recognizable as the standard weighted low-rank least-squares formulation implemented through whitening and SVD; alternating quantization and low-rank correction also has a close precedent in LoftQ. B combines DDPM denoising with a learned mode-transition predictor and an auxiliary transition loss. That latter block is less specifically placeable: I can locate it only broadly in latent-state/mixture generative-model literature, not identify a particular matching mechanism. However, B supplies neither its transition kernel nor its loss definition (B pages 2–3), so this uncertainty leaves potential originality unresolved rather than establishing a concrete technical invention. A’s assembly of familiar components is not itself evidence of new building blocks. For A’s constrained-compression task, the obvious approach is sensitivity-aware quantization with low-rank error compensation; for B’s task, it is to investigate reverse-diffusion mixing or introduce an explicit transition controller. A makes a modest but substantive departure by placing curvature weighting in the low-rank initialization and then alternating residual requantization with full-Hessian-weighted refactorization (A pages 4–6). B’s central move follows the explicit-controller direction, without specifying an unexpected transition strategy beyond naming the added predictor and loss. The decisive distinction is how far those proposals support their intended payoff. A gives an actionable algorithm: initialize rank-three factors from a diagonally weighted residual, requantize the weights minus their correction, and recompute factors through Cholesky-weighted SVD. Its reported artifact satisfies the size constraint, and removing refinement worsens BPB from 1.05999 to 1.06068 (A page 7). These results support a limited practical benefit. They do not establish every claim: the parent scores are estimated, the reported p≈0.13 does not establish conventional statistical significance, and one failed initialization run does not prove that Hessian weighting is necessary for stability (A pages 7–8). B’s central payoff is substantially less supported. Modes, transition targets, and the way predicted probabilities modify sampling remain undefined. Its FID results neither directly measure transitions nor explain an Inception-feature adaptation for the two-dimensional data; promised IS results are absent. Moreover, Moons FID worsens despite the claim of improvement on every dataset, and comparing rates 0.8 and 0.9 cannot establish general optimality (B pages 3–4). Thus A’s limited novelty and modest directional surprise are backed by an operational mechanism and bounded evidence, whereas B’s less attributable idea remains too underspecified and indirectly evaluated to outweigh that contribution.

Using work-function geometry to change predictive victim rankings—not merely delimit permissible evictions—is a more unexpected central move. Regarding New, Manuscript A breaks down into two standard building blocks: (1) the algorithmic grokking benchmark using a two-layer Transformer decoder trained with AdamW on modular addition, subtraction, division (mod 97), and S5 permutation group operations (A pages 4–5), which is taken directly from Power et al. (2022); and (2) five parametric dynamic batch size schedules—linear, exponential, logarithmic, cyclic, and cosine annealing (A page 4)—which apply standard learning-rate schedule functional forms (placeable in Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017 and cyclical schedule literature) to batch size scaling (placeable in Smith et al., 2017). Even the least placeable block in A—applying these parametric schedules to batch size on the grokking benchmark—consists entirely of standard mathematical formulations from those named works. In contrast, Manuscript B is built from three technical blocks: (1) Harmonic-Aware Spectral Decomposition (HASD), which identifies top-K fundamental FFT peaks, groups them with their integer overtones m * f_k within a discrete bin neighborhood tolerance Delta to absorb finite-window DFT leakage, masks entire harmonic sets coherently, and attenuates masking on non-periodic signals via a normalized spectral-entropy back-off factor gamma(X) = 1 - S(X) (B pages 4–5); (2) a Global-Local Dual-Context Prompt Router (Dual-MoP) that fuses a sequence-level spectral signature g_X with local patch tokens b_p via multiplicative sigmoid gating (B page 5); and (3) a Harmonic Phase-Conscious Dual-Domain Loss (H-Loss) combining time-domain MSE with L1 spectral magnitude and L1 complex FFT coefficient penalties (B pages 5–6). B's least placeable block—coherent fundamental-and-overtone set masking with leakage tolerance bands and spectral-entropy attenuation (plus a zero-parameter Gaussian low-pass pre-filter on the entropy estimator path under broadband noise, B page 17)—cannot be placed in a specific prior time-series paper; while energy-based spectral splitting appears in SEMPO (He et al., 2025) and harmonic overtone filtering exists broadly in audio/speech signal processing literature, this specific self-supervised pre-training mechanism is only placeable at the subfield level. Regarding Useful, Manuscript A proposes that dynamically varying batch size B(t) between 32 and 512 over T = 7,500 steps accelerates grokking and improves validation accuracy compared to a fixed batch size of 32 (A pages 1, 4, 7). While A reports that linear increase reduces steps to 99% validation accuracy by 24% on modular division (3,193 vs. 4,200 steps) and reaches 68.36% vs. 3.59% accuracy on S5 permutations (A page 7), the experimental design is in need of repair due to a major confounding flaw: all runs are fixed to 7,500 update steps (A pages 4–6) and compared only against a fixed small batch size of 32. Because linearly increasing B(t) from 32 to 512 processes 8.5x more training samples per step on average without adjusting the learning rate or comparing against a fixed large batch size or epoch-matched baseline, A never establishes whether the payoff comes from the dynamic schedule itself or merely from seeing 8.5x more data and altering the gradient noise scale. Additionally, A contains internal inconsistencies, such as stating that cyclic variation completes 10 cycles (A page 5) while defining the equation with a single cycle sin(2*pi*t/T) over T steps (A page 4), and its extracted figures (Figures 1–5, A pages 6–9) provide no additional quantitative tables beyond the sparse text mentions. Conversely, Manuscript B's mechanisms are fully worked out mathematically (Equations 1–12, B pages 4–6, 17; Table 6, B page 14) and validated under a tightly controlled, budget-matched protocol (pre-training both baseline SEMPO and HARMONIC-MoP from scratch on the same 10M-point UTSD corpus, random seeds, and single-A100 compute budget, B page 6). B demonstrates a 40.1% reduction in Stage-1 reconstruction MSE (0.0198 vs. 0.0329, B page 6) and consistent zero-shot forecasting gains across the 7-dataset TSLib benchmark (+3.1% overall MSE, with +8.2% to +10.1% gains on strongly periodic series ETTh1, ETTh2, and Electricity, Table 1, B page 7; Table 13, B page 19), the 97-configuration GIFT-Eval benchmark (+4.2% Mean MASE, Table 4, B page 9), and 10 unseen Monash datasets (+3.2% median MASE, Table 7, B page 14). Crucially, B's ablations directly prove its physical mechanism: Table 5 (B page 10) shows that applying HASD without complex phase loss (H-Loss) severely degrades zero-shot transfer (0.420 vs. 0.318 MSE) because temporal MSE allows phase-shifted overtone reconstructions, and Figure 6 (B page 16) shows that masking only fundamental peaks without their overtones performs worse than random masking (0.431 vs. 0.422 MSE). B also transparently addresses its primary tradeoff—slight regressions on highly stochastic series like ETTm1 (0.664 vs. 0.639 MSE, Table 1, B page 7)—by ablating alternative learnable back-off functions (Table 8, B page 15), lookback bin tolerances (Table 9, B page 16), and SNR noise levels (Tables 11–12, B page 18). B’s blocks are spectral partitioning, harmonic-family masking, leakage tolerance, entropy-based attenuation, global–local prompt gating, and spectral reconstruction penalties (B pages 4–6). Its least-placeable block is assigning one sampled corruption decision to an entire fundamental–overtone family: I can place that only broadly in harmonic-aware signal processing and structured spectral augmentation, not a specific predecessor. For B’s task, the obvious approach is masked time-series pre-training with patch or frequency augmentation and adaptive prompting. Treating overtone families as coherent corruption units, while using the sequence spectrum to condition local prompt selection, is a more substantial central departure from that approach. This is a specific inductive-bias intervention rather than simply a larger forecasting model. A provides an actionable training setup and reports meaningful results: 3,193 versus 4,200 updates to reach 99% validation accuracy on division, and 68.36% versus 3.59% final permutation accuracy (A page 7). However, increasing batches from 32 toward 512 against a fixed-32 baseline changes examples processed per update. Without exposure-matched comparisons or larger fixed-batch controls, these results establish fewer updates and better fixed-update performance, not computational savings or a benefit uniquely attributable to scheduling (A pages 4–5). Nevertheless, B’s phase explanation needs substantial repair. Time-domain MSE already penalizes phase errors, as follows from Parseval’s identity, contrary to B pages 5 and 10; complex L1 changes spectral error weighting rather than introducing otherwise absent phase sensitivity. Its phase-MAE table also shows virtually no improvement for the full loss over time-MSE alone (B page 17). Likewise, the changing corruption task prevents the reconstruction-loss reduction from independently proving better representations. I therefore credit B’s explicit harmonic-corruption design and its ablation-supported forecasting payoff, not its overstated phase guarantees. Despite those explanatory weaknesses, this experimentally supported, less expected methodological direction offers stronger overall creative quality than A’s useful but comparatively conventional schedule intervention with unresolved training-budget confounds.

Evaluated relative to their respective fields and research tasks, Manuscript A demonstrates substantially stronger overall creative quality than Manuscript B when considering New, Useful, and Surprising jointly. For New, breaking Manuscript A into its constituent building blocks yields three primary mechanisms: (1) Harmonic-Aware Spectral Decomposition (HASD), which partitions high- and low-energy FFT spectra, identifies top-K fundamental peak frequencies, groups each fundamental with its integer harmonic overtones within a discrete-bin tolerance band Delta to account for finite-window DFT spectral leakage, and modulates joint binary harmonic-set masking via the linear complement of normalized Shannon spectral entropy, gamma(X) = 1 - S(X) (A pages 4-5); (2) a Global-Local Dual-Context Prompt Router (Dual-MoP) that gates local patch token embeddings with a sequence-level MLP projection of top Fourier magnitudes and spectral entropy prior to softmax prompt-pool routing (A page 5); and (3) a dual-domain pre-training loss (H-Loss) combining time-domain MSE with L1 spectral magnitude and L1 complex Fourier coefficient penalties (A pages 5-6). While Dual-MoP and H-Loss draw on blocks placeable in standard formulations across Mixture-of-Experts/prompt-tuning literature (e.g., Shazeer et al., 2017; He et al., 2025) and frequency-domain reconstruction losses (e.g., Yi et al., 2023; multi-resolution spectral losses in audio generation), A's least placeable building block—sampling coherent binary self-supervised masks across integer harmonic overtone sets with leakage-tolerance neighborhoods attenuated by normalized spectral entropy (A pages 4-5)—cannot be placed in a specific prior named paper and is placeable only broadly within the subfields of harmonic comb filtering in signal processing and masked time-series pre-training. By contrast, Manuscript B breaks down into (1) five standard functional schedules (linear, exponential, logarithmic, cyclic sinusoidal, and cosine annealing) mapping training step t to batch size B(t) (B page 4), and (2) evaluating steps-to-generalization on four small algorithmic datasets (modular addition, subtraction, division mod 97, and S5 permutations) using a 2-layer decoder Transformer (B pages 4-5). Every building block in B is standard material directly placeable in named works: the algorithmic grokking tasks and Transformer setup come directly from Power et al. (2022) (B pages 2, 4-5), while dynamic batch size scheduling and cyclic/cosine schedules are standard formulations in optimization literature such as Smith et al. (2017) and Loshchilov & Hutter (2017) (B pages 2, 4). Because every individual block in B is specifically placeable in prior works, its novelty is much lower. For Surprising, the obvious approach to A's task of improving zero-shot cross-domain time-series foundation models is scaling backbone parameters and pre-training corpora or applying independent random patch or frequency-band masking with time-domain MSE loss (A pages 1-2); the obvious approach to B's task of accelerating grokking on algorithmic datasets is sweeping optimization hyperparameters or schedules (such as weight decay, learning rate, or batch size) on the standard Power et al. (2022) benchmark suite (B pages 1-4). B departs minimally from this expected direction, executing a direct empirical sweep of five textbook schedule curves applied to batch size without uncovering an unexpected mechanistic principle (B pages 4-7). A makes a central, non-obvious departure by diagnosing how independent frequency-bin masking and point-wise temporal MSE destroy the physical phase lock between fundamental frequencies and their higher-order harmonics during self-supervised pre-training, and redesigning the masking, routing, and loss around harmonic phase coupling and spectral entropy (A pages 2, 4-6). For Useful, A's central mechanism is mathematically worked out in full detail (Eqs. 1-12, A pages 4-6, 17) and validated under a strict apples-to-apples compute and data budget (10M UTSD time points, 6.88M parameters, 81.3 minutes on one A100 GPU; A pages 6, 14). The claimed payoffs follow with comprehensive support: a 40.1% reduction in Stage-1 reconstruction MSE over the identically trained SEMPO baseline (0.0198 vs. 0.0329; A page 6), +3.1% average zero-shot MSE improvement across the 7-dataset TSLib benchmark with +10.1% and +9.1% gains on strongly periodic ETTh1 and Electricity series (Table 1, A pages 6-7), +4.2% Mean MASE improvement across 87 strictly zero-shot GIFT-Eval configurations (Table 4, A page 9), and gains on 8 of 10 unseen Monash datasets (Table 7, A page 14). Crucially, A's ablations directly verify the physical mechanism: masking only fundamental peaks without their overtones degrades MSE worse than random masking (0.431 vs. 0.422, Figure 6, A page 16), removing complex H-Loss collapses zero-shot transfer (0.420 vs. 0.318 MSE, Table 5, A page 10), and adding a zero-parameter Gaussian pre-filter on the entropy estimation path restores 5 dB AWGN gate retention from 56% to 87% (Table 11, A pages 17-18). A's main tradeoff is that harmonic inductive bias slightly degrades MSE on highly stochastic series like ETTm1 (0.664 vs. 0.639, Table 1, A page 7) and Dual-MoP provides only a small standalone MSE gain in ablation (0.318 vs. 0.320, Table 5, A page 10), though A transparently analyzes both tradeoffs. Conversely, B's central mechanism and claimed payoff—that linearly increasing batch size from 32 to 512 accelerates grokking by 24% on modular division (3,193 vs. 4,200 steps) and reaches 68.36% vs. 3.59% accuracy on S5 permutations (B pages 1, 7)—suffer from a load-bearing experimental confound and incomplete evidence. Because B fixes total parameter update steps at T = 7,500 across all runs while comparing dynamic schedules reaching B_max = 512 exclusively against a small fixed baseline of B = 32 (B pages 4-6), the linear schedule processes ~8.5x more training examples (epochs) within 7,500 steps than the baseline, without any fixed-large-batch control (e.g., fixed B = 272 or 512) or epoch-matched comparison to isolate schedule dynamics from total data exposure. Moreover, B contains specification inconsistencies (defining cyclic batch size as a single-period sine wave in the equation on B page 4 but describing 10 complete cycles on B page 5, alongside an unresolved '?' citation on B page 3) and omits tabular numerical reporting for most tasks, relying on unextracted plot visuals (Figures 1-5, B pages 6-9). Even accounting for B's simplicity and A's minor stochastic-series tradeoff, A is far more rigorous, novel, and mechanistically insightful.

A offers the stronger overall creative contribution, though its explanation of phase preservation needs substantial qualification. Its building blocks are harmonic-group masking, entropy-dependent suppression, global/local prompt gating, and spectral reconstruction losses (A pages 4–6). The hardest block to place is treating a fundamental’s leakage-tolerant overtone family as one corruption unit: the closest prior art I can identify is harmonic signal processing and structured spectral augmentation, not a particular earlier formulation. B uses familiar batch-size schedules and a standard Transformer grokking testbed (B pages 4–5). Increasing batch size to alter optimization is specifically anticipated by Smith et al.’s “Don’t Decay the Learning Rate, Increase the Batch Size.” B’s least-placeable claim is instead the grokking-specific performance ordering of those schedules; I can locate that only within empirical grokking/optimization research, not attribute the reported finding to an earlier paper. Thus neither manuscript earns novelty merely from combining familiar components, and the exact contributions are not fully reducible to named prior formulations. For A’s forecasting task, the obvious approach is to refine generic masked pretraining and parameter-efficient adaptation; for B’s investigation, it is to compare fixed batches and familiar schedules on canonical grokking tasks. A departs further by making harmonic families determine what information is withheld and using whole-sequence spectral context to condition local prompt selection. B largely follows the expected experimental direction, although its reported permutation-task improvement is genuinely striking (B page 7). A also develops an actionable intervention with a same-data/epoch comparison showing forecasting MSE improving from 0.409 to 0.396, and component ablations distinguishing the substantial loss/masking effects from the small routing contribution (A pages 6–7, 10). These results support a bounded forecasting payoff, not all its physical explanations. In particular, temporal MSE already penalizes phase errors by Parseval’s identity, contrary to A’s central motivation; its spectral loss changes the error norm rather than introducing previously absent phase sensitivity. Table 10 also shows almost unchanged phase MAE despite improved forecasting (A pages 5, 17). The phase mechanism therefore needs repair even if the intervention helps empirically. B specifies its schedules and reports three-seed experiments, a useful strength. Its 3,193 versus 4,200 updates to reach 99% division accuracy and 68.36% versus 3.59% permutation accuracy support schedule-dependent learning behavior (B pages 4–5, 7). However, increasing batches processes substantially more examples per update, and the missing sample/compute-matched and larger-fixed-batch controls prevent interpreting fewer updates as training efficiency or isolating a benefit of scheduling itself. Neither paper fully establishes its explanatory mechanism, but A’s more unexpected structural intervention and ablated downstream payoff outweigh its overclaimed phase rationale; B’s intriguing observations leave the central efficiency interpretation more confounded.

For B’s task, the obvious approach is to fit low-rank neural dynamics and separate factors using instantaneous independence penalties or post-hoc ICA. Manuscript B relies on: (1) Stage-1 LoRA adaptation of a CLIP-ViT backbone with PCA projection and bucketed k-means prototype transport (B pages 3–4), placeable in RALI (Zhao et al., 2025) and LoRA (Hu et al., 2022 / Yin et al., 2023); (2) supervised adversarial content-quality disentanglement via a Gradient Reversal Layer (GRL) with sigmoid annealing trained against frozen k-means semantic cluster targets from unadapted CLIP features (B pages 4–5), whose GRL mechanism is placeable in Ganin & Lempitsky (2015); (3) extracting zero-FLOP spatial saliency weights directly from the negative self-attention entropy of the final ViT layer (B page 5); (4) training a patch quality segmentation head jointly on synthetic patch-box area-overlap severity targets and saliency-weighted Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) anchored to global MOS, aggregated via a Generalized Minkowski norm (B page 5); and (5) augmenting the quality state with extreme regional severity to dynamically anneal the prototype transport softmax temperature as an exponential function of local defect severity (B pages 6, 16). B's least placeable building blocks—using negative final-layer CLIP self-attention entropy directly as a zero-FLOP gaze-aligned MIL saliency prior (B page 5) and modulating prototype-transport temperature exponentially via Minkowski-pooled patch defect severity (B pages 6, 16)—cannot be placed in a specific prior paper and are only placeable at the broader subfield level of vision-transformer attention interpretability and metric prototype learning. For Surprising, the obvious approach to A's task of multi-cloud broadcast routing in an AI-driven systems benchmark is to apply an integer linear program, a standard constructive Steiner tree heuristic, or an LLM-driven evolutionary mutation loop over greedy edge-selection rules; the obvious approach to B's task of improving a lightweight prototype-distilled NR-IQA model on cross-domain and localized distortions is to fine-tune the vision backbone with standard contrastive objectives or multi-scale patch attention pooling under global MOS regression. A departs from naive edge-by-edge search and unconstrained LLM mutation by condensing the MCTS action space to unreached terminal selections connected via on-the-fly multi-source Dijkstra (A pages 2, 4–5). While this state abstraction is central to A's solver, it primarily repackages a classical constructive Steiner tree heuristic inside a 2-second MCTS wrapper and abandons the LLM neuro-symbolic integration promised in its abstract (A pages 1, 9). By contrast, B makes a multifaceted central departure: rather than relying on unsupervised PCA nulling or weak global MOS pooling, it uses frozen unadapted CLIP clusters as a self-supervised adversarial target to strip content bias while preserving orthogonal low-level quality directions (B pages 4–5, 10, 19), extracts human-gaze-aligned spatial saliency at zero extra FLOPs from self-attention entropy (B pages 5, 10), and bridges synthetic box-overlap segmentation with real-MOS MIL anchoring (B page 5). For Useful, the contrast is decisive. A's central proposal is in need of repair due to major internal contradictions, missing formal details, and unsupported claims. First, A's Abstract (A page 1) claims to propose a "hybrid neuro-symbolic solver that combines the global structural exploration of LLMs with an Action-Condensed Monte Carlo Tree Search," but Section 3 (A pages 3–5) describes a purely classical graph search with no LLM component, and Section 5 (A page 9) defers hybrid neuro-symbolic integration to future work; moreover, its UCB1/UCT modification for cost minimization is merely asserted in text without an equation (A page 5), and link throughput capacities th(u,v) introduced in Section 3.1 (A page 4) are omitted from the objective in Eq. 1 (A page 4) and acknowledged as unenforced in Limitations (A page 9). Second, A's reported empirical payoff is contradicted by its own tables and captions: the prose claims Action-Condensed MCTS achieves a transfer cost of 627.10 $/GB (or 627.09 on A page 3), slightly trailing Human SOTA (626.24) and Engram (622.00) (A pages 1, 2, 6, 8, 9), whereas Table 1 (A page 7) lists "Action-Condensed MCTS (Ours)" at 1090.78 $/GB (worse than every baseline, including OpenEvolve at 728.00), and Figure 3's caption (A page 8) contradicts both by claiming it achieves the lowest cost at $0.28/GB and outperforms all human and agentic baselines. Conversely, B's mechanism is thoroughly worked out with explicit equations (B pages 4–6, 16) and backed by rigorous empirical and diagnostic evidence across seven benchmarks and multiple OOD tests (B pages 6–10, 15–19). Although B has minor presentation gaps—such as Figure 1's caption mentioning a "Soft-TopK MIL aggregator" (B page 4) whereas Eqs. 6–7 use attention-entropy linear MIL pooling and a p=4 Minkowski norm (B page 5), and Eq. 8 (B page 5) linearly combining y_base, y_dis, and v_ext without explicitly notating how the metric-weighted transport score from Eq. 9/13 (B pages 6, 16) is substituted—its claimed payoffs are thoroughly verified. B demonstrates consistent PLCC/SRCC gains over RALI at <3 ms latency (Table 1, B pages 6–7), proves that its GRL adversary reduces content-probe accuracy from 0.868 to 0.138 while boosting OOD PLCC unlike HSIC or MINE (Table 2, B page 7), rules out proxy-cluster overfitting by showing semantic decodability collapses on unseen ImageNet-1k and MS-COCO labels while retaining 79–110% of low-level quality signals (B pages 9–10, Table 12 page 19), validates its zero-FLOP attention-entropy saliency against human gaze on SALICON (Table 11, B pages 10, 19), and matches Gemini 2.5 Flash on worst-region defect localization (89.6% vs. 89.3% hit-rate) at ~2,949x lower latency while generalizing to non-rectangular organic defect shapes (B pages 8–10, Table 13 page 19).

B has stronger overall creative quality, although neither manuscript introduces wholly unfamiliar machinery. A decomposes into UCT-style search, shortest-path terminal attachment, and randomized restricted-candidate rollouts (A pages 4–5). Its least readily placed block—the terminal-level tree-growth rule—still has a close antecedent in the Takahashi–Matsuyama shortest-path Steiner heuristic; its top-K randomization resembles GRASP construction. These are antecedents to the primitives, not claims that the complete directed-MCTS solver already appears there. B decomposes into LoRA adaptation, prototype regression, gradient-reversal content suppression, and spatial severity prediction and pooling (B pages 4–6). Most are readily recognizable, particularly the adversary and annealing schedule from Ganin-style domain-adversarial learning. Its least placeable ingredient is the attention-entropy-to-saliency rule: I can locate that only within transformer-saliency literature, not a particular prior formulation. This gives B modestly less specifically traceable material, without treating its assembly of familiar modules as novelty. For A’s routing task, the obvious approach is a directed-Steiner heuristic or mathematical optimization with shortest-path-based construction; for B’s lightweight IQA task, it is adapting a pretrained visual encoder to global quality scores, potentially with spatial attention or distilled language supervision. A’s search over terminal orderings rather than edges is a useful abstraction but remains close to conventional greedy tree construction. B’s deliberate suppression of the semantic information encouraged by its backbone, coupled with replacing scalar-only supervision by explicit defect-region targets, is a more consequential central redirection—though still within established invariant-representation and region-aware IQA approaches. A’s mechanism is sufficiently concrete to implement: each MCTS action selects a destination, multi-source Dijkstra attaches its cheapest incremental path, and randomized rollouts evaluate completion. However, exactness of each attachment does not establish optimality of the resulting Steiner tree; restricting construction to those attachments can exclude beneficial shared-relay structures. The implemented method also does not specify the neural exploration promised in the abstract. More importantly, its main payoff is unresolved in the supplied evidence: A page 6 reports 627.10, while Table 1 on A page 7 lists 1090.78 for the same method. A page 9 additionally acknowledges that throughput constraints and dynamic conditions are not addressed. These issues limit confidence in its claimed competitive, adaptive routing payoff. B more directly tests whether its proposed mechanisms accomplish their intended jobs. Its adversarial controls connect reduced semantic decodability with improved out-of-domain scoring (B page 7), while the localization ablation improves hit-rate from 46.4% under MOS-only supervision to 89.6% with synthetic regional targets (B page 8). Importantly, synthetic-only training already achieves that hit-rate, so the additional MIL contribution is modest. The overall scoring gains are also incremental rather than transformative. B overstates complete content invariance: independent COCO probe accuracy remains 33.5%, versus its stated 1.35% chance level (B page 9), and adversarial confusion does not mathematically guarantee orthogonality. Its entropy calculations and learned patch head are not literally zero-FLOP either. Nevertheless, narrowing these claims to semantic attenuation and inexpensive defect localization leaves a worked-out proposal with mechanism-specific supporting evidence. That supported, moderately unexpected redirection outweighs A’s appealing abstraction and simpler implementation, whose principal performance claim remains unreconciled.

Evaluated relative to their respective fields and research tasks—lightweight no-reference image quality assessment (NR-IQA) for A (A page 1–2) and multi-cloud broadcast routing optimization via directed Steiner trees for B (B page 1–3)—Manuscript A demonstrates substantially stronger overall creative quality when considering New, Useful, and Surprising jointly. For Surprising, the obvious approach to A's task of improving a lightweight distilled vision-encoder IQA model across domains and localized defects would be to apply contrastive degradation pre-training or add a multi-scale spatial attention pooling head trained end-to-end on global scalar MOS labels (A page 2–3). The obvious approach to B's task of constructing minimum-cost broadcast trees across ~10–50 node cloud graphs where naive LLM evolution or edge-by-edge search struggles would be to apply a standard Steiner tree approximation heuristic or an integer linear programming solver (B page 2–3, 9). B departs from naive edge-by-edge reinforcement learning and unconstrained LLM prompt evolution by defining the MCTS state as a partial broadcast tree and actions as selecting unreached destination terminals connected via multi-source Dijkstra (B page 2, 4–5). However, within combinatorial routing, iteratively connecting unreached terminals via shortest paths from the existing tree is the classic Shortest Path Heuristic (SPH), making B's search formulation an expected algorithmic refinement. A makes a more unexpected and central departure: first, it diagnoses that prototype transport in CLIP feature space remains dominated by object categories and actively strips them via a supervised Gradient Reversal Layer (GRL) trained against 100 k-means clusters of pristine frozen CLIP embeddings (A page 2, 4–5); second, it repurposes the vision transformer's final-layer negative self-attention entropy as a zero-FLOP perceptual saliency weight for a patch segmentation head trained jointly on synthetic fractional box-overlap targets and real-MOS Multiple Instance Learning (MIL), using the resulting Minkowski-pooled worst-region severity to dynamically sharpen prototype transport temperature (A page 5–6). For New, we examine the least placeable building blocks of each manuscript without judging their combination. B's building blocks—representing states as partial trees, expanding to unreached terminals via multi-source Dijkstra from current tree vertices (B page 4–5), UCT selection (B page 5), and randomized greedy rollouts over the top-K closest terminals (B page 5)—are all directly placeable in standard combinatorial optimization literature, specifically the Takahashi-Matsuyama shortest-path Steiner tree heuristic and Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedures (GRASP) combined with MCTS. In A, while LoRA adaptation (Yin et al., 2023; A page 3), bucketed k-means prototype transport (RALI, Zhao et al., 2025; A page 2, 4), and adversarial GRL (domain adaptation literature; A page 4) are placeable in specific works, its least placeable building blocks—such as using negative ViT self-attention entropy as a zero-FLOP human-gaze-aligned saliency prior (A page 5, 10) and modulating prototype-transport temperature via Minkowski-aggregated local defect energy (A page 5–6)—can only be placed more broadly at the level of the vision-language IQA and transformer attention-analysis subfield literatures. For Useful, A's mechanisms are fully worked out mathematically (Equations 1–9 on A page 4–6; Equations 10–13 on A page 16) and rigorously validated. A demonstrates that its GRL adversary reduces 100-cluster semantic probe accuracy from 0.868 to 0.138 while outperforming unsupervised PCA-nulling, HSIC, and MINE on out-of-domain PLCC (Table 2, A page 7). Crucially, A rules out self-referential proxy bias by showing that linear probe decodability on unseen ImageNet-1k and MS-COCO labels collapses toward chance while preserving 85–110% of low-level quality signals (Figure 3A, A page 9; Table 12, A page 10, 19). Its patch head achieves an 89.6% worst-region hit-rate matching a grounding MLLM (Gemini 2.5 Flash) at ~2,949x lower latency (A page 8–9), generalizes to non-rectangular organic shapes and QGround-100K annotations (Table 13, A page 10, 19), and validates its attention-entropy saliency against human gaze on SALICON 2017 (Table 11, A page 10, 19). The primary tradeoff in A is that its aggregate global score gain over the RALI baseline across the seven benchmarks is modest (+0.0062 average PLCC and +0.0084 average SRCC; A page 1, 6–7), though its new capabilities in verified content invariance and sub-millisecond defect localization are strongly supported. In contrast, B is in need of repair due to severe internal contradictions, missing specifications, and unsupported framing. First, B's abstract claims a "hybrid neuro-symbolic solver that combines the global structural exploration of LLMs with an Action-Condensed Monte Carlo Tree Search" (B page 1), yet Section 3 (B page 3–5) contains no LLM component at all, and Section 5 (B page 9) relegates hybrid neuro-symbolic integration to future work. Second, Section 3.3.1 (B page 5) asserts that it modifies the UCT formula to minimize costs rather than maximize rewards, but omits the formula entirely, and Section 3.1 (B page 3–4) introduces link throughput capacity th(u,v) only to ignore it in the objective (admitted on B page 9). Third, B's empirical evidence is self-contradictory: the main text claims Action-Condensed MCTS achieves a transfer cost of 627.10 $/GB (or 627.09 on B page 3), trailing Human SOTA (626.24) and Engram (622.00) (B page 1, 2, 6, 8, 9); however, Table 1 (B page 7) reports a score of 1090.78 $/GB for Action-Condensed MCTS (worse than every baseline in the table), while the Figure 3 caption (B page 8) contradicts both by claiming it achieves the lowest cost overall at $0.28/GB. Despite the simplicity and speed of B's 2.0-second multi-source Dijkstra MCTS (B page 5–6), A's cohesive, unexpected architectural design and thorough empirical verification make it the clear winner.

A offers the stronger overall creative contribution, although both manuscripts rely substantially on established machinery. For A’s lightweight image-quality task, the obvious approach is encoder adaptation followed by global score regression or prototype matching. For B’s broadcast-routing task, it is a Steiner-tree heuristic or mathematical optimizer using shortest-path primitives. A’s central departure is to suppress semantic information while explicitly learning localized degradation; B’s is to search destination-attachment order with MCTS rather than search individual edges (A pages 4–6; B pages 4–5). Both are meaningful departures, but B remains closer to a familiar greedy tree-construction direction. Breaking down the mechanisms, A uses LoRA, gradient-reversal adversarial learning, prototype regression, synthetic patch supervision, MIL, and Minkowski pooling—all recognizable established components. Its hardest individual mapping for me to place is inverse attention entropy as a human-gaze proxy: I can locate that only broadly in attention-based visual-saliency research, not confidently in a particular prior formulation (A pages 5 and 10). B decomposes into UCT search, shortest-path attachment to a partial tree, and randomized top-K rollouts. Even its less-routine tree-attachment abstraction closely resembles the Takahashi–Matsuyama shortest-path Steiner heuristic, adapted here to directed attachments; its randomized candidate selection is recognizable from GRASP-style restricted candidate lists (B pages 4–5). This does not establish prior publication of B’s complete algorithm, but its constituent mechanisms are more specifically placeable. The unusual assemblies matter as departures in direction, not as independent evidence of novelty. A also provides a more convincing connection between its mechanisms and their intended payoff. Its disentanglement comparison reports improved out-of-domain correlation while reducing semantic decodability, and its supervision ablation increases localization hit-rate from 46.4% with MIL alone to 89.6% with synthetic supervision (A pages 7–8). The later shape-generalization and real-region tests extend support beyond rectangular training masks (A pages 10 and 19). Important qualifications remain: synthetic-only training already achieves the same localization hit-rate, so the added benefit of MIL is limited; independent-label probe results remain substantially above chance and therefore support reduced semantic accessibility, not strict content invariance (A pages 8–9). The reported global scoring improvement is modest, but the localization mechanism has a separately demonstrated payoff. B’s algorithm is coherent as a bounded-budget heuristic: multi-source Dijkstra finds the cheapest next attachment, and MCTS explores how attachment order affects sharing. That does not guarantee optimal subtrees or globally optimal Steiner trees. More importantly, its comparative payoff is unresolved: the main results report 627.10, Table 1 reports 1090.78 for the proposed method, and Figure 3’s caption claims 0.28 and superiority to all baselines (B pages 6–8). These incompatible extracted claims cannot establish the advertised performance advantage. The promised neural–symbolic integration is also not operationally specified, while throughput constraints and dynamic-network evaluation are explicitly absent (B pages 1, 5, and 9). Thus, despite A’s overstatements and conventional ingredients, its less-readily-placeable mapping and experimentally supported move from global scoring toward content-resistant, localized assessment form a stronger creative contribution than B’s recognizable search abstraction with unresolved central evidence.

Evaluated relative to their respective fields and tasks, Manuscript B demonstrates substantially stronger overall creative quality than Manuscript A across New, Useful, and Surprising considered jointly. Regarding New (whether the building blocks have been written down before, independent of their combination), Manuscript A decomposes into four main blocks for tabular LLM prompt serialization: (1) global integer factorization of column-value pairs into an int32 matrix with squared string-length weights (A page 4), (2) dynamic prefix-trie row partitioning via vectorized histogram counting (`np.bincount`) and a max-heap (A page 4), (3) an adaptive Top-K (K=5) 2-step lookahead for partitions above 500 rows reverting to 1-step greedy below 500 rows (A pages 4–5), and (4) parent-minus-child histogram subtraction for non-matching row subsets (A page 5). Dictionary encoding, histogram subtraction, and bounded-depth lookahead in tree construction are standard algorithmic techniques across tabular data processing, while recursive column-value grouping for LLM KV-cache reuse is directly placeable in the relational LLM query optimization literature, specifically Greedy Group Recursion (GGR, Liu et al., 2024; A pages 2–3). Even A's least placeable block—the specific $(N_{c,v}-1)|v|^2$ 2-step lookahead splitting rule (A pages 4–5)—is a narrow heuristic variation within that exact problem formulation. Manuscript B decomposes into: (1) an invariant VQ-VAE and multi-hop residual GNN backbone from IA-GGAD (Zhang et al., 2025b; B pages 3–4), (2) Discrete Signed Forman-Ricci Simplicial Curvature (FRSC) node profiling that retains signed rank order rather than magnitude deviations (B pages 4–5, 13), (3) Multi-Scale Hodge-Simplicial Heat-Kernel Diffusion (MSH-HKD) on the 1st-order Hodge Laplacian ($e^{-tL_1}$ at $t=1$) conditioned on a global edge-density Gaussian gate $g_{hk}$ that also prunes simplicial matrix allocation on ultra-sparse graphs (B page 5), and (4) Curvature-Gated Reliability Consensus Fusion (CGR-Fuse) weighting topological consensus against 1-hop GNN affinity via clamped Spearman rank agreement and a triangle-free property switch (B page 5). While discrete Forman-Ricci curvature in graph anomaly detection (Chatterjee et al., 2021) and Hodge Laplacian simplicial diffusion (Schaub et al., 2018, 2021; Frantzen & Schaub, 2025) exist in the topological data analysis (TDA) and graph signal processing literature (B pages 2–3), B's least placeable blocks—specifically the global edge-density Gaussian gate $g_{hk}$ controlling 1st-order Hodge heat-kernel trace diffusion and the bounded Spearman rank-agreement gate bridging 1-hop GNN affinity with signed simplicial curvature for zero-shot cross-domain transfer (B page 5)—cannot be traced to a single prior work and are only placeable at the broader subfield level of topological graph anomaly detection. Regarding Surprising (departure from the obvious approach to each task), for Manuscript A's task of ordering tabular rows and columns to maximize LLM KV-cache prefix overlap, the obvious approach is static cardinality-based column sorting followed by lexicographical row sorting (as in GGR) or black-box evolutionary permutation search (as in AdaEvolve; A page 2). A departs from static column ordering by allowing different row branches in a prefix trie to select different subsequent columns dynamically and bounding search cost via integer vectorization and a 500-row lookahead cutoff (A pages 2, 4–5). While dynamic per-partition column selection is a sensible algorithmic refinement over static global column orderings, it remains an expected greedy/beam-search progression for trie construction. For Manuscript B's task of zero-shot generalist graph anomaly detection (GGAD) under severe Graph Structure Shift (GSS), the obvious approach would be to train deeper multi-hop parametric GNN encoders, apply spectral band-pass filters, or append standard absolute-deviation topological features ($|F|$ or $|z_{FR}|$) weighted more heavily whenever local 1-hop affinity disagrees with higher-order topology (B pages 2–3, 8). B departs from this expected trajectory in three central, counter-intuitive ways: first, it shows that learned multi-scale projections fail to transfer under zero-shot structure shift and replaces parametric structural layers with purely non-parametric simplicial operators at short-range scale $t=1$ (B pages 5, 8); second, it overturns the standard TDA convention of using absolute or two-tailed curvature deviations by proving theoretically and diagnostically that structural fraud cliques reside overwhelmingly in the positive signed curvature tail ($F gg 0$), so taking magnitudes folds positive clique anomalies onto normal and negative-curvature bridge nodes (B pages 5, 8, 13–15); third, it gates higher-order diffusion using global rather than local ego-net density and fuses scores using positive Spearman rank agreement rather than disagreement (B pages 5, 8–9, 14), demonstrating that local density gates and disagreement gates misfire on injected noise in sparse or structureless graphs. Regarding Useful (whether the mechanism is worked out and the claimed payoff follows), the tradeoff strongly favors B due to internal contradictions and incomplete evidence in A. Manuscript A works out its integer factorization, subtraction update, and lookahead equations clearly (A pages 4–5), but its empirical validation has major flaws: Table 1 compares A's Combined Score (0.7185) against unaligned baseline numbers (reporting raw Prefix Hit Rate ranges for GGR, raw PHR for AdaEvolve, and only a relative speedup for ADRS best, with missing unified scores; A page 6), the runtime text is inconsistent between claiming an average of 18.05 seconds per task (A page 2) versus 18.05 seconds total across all five datasets to meet a 12-second per-dataset cap (A pages 5–6), and most critically, A's own ablation study in Table 2 shows that a simpler "Lazy Greedy Prefix Trie" without the headline 2-step lookahead achieves a higher score (0.7299) than the proposed "Final Solution (Top-K Lookahead)" (0.7185; A pages 6–7). Thus, A's central lookahead mechanism actually degrades its stated benchmark payoff. In contrast, Manuscript B's mechanisms are fully specified mathematically and algorithmically (B pages 4–5, 13) and backed by rigorous, multi-faceted empirical evidence across 8 zero-shot target benchmarks and 3 large-scale financial graphs up to 3.7M nodes against 16 baselines (B pages 6, 9–10). Every component of B's mechanism delivers its claimed payoff under controlled ablations: combining signed curvature, clustering, and density-gated Hodge diffusion improves average AUROC by +2.12% and AUPRC by +6.23% (headlined by +13.50% AUROC and +34.65% AUPRC on dense Facebook) with zero regressions on sparse citation graphs (B pages 6–7); signed curvature avoids the catastrophic rank collapse of $|FR_{\text{raw}}|$ on Weibo (89.35% vs. 31.40% AUROC; B page 8); global density gating avoids the -10.51% AUPRC regression of local ego-net gating on ACM (B page 14); and forced-$H_1$ Chebyshev timing on 3.7M nodes confirms linear scalability (123.23s, 3.2 GB VRAM) while showing that density pruning simultaneously improves accuracy on sparse distributed-fraud graphs (B pages 9–10, 15).

The sequential-row description also needs a precise request contract: matching row beginnings inside one long causal prompt are not automatically reusable cached prefixes (A pages 1 and 4). Its component decomposition shows that Hodge signatures alone can hurt, while curvature, clustering, and conditional diffusion together improve the reported results; the signed-curvature and global-versus-local gating comparisons further investigate why (B pages 6–8 and 14). This supports a conditional detection mechanism, not merely an asserted benefit from adding topology. The evidence remains imperfect: the fusion equation’s minimum weight of 0.20 conflicts with reported weights below that minimum and claims of a zero-weight safety switch (B pages 5 and 8–9). Its strict clique/normal separation claim also requires assumptions about external degrees and normal topology that are absent (B page 13). Consequently, neither universal safety nor fully reproducible gating is established, and the largest supported gains are concentrated on the dense social-network case. Despite those substantive qualifications, B offers the stronger overall creative contribution: an unexpected conditional use of familiar topology with experiments that directly probe its benefits and failures. A’s clearer low-level implementation is valuable, but its distinctive extra search machinery and claimed inference acceleration receive weaker support relative to its own task.

Regarding New, we break each manuscript into its constituent building blocks and examine the least specifically placeable block independently of how blocks are combined. Manuscript A relies on: (1) a vector-quantized invariant feature pool and 1-hop GCN affinity backbone taken directly from IA-GGAD (Zhang et al., 2025b; van den Oord et al., 2017; A page 4); (2) discrete signed Forman-Ricci simplicial curvature profiling (FRSC), which builds on standard discrete Ricci curvature anomaly detection (Chatterjee et al., 2021; A pages 2, 4–5); (3) global edge-density-gated 1st-order Hodge Laplacian heat-kernel diffusion at short scale t=1 (MSH-HKD), drawing on simplicial signal processing (Schaub et al., 2018, 2021; Frantzen & Schaub, 2025; A pages 2, 5); and (4) Curvature-Gated Reliability Consensus Fusion (CGR-Fuse), which weights higher-order simplicial descriptors against 1-hop GNN affinity via a floored sigmoid of their Spearman rank correlation paired with a global density Gaussian gate (A page 5). This fourth block—conditioning zero-shot higher-order Hodge/curvature fusion on global graph density and positive rank correlation with a protective floor—cannot be placed in a single prior work and is placeable only broadly within the graph out-of-distribution and topological data analysis subfield literatures. By contrast, Manuscript B relies on: (1) integer factorization of (column, string) pairs with np.bincount frequency counting (B page 4), which is common knowledge in tabular data engineering; (2) recursive prefix partitioning scored by shared string length (Nc,v - 1)|v|^2 with parent-minus-child histogram subtraction (B pages 4–5), which is standard material across Greedy Group Recursion for LLM relational caching (Liu et al., 2024; B pages 2–3) and decision-tree histogram subtraction in gradient boosting; and (3) a hybrid 1-step/2-step Top-K (K=5) lookahead with a 500-row threshold (B pages 4–5), which is a standard bounded beam-search heuristic in combinatorial optimization. Thus, A's least placeable mechanism is harder to place specifically than B's. Regarding Useful, Manuscript A's central mechanism—upgrading IA-GGAD's structural branch with signed Forman-Ricci curvature, global-density-gated t=1 Hodge 1-Laplacian Chebyshev diffusion, and rank-agreement fusion (A pages 4–5, 13)—is fully worked out mathematically and algorithmically, and its claimed payoff is rigorously supported. Across eight unseen target benchmarks and three large-scale financial graphs up to 3.7M nodes, A achieves +2.12% average AUROC and +6.23% average AUPRC over IA-GGAD, including +13.50% AUROC and +34.65% AUPRC on dense social networks (Facebook) with zero regressions on sparse citation graphs (A page 6, Tables 1–2; A page 10, Table 7). Furthermore, A directly validates each mechanistic claim via controlled ablations: showing that 67%–87% of structural anomalies lie in the top positive curvature decile whereas absolute or two-tailed curvature folds positive cliques onto negative bridges (A page 8, Table 4; A page 10, Figure 7a; A page 15, Table 10), that local ego-net gating fails on injected cliques in sparse graphs compared to global density gating (A page 14, Table 9), and that forced Chebyshev H1 diffusion scales linearly on 3.7M nodes (A page 15, Table 11). Conversely, while Manuscript B works out a clear, fast algorithmic pipeline for integer-factorized prefix partitioning (B pages 4–5), its empirical payoff is undermined by two major flaws: first, its main comparison table reports incommensurable metrics copied from literature (comparing B's 0.7185 Combined Score against raw Prefix Hit Rates for GGR and AdaEvolve and a '3.9x faster runtime' string for ADRS best; B page 6, Table 1); second, in B's own ablation study, the simpler 1-step Lazy Greedy Prefix Trie (0.7299) outperforms B's proposed Final Solution with Top-K 2-step lookahead (0.7185) (B pages 6–7, Table 2), leaving the core lookahead mechanism's benefit empirically unsupported. Regarding Surprising, the obvious approach to A's task would be to train a deeper multi-hop GNN or adaptive prompt network to learn multi-node structural representations, whereas the obvious approach to B's task would be to greedily group rows and columns by value frequency and string length using vectorized integer operations. Manuscript B stays very close to that expected greedy partitioning direction, adding only a shallow 2-step lookahead and histogram subtraction (B pages 4–5). Manuscript A makes a much stronger central departure: instead of modifying the trainable GNN backbone, it injects training-free simplicial operators (signed Forman-Ricci curvature and edge-space Hodge heat kernels) and counterintuitively gates them via global rather than local edge density and positive rank agreement rather than disagreement (A pages 2, 5, 8–9), demonstrating both theoretically and empirically why the intuitive alternatives (absolute curvature, local density gating, and disagreement-boosted gating) fail under graph structure shift (A pages 8–9, 13–14). Although B offers a clean, lightweight engineering tradeoff for tabular preprocessing speed (B pages 4–5), A's superior conceptual departure, less specifically placeable gating mechanism, and thoroughly validated empirical payoff make A the clear overall winner.

Both manuscripts largely use established building blocks. Its least placeable substantive claim is that global graph density provides a useful safety rule for admitting higher-order diffusion; I can locate this only broadly in adaptive graph filtering, not in a specific prior work. B combines dictionary encoding, recursive prefix grouping, heap-based greedy search, bounded lookahead, and subtractive frequency updates (B pages 4–5). Its least placeable block is the particular repeated-value utility, (N−1)|v|²; I can place it only broadly in weighted trie/data-layout heuristics, not a named antecedent. Thus neither deserves novelty credit simply for assembling familiar techniques, and provenance alone gives no decisive distinction. For A’s task, the obvious approach would strengthen learned neighborhood representations or domain-invariant reconstruction; for B’s task, it would order low-cardinality columns first and group rows lexicographically. A’s central departure is to preserve signed geometric evidence and selectively admit nonlearned simplicial diffusion, including deliberately suppressing that richer representation where it hurts. B also departs meaningfully through branch-specific column choices rather than one global ordering, but its bounded lookahead remains closer to the expected optimization of prefix grouping. A’s departure is more substantial, although curvature and higher-order graph analysis themselves are established approaches. The usefulness comparison favors A’s demonstrated mechanism rather than its benchmark size. Its reported comparisons isolate benefits from signed rather than absolute curvature and show that Hodge diffusion helps when combined with the curvature/clustering core and density conditioning, while indiscriminate diffusion can damage sparse-graph detection (A pages 7–8). The Facebook improvement from 80.43 to 93.93 AUROC and 5.90 to 40.55 AUPRC therefore has supporting component-level evidence, not merely a headline result (A page 6). Important repairs remain: the clique calculation on A page 13 incorrectly evaluates the stated formula as m−4 rather than m, and the 0.20 gate floor on A page 5 cannot produce the sub-0.20 or zero weights reported on pages 8–9. These undermine the formal guarantees and exact reproducibility, so the supported payoff is empirical and conditional, not universal regression-free transfer. B provides a reasonably actionable algorithm and reports useful overlap and preprocessing-runtime measurements. However, its distinctive lookahead component scores below its own lazy-greedy variant, 0.7185 versus 0.7299, without evidence establishing the asserted robustness guarantee (B pages 6–7). Its baseline table also mixes raw hit rates, a combined score, and a runtime multiplier, preventing a like-for-like superiority conclusion; no serving-level experiment establishes the claimed downstream acceleration (B pages 5–6). Overall, A narrowly offers stronger creative quality: its more unexpected structural intervention has targeted evidence explaining when it pays off, whereas B’s coherent engineering proposal leaves the advantage of its central refinement unestablished. A’s specification problems materially temper, but do not erase, that distinction.

These results do not establish end-to-end serving gains: squared character-prefix overlap is not itself measured KV-memory or latency savings, and sharing prefixes between separately issued row prompts must be distinguished from matching row beginnings inside one concatenated context.
