Evaluated relative to their respective fields and research tasks, Manuscript B demonstrates substantially stronger overall creative quality than Manuscript A when considering New, Useful, and Surprising jointly. Regarding New (whether the building blocks have been written down before), Manuscript A breaks down into (1) formulating conflict-aware transaction makespan minimization as a permutation search (A page 4), (2) deterministic beam search over schedule prefixes (A page 4), (3) pruning redundant permutations by mapping prefixes to an unordered `frozenset` state signature and retaining the lowest-cost path per subset (A page 5), and (4) memoizing prefix evaluation costs (A pages 5–6). Even A's least placeable block—subset-based state deduplication in permutation search (A page 5)—is a standard textbook formulation directly placeable in classic combinatorial optimization works such as Held-Karp subset dynamic programming and standard beam search with transposition tables in AI planning and job-shop scheduling literatures. Manuscript B breaks down into (1) first-order context-tail delta projection for C0 boundary alignment of retrieved horizons (B page 5, page 14), (2) real-FFT low/high sub-band spectral residual splitting (B page 5), (3) content-plus-distance neighbour attention (B page 5), (4) a per-sample, per-band, per-timestep gating MLP conditioned on a (6L+8)-dimensional retrieval-trust feature vector (B pages 5–6, page 14), and (5) post-hoc dataset-level dual-metric validation calibration (D-Guard, B page 6). While spectral decomposition (e.g., FEDformer, Zhou et al., 2022b; FreTS, Yi et al., 2023) and time-series RAG (e.g., TS-RAG, Ning et al., 2025; RAF, Tire et al., 2024) appear in named works, B's least placeable block—gating frequency-split output residuals per timestep using joint neighbour spectral disagreement, boundary slope mismatch, and local AR(1) trend continuity features on top of a frozen foundation model (B pages 5–6, page 14)—cannot be placed in a single prior paper and is only placeable at the broader subfield level of retrieval-augmented forecasting and uncertainty-gated residual fusion. Regarding Surprising (departure from the obvious approach to each task), for A's task of offline algorithmic transaction scheduling without neural inference overhead, the obvious approach is to expand greedy lookahead into a standard beam or tree search over partial permutations with state deduplication and caching; A takes this expected direction directly (A pages 4–6). For B's task of zero-shot retrieval-augmented time series forecasting with foundation models, the obvious approach is to prepend retrieved analogues in-context or monolithically fuse retrieved horizon vectors via cross-attention or static scalar blending. B departs centrally from this paradigm by diagnosing three structural failure modes of monolithic fusion—boundary step-discontinuities at t = T + 1, destructive interference between reliable low-frequency trends and volatile high-frequency seasonality, and negative transfer on noisy domains (B page 2)—and reframing retrieval augmentation as a lightweight, boundary-aligned, frequency-disentangled output-space residual refinement with a validation-calibrated do-no-harm fallback (B pages 2, 4–6). Regarding Useful (whether the mechanism is worked out and the claimed payoff follows) and relevant tradeoffs, A's proposal requires major repair due to internal algorithmic and empirical inconsistencies. First, A claims that caching workload evaluations using a strictly ordered prefix key `memo[tuple(Sk)]` causes the cache hit rate to "climb exponentially" as branches converge on similar transaction subsets (A pages 5–6, Eq. 4; pages 8–9). However, in a deterministic single-run beam search where active prefixes at step k-1 are distinct and each is extended by an unassigned transaction, every generated ordered tuple `(s1, ..., sk)` is unique; two permutations reaching the same unordered subset have different ordered tuples and cannot hit the same cache entry. Second, A asserts without formal simulator specification that the unordered set of completed transactions completely determines future makespan conflicts (A page 5), which ignores staggered resource/lock release times across permutations. Third, A's main empirical table compares its raw score of 3636.36 against baseline scores reported on an incommensurate ~0–100 scale (SMF at 85.2, AdaEvolve at 89.2, ADRS best at 92.4; A page 7, Table 1) whereas its own internal ablations all score 3378–3460 (A page 8, Table 2), claims 5-seed variance aggregation for a deterministic algorithm (A page 6), and references unmentioned baselines (HEFT and CPOP) in Figure 3 (A page 7). By contrast, B's mathematical formulation and 0.27M-parameter architecture are fully worked out (B pages 4–6, page 14) and empirically supported across seven zero-shot benchmarks (reducing TS-RAG MSE from 0.1940 to 0.1892 and outperforming RAF/RAEF under an identical frozen Chronos-Bolt backbone; B pages 7–8, Tables 1–2), extended rolling horizons up to L = 720 (B page 10, Table 3), and zero-shot cross-domain transfer without retraining to GIFT-Eval (-5.6% average MSE, -46.1% on periodic solar; B page 8, Figure 3; page 15, Table 10). The main tradeoff in B is that several architectural sub-components yield modest incremental gains over simpler ablations—for instance, Full Dual-Band achieves 0.2199 MSE versus 0.2203 for Monolithic and 0.2205 for Low-Only (B page 14, Table 4), and learned Content+Distance Attention (0.1891 MSE) ties Inverse-Distance Softmax (0.1890) and Uniform Averaging (0.1891) (B page 15, Table 9)—and validation calibration remains vulnerable to validation-to-test shift on Electricity (B pages 6–7). Nevertheless, B transparently reports these exact tradeoffs while delivering a coherent, reproducible, and empirically validated mechanism.

B has stronger overall creative quality, although its supported contribution is narrower than its headline claims. A comprises beam search, memoization and subset-based representative pruning; its least routine operational block—retaining the cheapest prefix for each completed subset—is recognizable as the dominance-pruning pattern of subset dynamic programming and graph-search duplicate detection, rather than a new search principle (A pages 4–6). Those precedents do not establish that its proposed state is sufficient for transaction scheduling. B comprises endpoint alignment, Fourier filtering, attention, input-dependent gating and validation-selected blending. Its least readily placeable block is the specific retrieval-trust mapping used to generate temporal, frequency-band gates; I can locate that only broadly in confidence-aware ensemble forecasting, not in a particular prior work I can confidently name (B pages 5–6, 14). This leaves some component-level distinctiveness, but the assembly of familiar ingredients is not itself evidence of New. For A’s task, the obvious approach is conflict-aware greedy scheduling followed by broader search or lookahead; beam search with duplicate suppression develops that expected direction. For B’s task, the obvious approach is to retrieve analogous histories and incorporate their futures through attention or scalar blending. B’s central move—treating retrieved futures as separately trusted spectral corrections to a frozen prediction—departs more meaningfully from that direction, although spectral decomposition and adaptive blending are themselves familiar forecasting techniques (A pages 4–5; B pages 4–6). The usefulness comparison also favors B, but not because of benchmark size. A reports a makespan of 274 and improvements over alternative searches, providing some evidence for an offline heuristic (A pages 7–8). However, equal completed subsets need not imply equal resource-availability or conflict-completion times, so lower prefix makespan alone does not establish safe dominance. Moreover, convergence on unordered subsets does not explain cache hits when the cache is keyed by ordered tuples, and a fixed-width beam does not guarantee the claimed optimum (A pages 5–6). The score’s definition and workload-specific results are missing, and the filtering ablation changes other search features. Its approximately 150-second runtime supports, at most, the offline setting acknowledged on A page 9—not its earlier microsecond-scale deployment rationale. B specifies an actionable residual computation and provides targeted evidence: average MSE decreases from 0.1940 to 0.1892, while ablations test decomposition, gating and calibration (B pages 7, 14–15). Those tables also constrain the payoff: monolithic fusion and simpler gates recover most gains, and learned attention does not clearly surpass uniform averaging. Crucially, validation-selected blending guarantees only the combined validation objective, not either test metric; B page 15 explicitly reports regressions despite broader no-negative-transfer claims. Pooled in-domain training and dataset-specific validation calibration also weaken the strict zero-shot interpretation (B pages 6–8). Thus B needs qualification, not acceptance of its strongest guarantees. Nevertheless, its selective spectral-correction direction has a more directly worked-out mechanism and better-supported bounded payoff than A’s purported state-equivalence and caching advantages. That combination supports the overall choice.

For Surprising, the obvious approach to static combinatorial scheduling when greedy lookahead stagnates is to apply a broader tree or beam search with duplicate-state pruning; B follows this expected path directly (B page 2, 4-5). For zero-shot time series RAG, the obvious approach is to concatenate retrieved analogues in-context or train a monolithic cross-attention adapter inside the model. A departs more meaningfully by treating the foundation model as a frozen black box and reformulating retrieval fusion in output space as a boundary-aligned, frequency-disentangled residual control problem governed by explicit trust diagnostics and a post-hoc "do-no-harm" safety guard (A page 2, 4-6). For Useful, A's mechanism is mathematically complete and empirically validated across seven standard benchmarks, extended rolling horizons up to L=720, and five unseen GIFT-Eval datasets (-5.6% MSE zero-shot, A page 7-10, 14-16) with only 0.27M parameters and 4.02 ms/batch latency (A page 7, 10). First, B repeatedly claims that memoizing simulator calls with the strictly ordered prefix tuple `memo[tuple(Sk)]` produces an "exponentially climbing cache hit rate" as branches converge on similar subsets (B page 2, 5-6, 8-9); mathematically, because every beam branch at step k expands a distinct prefix by a distinct transaction, every queried ordered tuple `tuple(Sk)` is unique, yielding a 0% cache hit rate across branches and conflating ordered-tuple caching with unordered-set pruning. A offers the stronger overall creative contribution, although its supported achievement is narrower than its headline claims. Its building blocks are endpoint-relative analogue transfer, FFT decomposition, content/distance weighting, reliability-conditioned residual gates, and validation-selected blending (A pages 5–6). The least readily placeable block is the mapping from neighbour disagreement, boundary mismatch, and retrieval distance to local correction strength: I can place its principle in reliability-conditioned forecast combination and mixture-of-experts gating, but cannot name a specific earlier work containing that mapping. B comprises bounded-width prefix search, completed-subset filtering, and ordered-sequence memoization (B pages 4–6). Even its least routine operation—keeping the cheapest representative of each completed subset—is recognizable as standard best-cost-per-state duplicate pruning in graph search and subset dynamic programming. This comparison concerns the individual mechanisms, not novelty credited merely for assembling familiar tools. For A’s task, the obvious approach is to retrieve similar histories and blend their continuations with the foundation forecast; for B’s task, it is conflict-aware greedy scheduling followed by conventional search over alternative orderings. A makes a meaningful, though not radical, directional departure by treating retrieval as an optional, frequency- and timestep-specific correction rather than a whole-trajectory contribution. B’s subset-based diversity control is central and potentially useful, but remains closer to familiar search-space reduction; avoiding neural inference is not itself an unexpected scheduling strategy. A works out its correction mechanism mathematically and supplies evidence of a bounded practical payoff: average MSE decreases from 0.1940 to 0.1892, and the transferred module reports further gains on held-out domains (A pages 7–8). Its ablations also permit scrutiny of the proposed mechanisms. However, monolithic residuals and simpler gates perform nearly as well, limiting the demonstrated necessity of the elaborate decomposition and modulation (A pages 14–15). The safety guarantee applies only to the combined validation objective, not both test metrics: two datasets regress on at least one metric (A pages 6 and 15). Training on benchmark training splits and using target-domain validation calibration also qualify the end-to-end zero-shot claim. These limitations leave a usable forecasting refinement, rather than the claimed universal protection against negative transfer. B’s potential payoff requires more substantial repair. The manuscript does not establish that a completed subset and its scalar makespan constitute a sufficient scheduling state: different orderings can leave different resource or dependency-release times, so the cheaper prefix need not dominate every continuation (B pages 4–5). Moreover, convergence on an unordered subset does not produce cache hits when the cache key is the ordered sequence, undermining the explanation for exponentially increasing memoization efficiency (B pages 5–6). The reported makespan remains potentially encouraging, but the score lacks a defining formula, workload-level comparisons are missing, and the purported filtering ablation changes other search components simultaneously (B pages 6–8). Its 150-second runtime supports, at most, offline batch scheduling, as its limitations acknowledge (B page 9). Thus A’s comparatively traceable mechanism and demonstrated, qualified gains outweigh B’s interesting diversity heuristic whose state-validity and efficiency explanations are not established.

Evaluated relative to their respective fields and tasks, Manuscript B demonstrates substantially stronger overall creative quality than Manuscript A when considering New, Useful, and Surprising jointly. For New, breaking Manuscript A into its constituent building blocks yields a two-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron with Batch Normalization, ReLU, and Dropout trained with binary cross-entropy (A pages 4–5), a one-dimensional validation grid search over scalar probability thresholds to maximize Micro-F1 (A pages 5–6, Algorithm 1), and an unweighted average of predictions across ten model checkpoints and two input resolutions (336 and 448) (A page 6). Even A's least placeable building block—post-hoc grid-search threshold tuning on ensembled multi-resolution MLP predictions to handle missing-label skew—is standard, textbook machine learning practice and common knowledge in the genre of Kaggle competition pipelines. By contrast, breaking Manuscript B into its building blocks yields spherical tangent Langevin dynamics with radial retraction on the Gaussian hypersphere (placeable in the Riemannian MCMC literature such as Girolami & Calderhead 2011 and manifold-constrained diffusion sampling such as Shi et al. 2026; B pages 2–3, 5), a hinge-gated cross-attention alignment barrier paired with a Tweedie CLIP-cosine anchor (placeable in the subfield of attention- and CLIP-guided diffusion control such as Chefer et al. 2023; B pages 3, 5), a finite-difference directional score curvature potential evaluated strictly along the normalized classifier-free guidance vector at initialization (B page 4, Eq. 3–4), and batch-wise repulsion over spatial Query-Query Gram matrices extracted at pure noise t=T (B pages 4–5, Eq. 5). B's least placeable blocks—probing local velocity curvature specifically along the conditional guidance vector at t=T and orthogonalizing spatial Query Gram matrices across a batch at the pure-noise step—cannot be placed in a specific prior paper and can only be placed more broadly within the subfield literatures of curvature-aware diffusion initialization (such as Jeon et al. 2024 and Li et al. 2026) and attention-based layout control (such as Hertz et al. 2022), making B much stronger on New. For Surprising, the obvious approach to A's task of noisy hierarchical multi-label artwork tagging is either to design an explicit hierarchical or asymmetric loss function, or in a competition setting to ensemble multi-scale features with post-hoc F1 threshold tuning; A departs from the academic loss-engineering route only by reporting that its custom geometric loss search branches failed and falling back entirely on the standard competition heuristic of a vanilla BCE MLP, ensembling, and threshold shifting (A pages 2, 4, 7–8). For B's task of mitigating mode collapse and layout stereotypy in conditional diffusion models, the obvious approach is to apply particle repulsion or condition annealing across all reverse denoising steps t in [T-1, 0], or to perturb initial noise using Euclidean pixel/latent Tweedie differences (B pages 1–3). B makes a central, unexpected departure by extracting and repelling spatial composition priors via Query-Query Gram matrices strictly at pure Gaussian noise t=T—where one would not expect cross-attention queries to already encode actionable inter-sample spatial layout structure—and coupling this with directional curvature probing along the guidance vector and hyperspherical norm preservation (B pages 3–5). Furthermore, B delivers surprising empirical insights by rigorously testing and refuting naive expectations about its own components: showing that simple post-hoc Euclidean norm rescaling matches full tangent-space projection across multi-step sweeps because radial norm preservation on the sqrt(D) shell is the true operative mechanism (B pages 9–10, 18–19, Tables 8, 16–17), and demonstrating that while mid-block ResNet or TweedieGrams are more discriminative in isolation, raw Query Grams win in the full framework by avoiding low-rank noise degradation and reusing the curvature forward pass (B pages 14–15, Tables 10–11). For Useful, A's mechanism is fully specified and clears the Kaggle silver medal benchmark with a 0.6791 Micro-F1 on iMet 2020 (A pages 1, 5–8), but its evidence reveals extreme fragility and practical tradeoffs: its conceptual figures depict box embeddings and asymmetric losses not used by the actual model (A pages 2, 3, 5), its baselines are restricted to internal search branches (A pages 7–8, Table 1), and its ablations show catastrophic collapse to near-zero F1 (0.0030–0.0035) if the threshold is fixed at 0.5, if 448-resolution features are removed, or if inference uses a single checkpoint instead of ten, imposing heavy inference costs (A pages 8–9, Table 2). B's mechanism is not only mathematically derived and algorithmically complete (B pages 3–5, 14), but its payoff is demonstrated across a wide scope of tasks and architectures—improving diversity (Vendi, Recall) while preserving fidelity across Stable Diffusion v1.4 text-to-image and ImageNet generation both standalone and stacked orthogonally with trajectory guidance (CADS, IG, PG) at roughly 3% runtime overhead (B pages 6–7, 10, Tables 1–2), transferring verbatim to Diffusion Transformers (DiT-XL/2 and PixArt-alpha) (B pages 7–8, 17–18, Tables 3–4, 15), and maintaining compositional and socioeconomic benchmark performance (GeoDE, DollarStreet, GenEval, T2I-CompBench; B pages 8–9, Tables 5–6). Even where B encounters tradeoffs—such as precision/coverage dips under strong dispersal on DiT-XL/2 (B page 17, Table 15) or the failure of its cross-attention hinge to protect perceptual quality under aggressive dispersal—B diagnoses the limitation and provides a working CLIP-x0 anchor and a memory-frugal sequential bank (B pages 5, 16–18, Tables 12–14), establishing superior utility alongside its stronger novelty and departure from expected directions.

B likewise uses familiar ingredients: finite-difference sensitivity probes, Gram-based repulsion, hinge penalties, and projected Langevin updates (B pages 4–5). Its least-placeable block is the particular mapping from inter-seed spatial Query-Gram dissimilarity at initialization to diversity of generated compositions. I can situate that in attention-based diffusion control and kernel sample-repulsion literature, but cannot identify a particular prior work containing that exact surrogate. This distinction concerns an individual proposed mechanism, not merely B’s unusual assembly of familiar components. For A’s task, the obvious approach is noise-aware multilabel training with calibrated thresholds; for B’s task, it is weakening or annealing classifier-free guidance, or repelling samples during denoising. A’s retreat from explicit hierarchies is a potentially informative negative result, but its replacement remains conventional classifier engineering. B’s batch-level layout shaping exclusively before denoising is a more unexpected central direction. Initial-noise optimization itself is already familiar from InitNO, so the departure is specifically the cross-seed structural objective rather than initialization optimization alone. A provides an implementable pipeline and reports 0.6791 Micro-F1 with component ablations (A page 8). However, optimizing against incompletely annotated validation targets does not by itself establish recovery of genuinely omitted attributes or hierarchical consistency. No clean-label audit or direct hierarchy-consistency test supports that interpretation. The near-total collapse after removing checkpoints or one resolution also lacks sufficient recalibration detail to establish the proposed variance-based explanation. Thus, the demonstrated payoff is narrower than the claimed solution to asymmetric omission noise, and it depends on a costly ensemble (A pages 8–9). B supplies more diagnostic evidence for its narrower practical payoff: repulsion alone increases Vendi from 2.398 to 2.550 against a spherical random-walk control, while geometry ablations show that norm restoration limits quality degradation under aggressive updates (B pages 9–10). These experiments connect interventions to effects rather than relying only on headline benchmark scores. They also reveal that ordinary post-hoc rescaling nearly matches spherical tangent updates, limiting the distinctive value of the elaborate sampler. Important claims need repair: the Jacobian-vector norm is not the asserted Rayleigh quotient (B page 14); fixing the radius preserves energy, not the complete Gaussian distribution; the default fidelity hinge is dormant and its active version fails to protect quality (B page 16); and the roughly 3% overhead claim conflicts with the 63.7% overhead reported in Table 11 (B pages 10 and 15). Fidelity and coverage losses also make the evidence support a diversity–quality tradeoff, not universal Pareto improvement (B pages 6–8). Despite those substantial qualifications, B retains a less routine, explicitly specified intervention with experimental support for controllable diversity gains and an identifiable norm-stabilization mechanism. A’s useful result is primarily conventional score optimization, with its more ambitious noise-and-hierarchy interpretation unestablished. That substantive distinction supports B overall without crediting its breadth or accepting its strongest theoretical and efficiency claims.

Every building block in B—including its least placeable block, post-hoc grid search for an F1-optimal classification threshold combined with multi-resolution checkpoint ensembling—is common knowledge and standard textbook material across applied machine learning and multi-label classification literature (e.g., Pillai et al. 2013 for F-measure threshold tuning; Dietterich 2000 for ensembling). Regarding Surprising, the obvious approach to A's task (mitigating mode collapse and layout stereotypy in CFG diffusion models) is to apply step-wise guidance, condition annealing, or particle repulsion across intermediate latents along the reverse denoising trajectory t in [T-1, 0], or to perturb initial noise in Euclidean space using pixel-level Tweedie distances (A pages 1–3). For B's task (multi-label artwork classification under hierarchical label relationships and severe false-negative omissions), the obvious approach from the academic ontology literature is to train with an explicit asymmetric or hierarchical box-embedding loss, while from a practical competition standpoint it is to train a classifier head on pre-extracted visual features and tune the decision threshold on a validation set (B pages 1–4). B departs from the academic framing of its own introduction by abandoning explicit hierarchical losses after reporting that seven internal search branches failed, retreating to a standard BCE-trained MLP with scalar threshold tuning (B pages 2, 7–8). However, retreating to a routine competition baseline where a single global threshold shift uniformly lowers the cutoff across all classes rather than modeling directional parent-child containment is a shallow departure. Conversely, A makes a central, non-obvious departure by assembling its geometric and spectral mechanisms strictly at the pure white-noise boundary t=T: rather than steering partially denoised images during reverse sampling, A exploits the insight that single-pass Query projections at pure noise t=T already carry sufficient spatial composition priors to orthogonalize multi-seed object layouts when coupled with directional CFG curvature and hyperspherical norm preservation (A pages 4–5, 7, 15). Regarding Useful, A's central mechanism is mathematically worked out in full (A pages 3–5, 14) and empirically validated across Stable Diffusion v1.4, Diffusion Transformers (DiT-XL/2, PixArt-alpha), real-world geographic/socioeconomic benchmarks (GeoDE, DollarStreet), and compositional suites (GenEval, T2I-CompBench) at ~3% runtime overhead for K=1 (A pages 6–10, 17–18). We note important tradeoffs exposed by A's own ablations: its default Hinge-Gated Text-Fidelity Anchor (tau_fid = -0.22) is completely dormant (reproducing the unanchored baseline identically, A page 15 lines 805–806, Table 12 page 16) and fails when forced active under aggressive dispersal, requiring a 4x slower CLIP-x0 anchor to actually protect fidelity (A page 8 lines 427–431, page 15 line 809, Table 13 page 16); moreover, its Spherical Tangent Langevin update performs virtually identically to a simple Euclidean step with post-hoc norm rescaling across K in {1..10} (A page 9 lines 463–474, Table 8 page 10, Tables 16–17 page 19). Nevertheless, A's transparent diagnosis of these exact tradeoffs strengthens its usefulness, and the complete pipeline demonstrably expands the diversity–fidelity Pareto frontier when stacked with trajectory guidance (CADS, IG, PG) (A pages 6–7). In contrast, while B works out the basic equations for its MLP, threshold grid search, and ensemble average to reach a 0.6791 Micro-F1 on iMet 2020 (B pages 5–8), its usefulness is undermined by severe omissions, internal inconsistencies, and load-bearing citation errors. Specifically, B never identifies what visual backbone extracted the 3072-dimensional features at 336 and 448 resolutions (missing evidence on B pages 4, 6, 7), provides zero mathematical or implementation details for the seven "Search Branch" baselines in Table 1 (B pages 7–8), includes figures depicting box embeddings and asymmetric losses that its own captions admit are not actually used by the method (B pages 2, 3, 5), reports implausible ablation collapses (e.g., Micro-F1 dropping from 0.6791 to 0.0035 with 1 checkpoint and 0.0034 at 336 resolution, B page 8 Table 2) without explaining why dynamic threshold calibration failed to prevent near-zero predictions, and relies on misattributed or fabricated citations as factual support (e.g., citing a 2025 research-ethics statement as [Mun, 2025] for museum digitization and knowledge distillation on B pages 1 and 9, and Dietterich et al. 1997 on axis-parallel rectangles for multi-resolution neural ensembling on B page 6). Consequently, despite some over-parameterized components in A whose roles are simplified by its own ablations, A is far more rigorous, novel, surprising in its t=T assembly, and empirically substantiated than B.

A’s building blocks are guidance-direction finite differences, inter-seed spatial Query-Gram repulsion, a fidelity penalty, and spherical Langevin updates (A pages 4–5). Most are recognizable sharpness regularization, attention guidance, or manifold sampling. Its least placeable block is the specific mapping from initial-noise Query-Gram dissimilarity to eventual compositional diversity: I can locate that only broadly in attention-based diffusion control and feature-space repulsion literature, not a particular prior formulation. B’s blocks—an MLP trained with binary cross-entropy, validation-grid threshold selection, and multi-resolution checkpoint averaging—are standard constructions (B pages 5–6). Even its omission-compensating threshold shift is closely connected to established F1-threshold optimization, specifically Lipton and colleagues’ “Thresholding Classifiers to Maximize F1 Score,” and to positive-unlabeled learning. A’s stronger originality therefore rests on a specific representation-to-layout mapping, not simply on assembling four familiar components. For A’s task, the obvious approach is weaker classifier-free guidance or diversity-promoting intervention during denoising; for B’s task, it is a multi-label classifier with omission-aware training and tuned prediction thresholds. A’s central move is instead to separate prospective layouts jointly before denoising, while constraining seed norms. Existing initialization optimization, including InitNO, limits how surprising the initialization stage itself is (A page 3), but the batch-layout objective remains a meaningful departure. B’s rejection of explicit hierarchical geometry could constitute an informative negative result, yet its destination—MLP, threshold tuning, and ensembling—is a familiar practical classification recipe. Its search-branch comparisons do not establish a general failure of geometric approaches (B pages 7–8). Both manuscripts specify actionable mechanisms, but their supported payoffs need narrowing. A reports Vendi increasing from 2.485 to 2.633 while ImageReward decreases from 0.107 to −0.039, demonstrating a diversity–quality tradeoff rather than unconditional fidelity preservation (A page 6). Its component and geometry ablations support useful repulsion and norm restoration, while showing that simple rescaling closely matches tangent dynamics and that the default fidelity hinge is inactive (A pages 9–10 and 16). Important repairs remain: the norm of a Jacobian-vector product is not the Rayleigh quotient asserted in its derivation (A page 14), and the approximately 3% runtime claim conflicts with the 63.7% overhead reported in its deployment table (A pages 10 and 15). B reports 0.6791 Micro-F1 against its strongest search branch’s 0.6115, but threshold optimization against incomplete validation targets does not itself demonstrate recovery of missing true attributes or hierarchical consistency. Its near-zero single-model and single-resolution results also lack reported per-ablation threshold recalibration, leaving the claimed necessity of ensembling insufficiently isolated (B pages 6–9). Overall, A provides a more distinctive and partially tested diversity-control mechanism despite substantial theoretical and efficiency overclaims. B establishes a reported score for a conventional prediction pipeline more convincingly than it establishes its claimed mechanism for asymmetric missing-label recovery. That distinction supports A’s overall creative advantage.

Under New, each paper's individual components mostly come from known literature. In A, logit adjustment comes from Menon et al. (2020) (A page 3, 5), taxonomic tree-level overlap is standard in hierarchical classification (A page 4), and multi-layer feature prototypes are standard in metric learning (A page 5); A's least placeable building block is the specific multiplicative pairwise margin formulation M_{y,j} = tau * V_{y,j} * (1 - T_{y,j}) that scales visual prototype similarity by taxonomic dissimilarity (A page 5), which is placeable to the subfield literature of hierarchy- and confusion-aware margin losses in fine-grained recognition. In B, affine nullspace elimination y = y_p + Vw (B page 3), Douglas-Rachford (DR) operator splitting with implicit differentiation (B pages 3-4, following Pi-net and OSQP), and row equilibration are established in numerical optimization and constrained learning; B's least placeable block is the Diffeomorphic Log-Barrier Feasibility Flow (DLFF) step w - grad(phi_B)/(1 + eta * ||grad(phi_B)||_2) used as a smooth post-processing layer for truncated splitting iterates (B page 4, 10), which is placeable to the subfield of barrier and interior-point feasibility restoration. Under Surprising, for A's task of long-tailed fine-grained species classification on iNaturalist 2019, the obvious approach is frequency-based logit adjustment or class re-weighting paired with a taxonomic hierarchy loss. A departs from this by dropping frequency from the margin and instead penalizing visually similar but taxonomically distant classes while applying a softer penalty to close taxonomic neighbors in the same genus (A page 5), and by candidly reporting that its proposed margin contributes almost nothing compared to basic data augmentation (A pages 7-8). For B's task of accelerating and stabilizing hard-constrained neural networks (HCNNs), the obvious approach is to accelerate the lifted-space factorizations or use sophisticated deflated/recycled Krylov solvers for the ill-conditioned implicit backward pass. B makes a much stronger central departure: by projecting the problem into the equality nullspace R^{d - n_eq} and applying a simple unit-norm row scaling to the reduced inequality matrix C_r = C V (B pages 3-4), B reveals that even though the normal matrix condition number kappa(C_r C_r^T) barely changes (4.98e5 to 4.78e5), the lifted DR operator condition number collapses from 12.99 to 2.13 (B page 3, page 6 Table 2b). Consequently, complex deflated-Krylov (DKSR) and residual-correction backward machinery become unnecessary—plain matrix-free BiCGSTAB matches dense LU to 2.4e-10 relative L2 error in 4.9ms (B page 4, pages 6-7 Figure 4)—and models trained with a small iteration budget (K_train = 20) generalize flatly to deep test-time budgets (K_test = 200) (B pages 6-7 Figure 5). Under Useful, the tradeoff between the two papers heavily favors B. In A, although the offline prototype and taxonomic margin pipeline is clearly specified (A pages 4-6), the mechanism is fundamentally mismatched to its stated long-tailed goal: because both V_{y,j} and T_{y,j} are symmetric, the margin M_{y,j} = M_{j,y} is symmetric and completely ignores class frequency, so it cannot asymmetrically shift decision boundaries to protect rare tail species from common head species as claimed (A page 2, page 8 Figure 3). Empirically, A's ablation study (A pages 7-8 Table 2) shows that removing the entire logit adjustment degrades Top-1 error by just 0.0018 (0.2445 vs. 0.2463), which is smaller than removing standard label smoothing (+0.0032) and an order of magnitude smaller than removing standard data augmentation (+0.0242), and A omits any baseline comparison to standard frequency-based logit adjustment (A page 9). B is not without minor flaws requiring repair: its title highlights an 'Amortized' Stiefel hypernetwork that actually fails in Ablation 1 (0% feasibility and 0.38 violation in Table 2a, B page 6, forcing reliance on exact SVD/QR nullspace bases, B pages 3, 8), and the DLFF log-barrier formula phi_B(w) = -sum log(u_tilde_{r,i} - [C_tilde_r w]_i) (Equation 6, B page 4; Theorem 3, B page 10) is strictly defined only on the interior where slacks are positive, leaving unstated how negative (violated) slacks from truncated iterates w_K are clamped or reflected before evaluating the barrier gradient. A narrowly offers stronger overall creative quality: its departure is modest and imperfectly justified, but remains an executable, directly tested hypothesis, whereas B’s more adventurous feasibility-restoration mechanism fails in its advertised operating regime. A’s building blocks are hierarchical label similarity, averaged multilayer visual prototypes, and class-pair logit offsets (A pages 4–5). Logit adjustment is specifically recognizable from Menon et al.’s work; prototypes and hierarchical costs are established classification tools. Its least specifically placeable block is the policy of discounting visual-confusion costs by taxonomic proximity. I can place that only in hierarchy-aware, cost-sensitive fine-grained recognition, not identify an exact antecedent. B builds on nullspace elimination, Douglas–Rachford splitting, row equilibration, log barriers, and Krylov-based implicit differentiation—all recognizable numerical-optimization machinery (B pages 3–4). Its least placeable block is the asserted globally interior-restoring, diffeomorphic barrier update: I can relate it to barrier-based feasibility-restoration literature, but cannot identify an established result supplying that property. Neither manuscript earns novelty merely from assembling familiar components; the specificity of these placements does not establish a decisive novelty gap. For A’s task, the obvious approach is frequency-based rebalancing combined with stronger fine-grained representations. Its central deviation is to distinguish visually confusing but taxonomically distant pairs from close relatives. For B’s task, the obvious approach is affine elimination or projection followed by a sufficiently converged inequality solver and implicit differentiation. Nullspace coordinates are therefore not themselves unexpected; B’s genuinely larger departure is promising smooth, strict feasibility independently of the truncated solver’s convergence (B pages 3–4). The mechanism-and-evidence comparison limits the value of that larger departure. A specifies a computable loss and reports error of 0.2445 versus 0.2463 without adjustment, but provides no uncertainty estimates, and explicitly lacks a standard frequency-adjustment comparison (A pages 7 and 9). Moreover, subtracting a positive margin from competing logits makes those competitors easier to overcome in training, rather than increasing their cross-entropy penalty as claimed (A page 5). This undermines the proposed explanation, although it does not make the evaluated heuristic undefined. The evidence supports, at most, a small task-specific benefit—not the broader decision-boundary claims. B deserves credit for the exact static-matrix nullspace mechanism and reported roughly threefold training speedups (B pages 3 and 5). However, its log barrier is undefined whenever an inequality slack is nonpositive—precisely the infeasible truncated outputs it purports to repair. Even from an interior point, a bounded explicit gradient step does not automatically remain interior or become a diffeomorphism; the argument on B page 10 establishes neither guarantee. The low-budget restoration results on B page 6 therefore require an unstated repair or different mechanism. Its factorization-free exactness is also restricted: changing equality matrices require exact QR or an approximate hypernetwork, whose reported residual is 0.38 with zero feasible instances (B pages 3 and 6). Thus B has a more surprising direction and meaningful reported benefits for its conventional reduced solver, but its defining restoration promise needs fundamental repair. A’s small, uncertain empirical gain and incorrect penalty interpretation prevent a strong endorsement; nevertheless, its distinctive intervention can actually be applied as written. That narrower connection between proposal and supported payoff tips the overall judgment toward A.

Manuscript B can be broken into three building blocks: (1) a taxonomic similarity matrix T_{i,j} counting shared hierarchy levels from kingdom to genus (B page 4), which is standard in hierarchical classification literature (e.g., Wu et al., 2020); (2) offline multi-layer visual feature prototypes with cosine similarity V_{i,j} (B page 5), which is standard in metric and few-shot learning (e.g., Prototypical Networks); and (3) its least placeable block, the pairwise difficulty-aware logit margin M_{y,j} = tau * V_{y,j} * (1 - T_{y,j}) subtracting penalties scaled by visual similarity and taxonomic distance (B page 5), which is placeable in the subfield of dynamic logit adjustment and hierarchical margin losses (extending Menon et al., 2020 and Zhang et al., 2024b). Both papers rely largely on established building blocks with one subfield-level heuristic formulation, though A develops a more intricate mathematical assembly. Under Surprising, the obvious approach to A's task of enforcing hard affine equality and inequality constraints in neural networks is either adding soft penalty/correction terms (as in DC3) or running operator splitting in a full or slack-lifted primal-dual space (as in Pinet) (A pages 1-2). A departs centrally from this expected direction by eliminating equalities via nullspace parameterization, showing that simple row scaling of the reduced inequality matrix collapses the lifted DR operator condition number from 12.99 to 2.13 despite barely changing kappa(C_r C_r^T) (A pages 3, 6), and decoupling test-time iteration depth from training depth via implicit BiCGSTAB and barrier polishing (A pages 4, 6-7). For B's task of long-tailed fine-grained species recognition, the obvious approach is scaling logit margins by static class frequencies (Menon et al., 2020) or penalizing confusion among closely related species within the same taxon (B pages 1-3). B departs in an unexpected conceptual direction by multiplying visual prototype similarity V_{y,j} by the complement of taxonomic similarity (1 - T_{y,j}) to penalize cross-taxon visual lookalikes while softening penalties for close taxonomic relatives (B pages 4-5), and by candidly reporting negative/limiting ablation findings (B pages 7-9). However, under Useful, the tradeoff overwhelmingly favors A. A works out its reduced-space equilibrated DR and matrix-free BiCGSTAB mechanisms and substantiates its payoff across convex and non-convex QP benchmarks up to d=1000 (A pages 4-5, Table 1), five ablations (A pages 5-7, Table 2), SOCPs (A page 10, Table 3), and multi-vehicle motion planning (A page 10), achieving 2.9x-3.2x faster training than Pinet, machine-precision equality satisfaction (10^-14), and gradient accuracy within 2.4e-10 of dense LU in 4.9ms (A pages 5-7). A does have notable limitations: its learned Stiefel hypernetwork fails to maintain feasibility in Ablation 1 (0% feasible, 0.38 violation on A page 6, Table 2a), restricting exact equality enforcement to static M via offline SVD or batched QR (A pages 3, 8), and DLFF's log-barrier potential log(u_r - C_r w) in Equation 6 and Theorem 3 (A pages 4, 10) is mathematically undefined if a truncated iterate w_K lies strictly outside the inequality polytope (where u_{r,i} - [C_r w_K]_i <= 0), meaning it can only push interior points further inward rather than map arbitrary exterior points into the interior as claimed. Even accounting for these flaws in A's secondary components, A's core reduced-space equilibrated splitting and implicit differentiation pipeline works and delivers large, verified gains. Conversely, B's central proposal scarcely works relative to its claimed payoff: in B's own ablation study (B page 7, Table 2), removing the entire logit adjustment mechanism degrades Top-1 error by just 0.0018 (0.2445 vs. 0.2463), an order of magnitude smaller than standard data augmentation (+0.0242). Furthermore, B leaves three baseline rows blank in Table 1 (B page 7), omits any comparison to standard frequency-based logit adjustment (explicitly admitted on B page 9), never incorporates class frequency into its long-tailed margin formula (B page 5, Equation 3), and assigns zero margin penalty (1 - T_{y,j} = 0) whenever two species share a genus. Thus, A's substantive algorithmic mechanisms and well-supported empirical payoffs outweigh B's minimally effective heuristic.

A’s least-placeable block is the claim that evaluation-only pauses themselves alter grokking (A page 3): I cannot name a specific antecedent beyond the grokking/training-schedule literature. The surrounding experimental paradigm is readily located in Power et al.’s Grokking. B’s least-placeable block is its success-conditioned mirrored-sampling rule (B page 5), which I can locate only within adaptive evolution-strategy sampling, not a particular prior paper. Its classical optimizer is readily located in Hansen’s CMA-ES tutorial, while residual adaptation and identity ablations are familiar mechanisms. Thus neither manuscript earns novelty merely from assembling established components, and A’s unfamiliar hypothesis deserves consideration independently of whether it works. For A’s task, the obvious approach would be to vary optimization or regularization and compare generalization at matched training-update counts; replacing updates with extended evaluation is a genuinely unexpected central hypothesis. For B’s attribution task, the obvious approach would be matched comparisons with the learned modules removed. B develops that expected direction further by designing an exactly recoverable identity control and demonstrating that an apparent transfer success becomes a scaffolding-dominated, metric-dependent result. Its central departure is not simply another learned optimizer: learning improves early progress while worsening the eventual solution (B pages 6–9). The decisive difference is how these directions become usable scientific contributions. A specifies 200 training steps followed by 100 evaluation steps without weight updates (A page 3), but supplies no mechanism by which the pause changes learning. Under ordinary evaluation semantics, holding the optimizer schedule, other training state, and training randomness fixed leaves the parameter trajectory unchanged as a function of update count. Effects through altered schedules or state would require identification and controls that A does not provide. A page 4 asserts significant improvements and ablation results, but the extracted text supplies no numerical baseline comparisons, confidence intervals, or p-values; the figure captions on A pages 4–5 cannot establish those results. B instead works out gates that equal one at initialization and can be pinned to one throughout execution, recovering the same separable-CMA-ES core and fixed sampling machinery (B pages 4–5). That makes its main attribution comparison operational rather than rhetorical. The reported full score is 1.191 versus 1.107 for the identity control, with a paired learned increment of 0.083 across all eight evaluation seeds; nevertheless, the identity control finishes 220.7 return higher on average (B pages 6–9). These results support a specific payoff: distinguishing inherited optimizer performance from a conditional learned improvement. They do not establish broad transfer superiority. Configuration selection reused the evaluation seeds, there was only one meta-training run per configuration, several secondary ablations involve different learned weights, and the endpoint reversal lacks paired seed-level evidence (B pages 7 and 10). Those limitations narrow B’s conclusions without disabling its central identity-control comparison. Overall, B turns familiar ingredients into a consequential, testable reinterpretation of performance, whereas A’s unusual intervention remains causally unexplained and empirically unsupported in the supplied evidence.

Regarding Surprising, for B's task of modeling 2D toy distributions with diffusion models, the obvious approach is mapping the 2D coordinates through trigonometric sinusoidal or Fourier encodings before an MLP denoiser; B barely departs from this expected direction, simply concatenating the two standard encodings (B page 2). (2022), parameter efficiency, and an ablation study (B pages 2, 4) while reporting only single-method numbers in Table 1 with zero baseline or ablation evidence in the extracted text (B pages 3–5). Conversely, A's central mechanism—scoring query tokens against chunk tokens via average maximum cosine similarity in the frozen encoder to select the dominant chunk adapter, placing the adapter atom on the relevance peak, and aligning chunk cuts to generator delimiters (A pages 3–4)—is thoroughly worked out and validated across 30 valid trained configurations spanning 128 to 65,536 tokens under a controlled three-hour single-GPU budget (A pages 4–8). Regarding direction and departure from expectation, for A's task of fast deterministic tabular reordering for prefix caching, the obvious approach is sorting columns by low cardinality and rows lexicographically, weighting column priority by string length so longer repetitive cells come first; A departs minimally from this expected path, simply inserting mean squared string length into the numerator of GGR's cardinality heuristic and abandoning its initially planned dynamic per-row ordering in favor of a single static sort_values call (A page 2, page 4-5, page 8). For B's task of meta-evolving an evolution strategy on cheap low-dimensional functions to transfer to a high-dimensional control task, the obvious approach is parameterizing the update rule with a neural network, meta-training it, and reporting its win margin over an external baseline; B departs fundamentally and centrally from this expected direction. B’s stronger overall contribution is an experimentally supported attribution mechanism, rather than simply a better reported optimizer score. A’s building blocks are length/repetition-based column priority, lexicographic row grouping, and a runtime-adjusted prefix metric. Its least placeable block is the precise mean-squared-length/unique-ratio priority (A pages 4–5): I can place its rationale in database layout and compression heuristics, but cannot name an earlier work containing that exact rule. B builds on recognizable separable CMA-ES updates, equivariant networks, residual modulation, and antithetic sampling. Its least placeable individual rule is the success-rate-dependent mirroring probability (B page 5), which I can place only broadly in mirrored-sampling evolution-strategy research, not a specific matching prior formulation. Thus both contain custom mechanisms, but neither deserves novelty credit merely for assembling established components. A provides an actionable, inexpensive algorithm: prioritize long repetitive columns, then sort rows to group their prefixes. Its reported 0.6984 combined score versus GGR’s 0.692, approximately 0.95-second runtime, and static-versus-dynamic ablations support a modest payoff on its layout benchmark (A pages 6 and 8). The claimed serving payoff is less established. Character-prefix overlap is not itself a measurement of token-level cache reuse or latency, and matching prefixes of adjacent rows inside one concatenated table does not suffice for ordinary causal KV reuse because their preceding contexts differ. A does not clearly establish the separate, identically contextualized row-prompt workload needed to resolve this issue, nor demonstrate end-to-end serving savings (A pages 3–6). Its treatment of AdaEvolve’s result as both raw PHR and a comparable score also weakens the claimed efficiency tradeoff. B’s bounded multiplicative gates are worked out sufficiently to make an exact intervention possible: forcing every gate to one removes learned modulation while preserving the implementation’s fixed machinery (B pages 4–5). That control scores 1.107 against the full method’s 1.191, with a reported paired learned increment of 0.083 across all eight evaluation seeds; importantly, the control finishes 220.7 return higher despite losing on anytime performance (B pages 6–9). This directly supports B’s narrower payoff: distinguishing learned acceleration from inherited algorithmic performance. Generalization remains limited by one transfer environment, one meta-training run per configuration, development-time reuse of evaluation seeds, and retraining-confounded secondary ablations (B page 10). Those limitations do not invalidate the central identity-gate comparison, whose weights cannot affect its updates. For A’s task, the obvious approach is low-cardinality prefix grouping; for B’s attribution task, it is to disable learning and compare with the classical backbone. A develops the expected direction through length weighting and finds that static ordering beats more elaborate alternatives. B goes beyond a conventional one-number ablation by making the classical behavior exactly recoverable and showing that the apparent benefit changes with budget and reverses between anytime progress and final quality. That reversal is central, not incidental. Although A offers a useful lightweight heuristic and B does not establish a generally superior optimizer, B’s recoverable control and supported reinterpretation of transfer performance constitute the more consequential creative departure.

For New, we break each manuscript into its constituent building blocks rather than judging their assembly. Manuscript A relies on: (1) chunked context-to-LoRA hypernetwork generation and rank-axis adapter concatenation (A pages 1–3), which is standard material in hypernetwork and adapter-composition works such as HINT (Ivison et al., 2023) and LoRAHub (Huang et al., 2023); (2) token-level maximum cosine similarity (MaxSim) late-interaction scoring (A pages 2–4), which comes directly from a specific named formulation, ColBERT/ColBERTv2 (Khattab et al., 2021; Santhanam et al., 2022b); (3) negative-control architectural read-out modifications and auxiliary margin/binding losses (A page 4), which are standard across representation learning; and (4) relevance-profile peak windowing ('atom placement') with delimiter-aligned chunk cuts to center the adapter-generating span on the highest-scoring token window (A page 4). A's least placeable building block is this relevance-profile atom placement for adapter span extraction, which cannot be pinned to a single prior hypernetwork paper and is placeable only at the broader subfield level of passage-granularity dense retrieval and context pruning (e.g., the dense-retrieval span selection literature surveyed on A page 3). Manuscript B relies on: (1) a three-stage hierarchical placement pipeline of node-level packing, intra-node replication, and GPU-level packing (B pages 3–4), which appears in hierarchical MoE placement works such as Yao et al. (2024) and the distributed MoE serving literature; (2) 'snake-like' (boustrophedon) assignment on sorted weights (B pages 4–5), which is standard textbook material in combinatorial partitioning and zig-zag scheduling heuristics; (3) parallel D'Hondt apportionment via a dense weight-over-divisor quotient matrix and top-k selection with an epsilon tie-breaker (B page 5); and (4) asynchronous step-(t-1)-to-(t+1) placement calculation (B pages 5–6), which is standard in overlapping MoE scheduling systems. B's least placeable building block is the tensorized quotient-matrix formulation of D'Hondt proportional apportionment for GPU slot replication, which as a mathematical mechanism is standard material in the proportional apportionment and resource-allocation literature (specifically Jefferson/D'Hondt divisor methods) implemented via standard tensor broadcasting. Thus, both papers build primarily on identifiable primitives from existing subfields and named works, with A's span-level atom placement for weight generation and B's tensorized D'Hondt matrix both sitting at the level of subfield adaptations of known mechanisms. For Surprising, for A's task of fixing multi-needle retrieval failures in long-context hypernetwork-generated LoRA adapters, the obvious approach a competent researcher would take is to increase the hypernetwork's read-out/head capacity to encode multiple key-value bindings or add auxiliary training losses that penalize distractor interference; for B's task of fast topology-aware MoE expert load balancing, the obvious approach is to apply iterative greedy heuristics (such as sequential Longest Processing Time bin-packing and step-by-step replica assignment) or a linear program over the node/GPU hierarchy. Both papers depart centrally from these expected directions, but in different ways. B departs from sequential heuristics by reformulating iterative proportional slot allocation and bin-packing into loop-free tensor operations using electoral D'Hondt apportionment and boustrophedon index scattering (B pages 2, 4–5). A makes an even sharper conceptual departure: instead of merely proposing a better module, A turns the two obvious directions (head redesign and auxiliary binding supervision) into systematic negative controls, proves empirically that both fail to breach a 0.52 superposition ceiling (A pages 2, 4, 6), and reframes weight-space context internalization at long context as an inference-time routing problem solved by repurposing a frozen encoder's ColBERT-style MaxSim score at adapter merge time with zero new parameters and no retraining (A pages 3–4). The decisive separation between the two manuscripts emerges under Useful, where A's mechanism is thoroughly worked out and achieves its claimed payoff, while B is in need of repair due to unsupported payoffs and internal contradictions. A's central proposal is to replace query-blind rank concatenation of per-chunk LoRA adapters with a parameter-free, merge-time MaxSim router in the frozen encoder's representation space, supported by relevance-profile atom placement and delimiter-aligned chunking (A page 4). Under a controlled 30-model comparison across 128 to 65,536 tokens on a fixed three-hour GPU budget, A demonstrates that while head redesigns plateau at 0.32, auxiliary losses at 0.46, and the strongest query-blind merge at 0.52, adding merge-time MaxSim selection alone lifts exact-match accuracy to 0.91, and adding the two chunk-level components reaches 0.98 (A pages 5–7, Table 1, Figures 2–4), while transparently accounting for run-to-run training collapse variance (A pages 4, 7–8). In contrast, B's central proposal—using O(1) boustrophedon scatter and parallel D'Hondt quotient-matrix ops to achieve competitive MoE load balancing within a microsecond-level (<2ms) latency budget (B pages 1–3)—fails on its own primary evaluation metric. In Table 1 (B page 6), B's proposed method achieves a Combined Score of just 0.1287, which is more than two orders of magnitude worse than the simplest topology-agnostic baseline, Standard EP (Round-robin), which scores 19.0 and is explicitly described as 'establishing the performance floor' (B page 6), as well as AdaEvolve (22.06) and MicroMoE (100.0). Furthermore, B repeatedly claims to satisfy 'strict microsecond-level latency budgets (e.g., < 2ms)' (B pages 1, 3, 8), yet reports an actual execution time of 3.05ms (3,057 microseconds), missing the 2ms budget and incurring a near-zero speed score of 0.006773 (B page 7). B also contains a direct methodological contradiction: Section 3.4 presents asynchronous step-(t-1)-to-(t+1) execution as part of its implemented system that 'completely hide[s] the solver latency' (B pages 3, 5–6), whereas Section 5 admits that asynchronous execution is unimplemented future work that 'Future research should explore... to completely hide the residual algorithmic latency' (B page 8). Even within B's ablation table, the designated 'Final solution (best)' (0.1287) is outperformed by its own anti-affinity redundancy variant (0.1461) (B page 7, Table 2). Weighing the tradeoffs across all three criteria, although B offers an interesting mathematical mapping between electoral D'Hondt apportionment and tensorized GPU replica allocation, its mechanism fails to beat the most basic round-robin baseline, misses its stated latency requirement, and suffers from internal inconsistencies regarding asynchronous execution. Manuscript A pairs an unexpected diagnostic reframing and cross-domain mechanism transfer with rigorous negative controls and a fully supported empirical payoff (from 0.52 to 0.98 exact match with no added parameters), giving A far stronger overall creative quality.

Its experiments make that change of intervention point consequential. The supported payoff separates the papers more strongly. Its measured 3.05 ms exceeds its stated 2 ms target, and its reported combined score is below even round-robin; because baseline scores are described as theoretically converted and comparative timings are missing, these results establish neither a convincing speed advantage nor a useful balance–latency tradeoff (A pages 6–7). Important limitations remain: single-run configuration comparisons, training collapses, pooled results, synthetic templated facts, and unquantified routing/storage costs restrict reproducibility and deployment claims (B pages 4–8). Moreover, unsuccessful alternatives do not prove that query-blind composition has a fundamental ceiling: the decoder still receives the query. That demonstrated payoff, coupled with the meaningful shift from learning better memories to selecting their weight-space expression, outweighs A’s clever apportionment transfer.

Thus the specificity of identifiable prior material does not by itself decisively separate them. The obvious approach for A’s task would be to improve binding capacity or supervision while retaining a reusable, query-independent adapter; for B’s task, it would be to score markdown against ordered code anchors and predict relative positions. Page 6 allows multiple markdown cells per gap while invoking ordinary linear sum assignment, whereas page 8 asserts strict one-to-one matching. Moreover, the continuous expectations and row-wise argmax described on page 6 do not themselves enforce global assignment constraints, and ordering multiple markdown cells within one gap remains unresolved. Consequently, the reported performance can support useful local alignment without validating the advertised global-resolution explanation. A’s bounded but intelligible intervention therefore offers the stronger overall creative contribution: an unexpected central reframing with directly relevant empirical support, rather than a familiar structural formulation whose claimed mechanism conflicts with its implementation description.

(2020) (B page 3, page 5); quantifying taxonomic similarity as the normalized count of shared hierarchy levels from kingdom to genus (B page 4, Eq. 1) is a standard tree-similarity formulation in hierarchical classification (e.g., Wu et al., 2020, B page 1); averaging L2-normalized features across layers to form class prototypes and cosine similarity matrices (B page 5, Eq. 2) is standard in prototypical networks and multi-layer feature fusion; and scaling logit margins by pairwise confusion or class difficulty (B page 5, Eq. 3) appears in the dynamic logit adjustment literature (e.g., Zhang et al., 2024b; Low et al., 2025, B page 1, page 3). In A, the core blocks also come from named works: context-to-LoRA hypernetwork generation and rank-axis adapter concatenation (A page 1, page 3) follow hypernetwork instruction tuning (HINT, Ivison et al., 2023) and adapter merging (Huang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023), while token-level maximum cosine similarity (MaxSim) scoring (A page 2, page 4) comes directly from ColBERT (Khattab et al., 2021; Santhanam et al., 2022b). However, A's supporting block—relevance-profile 'atom' placement, which shifts the internal span representation from which the hypernetwork constructs a chunk's weight adapter onto a token-level relevance peak alongside generator-delimiter-aligned cuts (A page 4, page 6)—cannot be pinned to a single named equation and is placeable only at the broader subfield level of span-based dense retrieval and hypernetwork representation pooling. Regarding Surprising, the obvious approach to A's task (resolving multi-fact retrieval failures in chunked context-to-LoRA hypernetworks) is to increase the hypernetwork's read-out/output head capacity or add auxiliary training losses that supervise key-value binding and penalize distractor interference (A page 2, page 3); the obvious approach to B's task (long-tailed fine-grained species classification without foundation-model leakage) is to modify class-frequency logit adjustment margins using taxonomic tree distances or empirical class confusion priors (B page 1, page 3). B stays close to this expected path, assembling taxonomic distance and offline visual prototype cosine similarity into a multiplicative logit margin $M_{y,j} = \tau \cdot V_{y,j} \cdot (1 - T_{y,j})$ (B page 5, Eq. 3), with only the modest conceptual twist of penalizing visually similar but taxonomically distant species more heavily than within-genus neighbors. In contrast, A makes a sharp, central departure: it first proves that the obvious architectural and training-loss approaches fail because query-blind adapter merging superposes co-resident facts in weight space (A page 2, page 6, page 7), and then repurposes ColBERT-style token-level late interaction from document retrieval as a parameter-free, inference-time router inside a frozen encoder's representation space to select which generated weight adapter dominates composition (A page 3, page 4). Regarding Useful, A's central mechanism is thoroughly validated with a decisive empirical payoff, whereas B's central mechanism yields an almost negligible payoff and suffers from structural gaps. A tests 30 valid trained models across four mechanism families under a strict three-hour single-GPU budget and fixed ~2B base model (A page 4, page 5). Using two falsifiable negative-control families, A shows that head redesigns plateau at 0.32 exact match, auxiliary binding/selection losses plateau at 0.46, and the strongest query-blind merge (incorporating redundancy weighting, competitive gating, and magnitude priors) hits a hard ceiling of 0.52 (A page 3, page 6, Table 1). Introducing query-conditioned MaxSim routing at merge time alone lifts accuracy from 0.52 to 0.91, relevance-profile atom placement raises it to 0.93, and delimiter-aligned chunking reaches 0.98 across context lengths from 128 to 65,536 tokens without adding parameters or retraining (A page 6, page 7, Figure 3). In B, although the equations and offline-online training algorithm are clearly specified (B page 4–6, Eq. 1–4, Algorithm 1) and evaluated on a realistic 1,010-species benchmark (iNaturalist 2019, B page 6), the ablation study reveals that removing the entire proposed logit adjustment degrades Top-1 Error by only 0.0018 (from 0.2445 to 0.2463), whereas standard data augmentation accounts for 0.0242 (B page 7, page 8, Table 2). Furthermore, as B candidly acknowledges (B page 9), it omits a baseline comparison against standard frequency-based logit adjustment (Menon et al., 2020), leaving unproven whether its taxonomic-visual margin beats static frequency scaling. Worse, B's margin $M_{y,j}$ is extracted offline before fine-tuning (B page 5, page 6) and is completely symmetric between classes ($V_{y,j} = V_{j,y}$ and $T_{y,j} = T_{j,y}$) with no class-frequency term, contradicting the central claim that it asymmetrically shifts decision boundaries to prevent common head species from cannibalizing rare tail species (B page 2, Figure 1; page 8, Figure 3). Weighing the tradeoffs, B deserves credit for evaluating on a large-scale real-world ecological dataset, providing explicit mathematical equations, and transparently reporting its near-zero ablation delta and missing baseline (B page 5, page 7–9), whereas A relies on a single synthetic multi-needle benchmark, assumes single-fact queries, and describes its sub-mechanisms (such as atom placement and negative-control heads) in prose without formal equations (A page 4, page 8). Nevertheless, A's creative diagnosis of weight-space superposition, its unexpected cross-domain synthesis of token-level late interaction as a zero-parameter merge-time weight router, and its rigorous, falsifiable empirical payoff (lifting accuracy from 0.52 to 0.98) far outweigh B's incremental and empirically marginal heuristic.

Preferred: Addressing Beats Architecture: Query-Conditioned Merge-Time Selection for Context-to-LoRA Hypernetworks on Multi-Needle Retrieval

A offers the stronger overall creative contribution: a useful change in where retrieval happens, supported by component-level evidence, rather than principally a new adjustment rule whose intended effect remains doubtful. A’s building blocks are hypernetwork-generated LoRA, adapter composition, ColBERT-style MaxSim, and relevance-preserving chunking (A pages 3–4). B’s are taxonomic similarity, multi-layer class prototypes, cosine similarity, and pairwise logit adjustment (B pages 4–5), with frequency-based adjustment specifically identifiable in Menon et al.’s Long-tail Learning via Logit Adjustment. For New, A’s least-placeable substantive block is its diagnosis that query-blind composition, rather than generation capacity, creates the binding bottleneck; I can place that only broadly in neural-binding and content-addressable-memory literature. B’s least-placeable block is the particular visual-similarity times taxonomic-distance margin, which I can place only broadly in hierarchy-aware cost-sensitive classification, not an exact prior formulation. Both therefore contain a subfield-placeable claim or rule beyond their readily recognizable primitives; merely assembling those primitives is not itself evidence of newness. For A’s task, the obvious approach would be to improve adapter capacity or binding supervision, or retrieve relevant text into the prompt. Its central departure is instead to use query–chunk matching to select already-generated weight updates at composition time. This is recognizably retrieval-inspired, but changes the locus of intervention rather than just improving the expected machinery. For B’s task, the obvious approach would be frequency rebalancing and stronger fine-grained representations. Adding taxonomic relationships and visual prototypes to class margins departs from frequency-only adjustment, but remains a relatively natural direction for biological classification. B’s finding that ordinary augmentation matters much more than its proposed adjustment is informative, though it does not establish a comparably unexpected mechanism. On usefulness, A describes an actionable frozen-encoder MaxSim router and reports a particularly relevant ablation: selection alone raises exact match from 0.52 to 0.91, with relevance placement and boundary alignment reaching 0.98 (A page 6). That directly supports selection as a productive intervention in its stated task. However, single evaluations per configuration, training collapses, and the synthetic single-fact setting limit confidence and generalization (A pages 4, 7–8). The failed architecture and loss variants also do not prove that query-blind composition inherently prevents query-conditioned decoding. B supplies explicit equations and real classification results, but its own ablation changes error only from 0.2463 without adjustment to 0.2445 with it, without reported uncertainty, and it lacks the standard frequency-adjustment comparison (B pages 7–9). More fundamentally, as written, subtracting a positive margin from non-target logits makes those competitors easier to defeat in the training loss, rather than imposing stronger separation against the supposedly troublesome confusions; this direction appears in both the equations and algorithm (B pages 5–6). Thus B’s central explanatory mechanism needs repair despite the functioning classifier. A’s bounded but substantial mechanistic payoff outweighs its incomplete causal claims and narrow scope, making its relocation of retrieval the more convincing creative advance.

Regarding Surprising, for Paper A's task of long-tailed fine-grained species recognition without foundation-model leakage, the obvious approach is to combine class-frequency re-balancing or logit adjustment with a taxonomic hierarchy prior or visual confusion penalty; A stays closely aligned with this expected direction by fusing taxonomic and prototype similarities into a logit margin (A page 2, page 5), departing mainly in its honest admission that the margin barely helps compared to basic augmentation (A page 7, page 8). In contrast, for Paper B's task of resolving multi-fact retrieval failures in context-to-LoRA hypernetworks, the obvious approach is to increase the hypernetwork's read-out/output head capacity or add auxiliary training losses that supervise key-value binding; B explicitly implements these expected directions as formal negative controls to prove they fail due to weight-space superposition (B page 2, page 3-6), and makes a central, unexpected departure by reframing long-context weight internalization as a merge-time routing problem, importing ColBERT-style token-level late interaction into hypernetwork adapter composition (B page 2-4, page 9). Regarding Useful, Paper A's mechanism pre-computes offline 30-image multi-layer prototypes and taxonomic overlap to adjust non-target logits during training (A page 4-6), clearing a 0.2445 Top-1 error threshold on iNaturalist 2019 (A page 7). Both manuscripts use recognizable ingredients, but B turns them into a more consequential, experimentally supported change of direction. A comprises hierarchical taxonomic similarity, averaged multi-layer visual prototypes, cosine similarity, and class-pair logit adjustments (A pages 4–5). Frequency-based adjustment is specifically placeable in Menon et al.’s Long-tail learning via logit adjustment; A’s least placeable block is its policy of prioritizing visually similar but taxonomically distant confusions. I can locate that only broadly in hierarchy-aware cost-sensitive recognition, not an exact prior formulation. B comprises hypernetwork-generated adapters, low-rank composition, token-level retrieval, and relevance-aligned segmentation (B pages 3–4). Its MaxSim operation is specifically recognizable from ColBERT. Its least placeable block is the diagnostic claim that adapter composition, rather than binding capacity, is the operative bottleneck; I can associate this with adapter-interference and conditional-routing research, but cannot name an earlier demonstration of that particular claim. Neither manuscript deserves novelty credit merely for assembling familiar components. For A’s task, the obvious approach is frequency rebalancing alongside better fine-grained representations or hierarchy-aware learning; for B’s task, it is improving the adapter generator’s binding capacity or supervision, with query-based text retrieval an established alternative. A’s emphasis on taxonomically distant lookalikes departs somewhat from the usual focus on closely related species, but remains a classifier-cost modification. B makes the more substantial central redirection: use the query to decide which generated parameters enter the model, rather than improve a single query-blind memory or retrieve text into the prompt. Query-aware selection itself is familiar; relocating the retrieval decision to adapter composition is the meaningful surprise. The demonstrated mechanisms favor that redirection. A provides real-species evaluation, but its core adjustment improves error only from 0.2463 to 0.2445, while augmentation accounts for a substantially larger difference (A page 7), and the standard frequency-adjustment comparison is missing (A page 9). More importantly, the stated mechanism needs repair: subtracting a positive margin from non-target logits makes those competitors easier to defeat in cross-entropy, rather than imposing the claimed stronger penalty for confusing them. This operation appears in both the equations and algorithm, not merely an ambiguous figure (A pages 5–6). B specifies a workable frozen-encoder MaxSim router and reports a directly relevant intervention: query-conditioned selection alone raises exact match from 0.52 to 0.91, with relevance placement and aligned boundaries reaching 0.98 (B pages 4 and 6). Its negative controls make the selection explanation substantially better supported than A’s claimed margin mechanism. Nevertheless, B’s synthetic single-fact retrieval setting, best-configuration reporting, and training collapses limit reliability and generalization (B pages 4, 7–8). Nor do unsuccessful head and loss variants establish an intrinsic query-blind ceiling: the downstream decoder still receives the query and could, in principle, recover preserved bindings. These qualifications narrow B’s conclusion to the tested substrate. Within that scope, however, its central departure has a much clearer supported payoff, outweighing its familiar primitives and narrower application evidence.
