Evaluated relative to their respective fields—meta-black-box evolutionary optimization for Paper A and spectral-manifold optimization for large language model (LLM) pretraining for Paper B—Paper A demonstrates substantially stronger overall creative quality when considering New, Useful, and Surprising jointly. For Surprising, the obvious approach to Paper A's task of evaluating a meta-learned evolution strategy on continuous control is to meta-train a neural update rule on cheap analytic functions, deploy it on a target control benchmark, and report the headline margin over an external classical baseline; the obvious approach to Paper B's task of improving spectral-sphere LLM optimizers is to combine Riemannian tangent projection, a spectral regularizer for secondary singular values, and a reduced-order approximation for the inner-loop Lagrange multiplier solver. Paper A makes a central, expectation-defying departure from its field's standard practice: instead of claiming a transfer victory from its 1.191 normalized anytime score over a pinned CMA-ES reference (1.000) on a 704-dimensional Brax Ant policy (A pages 1, 6), it architectures the optimizer so every learned output is a zero-initialized bounded multiplicative gate on separable CMA-ES, allowing the learned modulation to be switched off exactly ($g \equiv 1$) on the same code path (A pages 1–2, 4). This central move overturns the headline conclusion by showing that 55.8% of the apparent transfer gain comes from the classical anchor and fixed sampling machinery (scoring 1.107), that the learned increment (+0.083 paired) shrinks from 86.5% of the margin at generation 1,000 to 44.2% at generation 2,000, and that on final return the unlearned anchor actually overtakes the learned optimizer at generation 1,216 and finishes 220.7 points higher (3709.2 vs. 3488.5), even though meta-learning genuinely succeeded in-distribution by cutting log regret by 50.8% on training functions (A pages 6–9). Paper B stays much closer to the expected multi-pillar improvement template for manifold optimizers (B pages 1–5), and its most notable assembly move—compressing full-tensor matrix-sign root-finding into a 2D subspace complemented by step-wise spectral retraction (B page 5)—is undermined by mechanical breakdowns. For New, breaking Paper A into its building blocks yields: (1) separable CMA-ES with cumulative step-size adaptation and diagonal covariance updates (A pages 2–5), (2) Deep-Sets permutation-equivariant population encoding and coordinate-shared networks with scale-free features (A page 4), (3) zero-initialized bounded multiplicative residual gates $g(v) = \exp(\ln 2 \cdot \tanh(3v)) \in [1/2, 2]$ for exact classical recovery (A page 4), and (4) success-gated partial mirrored sampling paired with a pair-consistent evolution-path normalization $\mu_{\text{eff}}^{\text{path}} = (\sum_{\text{pairs}}(w_a - w_b)^2 + \sum_{\text{unpaired}} w_i^2)^{-1}$ (A page 5). Paper A's least placeable block is this pair-consistent path normalization under success-gated mirrored recombination weights (or the exact multiplicative gate subtraction formulation for meta-ES), which cannot be placed in a specific named paper from existing knowledge and is placeable only at the level of the subfield literatures on mirrored-sampling evolution strategies (e.g., Hansen's CMA-ES tutorial literature) and meta-black-box optimization (e.g., Lange et al., 2023). Breaking Paper B into its building blocks yields: (1) spectral-sphere constrained optimization $\|W\|_2 = R$ using rank-1 normal $\Theta_t = u_1 v_1^\top$, matrix-sign updates $\text{msign}(G + \lambda \Theta_t)$, and radial retraction (directly from the Spectral Sphere Optimizer of Xie et al. and Muon of Bernstein & Newhouse, B pages 1–3), (2) Euclidean tangent-space projection of momentum $M_{t-1}^\parallel = M_{t-1} - \langle \Theta_t, M_{t-1}\rangle \Theta_t$ (standard in Riemannian optimization literature such as Bonnabel, 2011 and Boumal, 2023, B pages 2–4), (3) the Euclidean gradient of effective rank $r_{\text{eff}}(W) = \|W\|_F^2 / \|W\|_2^2$ on a fixed-spectral-norm sphere (standard quotient-rule derivative in stable-rank regularization literature such as Sanyal et al., 2019, B pages 3–4, 15), and (4) projecting the scalar Lagrange dual equation $\langle \Theta_t, \text{msign}(\hat{M}_t^{\text{iso}} + \lambda \Theta_t)\rangle = 0$ onto a $2\times 2$ Gram-Schmidt subspace (B page 5). Paper B's least placeable block is the $2\times 2$ subspace reduction of the matrix-sign dual root equation, which is placeable only in the subfield literatures of Krylov matrix-function approximation and spectral-sphere optimization. Both papers thus contain a building block placeable only at the subfield level, though Paper B relies more heavily on standard textbook projections and prior SSO equations. For Useful, the difference is decisive. Paper A's central mechanisms are worked out in complete mathematical and algorithmic detail—specifying exact feature transformations, parameter counts (364 total), update equations, and ablations (A pages 4–6, 8–9)—and every claimed payoff follows transparently. For instance, Paper A's ablation of pair-consistent path normalization empirically verifies its theoretical prediction: reverting to textbook $\mu_{\text{eff}}$ while keeping mirrored sampling biases the step-size controller and freezes return at 2527.8 after generation 500, costing 0.294 paired across 8/8 seeds (A pages 5, 8–9). Paper A also candidly audits its own threats to validity, explicitly reporting that separate meta-training runs for ablations landed at different weight norms (20.62 vs. 19.12, 13.50, and 9.90) while proving its central identity-gate control is immune to this confound by construction (A page 10). By contrast, Paper B's three central mechanisms suffer from severe internal contradictions where the claimed payoffs do not follow from its own math and tables: (1) Pillar 3 projects the full-tensor nonlinear $\text{msign}(\hat{M}_t^{\text{iso}} + \lambda \Theta_t)$ onto a $2\times 2$ block $m_2 = Q_U^\top \hat{M}_t^{\text{iso}} Q_V$ whose entries are suppressed by $O(1/\sqrt{d})$ relative to $\|\theta_2\|_2 = 1$, leaving a full-dimensional tangent constraint violation of $R_{\text{full}} = |\langle \Theta_t, \Phi_t^*\rangle| \approx 0.394$ (B pages 5, 16, Table 8)—nearly 40% of the theoretical maximum of $1.0$ for unit spectral and nuclear norms, meaning the 2D solver fails to enforce $\langle \Theta_t, \Phi_t^*\rangle = 0$ and relies entirely on post-hoc radial retraction to prevent drift; (2) Pillar 2 claims existing spectral-sphere optimizers (SSO) suffer from severe rank collapse and that RMTS's $R_{\text{iso}}$ actively expands stable rank (B pages 1–2, 4), yet in Tables 2 and 3 (B page 7) base SSO without $R_{\text{iso}}$ achieves a much higher stable rank ($r_{\text{eff}} = 144.0$ at 10k steps and $135.2$ at 3.06B tokens) than RMTS ($89.4$ and $86.9$), and RMTS's step-2,000 stable rank is reported inconsistently across the paper as 183.7 in Section 4.5 (B page 8), 153.8 in Table 6 (B page 16), and 55.2–58.0 in Section 4.7 (B page 9); and (3) Pillar 1 defines RMTS's transport as exact orthogonal tangent projection with zero normal leakage (B page 4 Eq. 3, page 15 Proposition 1), yet Table 6 (B page 16) reports non-zero leakage (0.0017) for RMTS, lists "Tangential Projection" as a separate baseline with lower leakage (0.0006), and shows both Tangential Projection (3.7583) and Euclidean Accumulation (3.7601) beating RMTS's transport (3.7629) in validation loss, alongside runtime anomalies where RMTS (7,212 s) is reported as faster than MuonSphere (8,377 s) despite doing strictly more per-step work (B page 7, Table 2). Weighing the tradeoffs, Paper B tackles a large-scale LLM pretraining benchmark (up to 3.06B tokens across eight downstream tasks, B pages 6–7) while Paper A evaluates transfer on a single 704-dimensional control task with one meta-training run per configuration (A page 10). However, Paper A's narrow scope is paired with complete mechanical soundness, diagnostic precision, and a genuinely surprising methodological re-framing of meta-learned optimizers, whereas Paper B's broader empirical claims are compromised by mathematical and empirical contradictions across all three of its proposed pillars.

A offers stronger overall creative quality through a modest but effective construction that supports an unexpected attribution result. Its building blocks are separable CMA-ES, identity-initialized neural residuals, permutation-equivariant conditioning, and antithetic-sampling corrections (A pages 4–5). The core and architecture are readily placeable in Ros–Hansen’s separable CMA-ES and Deep Sets. Its least placeable individual mechanism is the success-dependent mirroring rule: I can identify mirrored-sampling evolution-strategy literature as a broad precedent, but not a particular work containing that rule. B comprises projected momentum, a quotient-rule stable-rank gradient, and a reduced dual solver (B pages 3–5). The first two are familiar Riemannian-optimization and matrix-calculus building blocks; its particular 2×2 multiplier surrogate is harder to place than those, with projected matrix-function/Krylov methods the closest literature I can identify, not an exact antecedent. Neither manuscript’s assembly of familiar ingredients alone establishes novelty. For A’s stated attribution task, the obvious approach is a matched learned-versus-unlearned ablation. Its extension is to make that control exact architecturally and use it to reveal that learning’s contribution depends on both budget and performance metric. For B’s efficient spectral-training task, the obvious approach is to improve constrained-update geometry and accelerate matrix-sign calculations. Replacing the full multiplier search with a 2×2 surrogate is a more adventurous algorithmic departure; A’s surprise instead lies in the substantive reversal uncovered by its experiment, not simply its critical framing. A works out the mechanism needed for its central claim: setting every gate to one removes learned influence while retaining the same fixed machinery. The full method scores 1.191 against the control’s 1.107, with a positive paired learned increment on all eight seeds, yet the control achieves higher mean final return (A pages 6–7). This directly answers its attribution question. One environment, selection using the evaluation seeds, one meta-training run, and retraining-confounded secondary ablations constrain generalization; the final-return reversal also lacks paired seed-level evidence (A pages 7 and 10). B provides meaningful timing, component-ablation, and longer-horizon evidence for a practical heuristic, including the reported twofold acceleration over SSO (B pages 7–9). However, its stronger geometric explanation needs repair. Projecting historical momentum does not make the subsequent accumulation tangent when the newly added gradient is unprojected (B page 4). Moreover, the reported full-space constraint residual of approximately 0.394 produces a first-order spectral-norm change under B’s own expansion, contrary to its second-order-drift explanation. Retraction can restore the radius without establishing that the surrogate recovers the tangent-constrained optimum (B pages 3, 5, and 16). Single-seed quality comparisons further limit confidence in its smaller performance margins. These gaps do not erase B’s inventive computational shortcut, but A more successfully converts its design into a supported, counterexpectational scientific conclusion whose scope is identifiable.

B builds from separable CMA-ES, pooled/shared neural modules, identity-initialized multiplicative gates, and modified mirrored sampling (B pages 4–5). Most have recognizable precedents in Hansen’s CMA-ES tutorial, Deep Sets, residual learning, and antithetic sampling. Its least-placeable ingredient is the success-rate-conditioned mirroring rule, which I can locate only in adaptive/mirrored evolution-strategy literature, not a particular work. Thus neither manuscript’s unfamiliar assembly alone establishes novelty, and B’s advantage does not depend on claiming more unprecedented ingredients. The important distinction is how effectively the central mechanisms support their intended payoff. A gives a plausible acceleration mechanism: replace repeated full-matrix sign evaluations with small surrogate solves and one full evaluation. Its reported speedup and component ablations support practical value (A pages 7–8). However, the admitted full-space tangent residual of approximately 0.394 means the surrogate has not recovered the claimed constrained direction. Spectral retraction can restore the weight norm, but cannot establish that this direction solves the original tangent optimization problem; with a nonzero tangent residual, the description of unretracted drift as merely second-order is also unjustified (A pages 5 and 16). Its reported training improvements therefore support a useful heuristic more strongly than its geometric guarantees. B’s central mechanism is simpler but better matched to its attribution task: forcing every learned gate to one removes learning while retaining the same classical core and fixed machinery. The resulting comparison—1.191 for the full method versus 1.107 for the identity control—supports a learned anytime increment without attributing the entire external-baseline margin to learning (B page 6). The budget analysis and mean final-return reversal further establish what that increment does and does not buy (B pages 7–9). One environment, one meta-training run, configuration selection on evaluation seeds, and retraining-confounded secondary ablations limit generalization, but do not erase the central identity-control comparison (B page 10). For A’s task, the obvious approach is geometry-aware corrections and cheaper spectral computations; replacing the full dual solve with a tiny surrogate is a substantive departure, albeit incompletely justified. For B’s attribution task, the obvious approach is an on/off ablation at the headline metric. Its more consequential departure is showing that the attribution changes with budget and reverses on final quality, while analytic-task probes distinguish successful in-distribution learning from limited transfer (B pages 7–8). That is a supported change in scientific interpretation, not merely cautious presentation. Despite A’s more adventurous numerical shortcut, B more successfully converts its design into an unexpected, actionable finding with clearly bounded evidential scope.

A offers the stronger creative reframing, although B provides a more explicit implementation and more extensive transfer evidence. A decomposes into hypernetwork-generated LoRAs, MaxSim retrieval, query-dependent routing, relevance-driven span placement, and aligned chunking (A pages 3–4). B decomposes into Fisher scatter weighting, trace-target covariance shrinkage, relative-Mahalanobis and energy scores, robust standardization, and gated weighted addition (B pages 4–5). These are largely recognizable primitives: MaxSim appears specifically in ColBERT, while B’s covariance rule is standard identity-target linear shrinkage. A’s least specifically placeable block is relevance-peak “atom” placement, which I can locate only in retrieval-guided span-selection literature, not a particular prior work; its underdescription limits confidence that it constitutes a distinct algorithm. B’s least specifically placeable block is the mid-layer residual correction, whose role belongs to OOD score-fusion literature and whose mathematical gate is a standard negative hinge. Neither paper earns novelty simply from assembling these components. For A’s task, the obvious approaches are improving adapter binding/capacity or retrieving query-relevant chunks; its departure is to use retrieval to select generated weights at composition time rather than supply retrieved text or retrain the generator. For B’s task, the obvious approach is regularized feature-distance detection combined with classifier confidence. Its class-aware weighting and relocation of gating from features to scores develop that expected direction. A’s unexpected central move is therefore the placement and diagnostic role of routing—not the invention of query-dependent retrieval. A supports this move with a targeted intervention: frozen-encoder token similarities select the relevant chunk adapter without new trainable parameters, raising reported exact match from 0.52 to 0.91; relevance placement and boundary alignment then reach 0.98 (A pages 4 and 6). The unsuccessful head and loss alternatives provide useful evidence for a local composition bottleneck. Nevertheless, one evaluation per configuration, training collapses, and the synthetic single-fact task constrain that conclusion (A pages 4–5 and 7–8). These experiments do not establish the stronger assertion that query-blind composition necessarily destroys binding: the downstream model still receives the query, and unsuccessful finite-budget alternatives cannot prove impossibility. B’s mechanism is more fully actionable: its equations specify stable distance estimation and complementary score fusion. Reported CIFAR-100 FPR95 falls from 4.17% to 2.17%, while fixed-setting improvements across adaptation strategies and backbones support transfer beyond one feature geometry (B pages 6–8). However, not every advertised mechanism receives equally strong support: deployed tied shrinkage essentially matches tied empirical covariance, at 4.38% versus 4.37% FPR95 (B page 7). Its DS derivation establishes additivity for the specified zero-ignorance sigmoid masses, not a general inability of DS methods to incorporate reliability weighting (B page 11). These qualifications temper the explanatory claims without negating the detector’s demonstrated utility. Overall, B supplies useful engineering of established scoring ingredients, but A’s controlled relocation of retrieval into weight composition yields a more distinctive, empirically grounded explanation of its task’s failure mode. That explanatory departure narrowly outweighs B’s stronger specification and broader demonstrated applicability.

Its equations specify the detector, and its reported CIFAR-100 FPR95 improvement from 4.17% to 2.17%, together with adaptation/backbone comparisons, supports a useful post-hoc method (A pages 6–8). However, the component evidence does not support every explanatory claim: tied shrinkage essentially matches the unregularized tied estimator, at 4.38% versus 4.37% FPR95 (A page 7), and the gate’s formula does not guarantee that every ID or near-OOD input remains unaffected. Its DS calculation also establishes collapse for a particular belief parameterization, not a general inability of evidential fusion to incorporate reliability (A page 11). B’s reported intervention is more directly diagnostic: query-conditioned selection alone raises exact match from 0.52 to 0.91, with placement and chunk alignment subsequently reaching 0.98 (B page 6). That isolates a substantial supported payoff for the central change rather than attributing everything to a bundled redesign. Important qualifications remain: the evidence concerns one synthetic task, implementation details and repeated-seed uncertainty are incomplete, and unsuccessful capacity/loss variants do not prove that query-blind composition structurally cannot preserve bindings (B pages 3–8). Thus its general impossibility rhetoric exceeds its evidence. Nevertheless, the narrower demonstrated result remains an incisive reframing of where to intervene. That experimentally supported change of direction gives B the stronger overall creative quality, despite A’s greater implementation specificity and wider practical testing.

A’s building blocks are hypernetwork-generated adapters, conditional adapter composition, MaxSim retrieval, relevance-based span placement, and boundary-aware chunking (A pages 3–4). HINT and ColBERT provide identifiable precedents for major primitives. Its least-placeable claim is the diagnosis that composition, rather than adapter generation, causes the observed binding failure; I can locate this only in adapter-interference and content-addressable-memory research, not a specific prior demonstration. B combines regression-based VI, orthogonal-polynomial features, a whitening/change-of-basis identity, block-Jacobi conjugate gradients, and smoothed score control variates (B pages 4–6). These ingredients are recognizable from Salimans–Knowles’s regression VI, Wiener–Askey polynomial-chaos literature, and standard numerical methods. B’s least-placeable claim is that its exact polynomial-to-natural-statistic mapping extends across the stated non-Gaussian families; I cannot identify a particular prior construction supporting that scope. Neither manuscript earns novelty simply from assembling familiar components. For A’s task, the obvious approach is to improve the adapter generator, binding supervision, or static merge. Its central departure is to postpone selection until the query arrives and use token-level retrieval to choose weights rather than prompt text. Query-dependent retrieval itself is familiar, so the surprise lies in relocating the decision and challenging the presumed upstream bottleneck. For B’s task, the obvious approach is Fisher regularization or structured, matrix-free solves plus variance reduction. Replacing empirical curvature estimation with analytically orthonormal features is a more adventurous central shortcut; its PCG and control-variate components follow expected directions. That directional ambition deserves credit independently of whether the mathematics succeeds. A supports its intervention with a clear mechanism and useful component comparisons: frozen-encoder MaxSim selects the relevant chunk’s adapter, relevance-based placement focuses its content, and aligned boundaries prevent fragmented facts. Reported accuracy rises from 0.52 to 0.91 with query conditioning alone, then to 0.98 with the supporting changes (A pages 4 and 6). This is substantial evidence for the particular intervention, although not for a universal impossibility of query-blind storage: a merged model could in principle retain bindings and use the downstream query. One scored model per configuration, training collapses, and a single synthetic benchmark also limit the causal attribution and generality (A pages 4, 7–8). B reports meaningful benchmark improvements and informative variance-reduction ablations (B pages 8–9), but its principal generalization needs mathematical repair. The identity F⁻¹ = MᵀM is valid if the orthonormal features and sufficient statistics span the same space. B assumes that premise for its classical families (B pages 5 and 14), yet ordinary Gamma statistics include log x, and Beta statistics include log x and log(1−x); finite Laguerre or Jacobi polynomial vectors cannot be an invertible linear transformation of those statistics. Thus the claimed exact non-Gaussian natural-parameter update does not follow. The dense mapping also costs O(m²), with the stronger complexity claim requiring additional structure acknowledged on page 5. Reported payoff is conditional rather than uniformly stabilizing: adding control variates worsens Poisson KL from 2.846 to 2545.219 at N=50 (B page 15). Overall, A’s narrower but mechanistically supported redirection outweighs B’s ambitious connection, whose central advertised scope remains unsupported by its derivation.

Replacing its estimation with analytic polynomial orthogonalization is a meaningful departure, although PCG and control variates follow familiar directions. For B’s context-internalization task, the obvious approach is to improve the adapter generator or teach stronger key–value binding. The decisive tradeoff is mechanistic support. A specifies an implementable supervised head and reports angular errors alongside nearly unchanged noise-prediction losses (A page 8). Its evidence supports only a diagnostic readout: the architecture does not feed the auxiliary variable back into denoising, and the increased dino KL divergence limits the claim of unchanged generative quality (A pages 6 and 8). B supplies useful evidence for contrastive fine-tuning and small additional AUROC improvements, but its distinctive physical interpretation has a concrete mathematical problem. With p_s = q_s − x̄, its coupling reduces to tanh[x̄·(q_s − q_t)], becoming identically zero when coordinates are centered; this does not substantiate the claimed inter-pocket topology mechanism (B page 4). The detector experiments compare against frozen DrugCLIP rather than that trained control, so they do not isolate geometry as the source of robustness (B page 13). These are not objections to unconventional invention itself: they disconnect B’s most unexpected mechanisms from their claimed useful effects. A therefore provides the stronger, though limited, realized creative contribution.

Regarding New, Manuscript A can be broken into five main building blocks: (1) dual-tower contrastive retrieval over frozen Uni-Mol encoders with listwise and tri-modal SigLIP objectives (A pages 3, 5), which is placeable in DrugCLIP (Gao et al., 2023) and SigLIP (Zhai et al., 2023); (2) an entropic Sinkhorn optimal-transport atom-alignment channel (A page 5), which is standard material in optimal-transport matching for biomolecules and point clouds; (3) a ligand-conditioned 4-step RK4 coordinate flow combining a Gaussian kernel density gradient with radial expansion to reopen collapsed pockets in embedding space (A page 4); (4) a quaternionic spectral matcher that reshapes 128-d atom projections into 32 4-d blocks and concatenates per-block Euclidean norms with their 1D real FFT magnitudes (A page 4); and (5) a symplectic sub-pocket hypergraph that clusters pockets into k-means sub-pockets, assigns Darboux coordinates from sub-pocket centroids and centroid-relative offsets, and propagates embeddings via a skew-symmetric bilinear coupling tanh(p_s^T q_t - q_s^T p_t) (A page 4). The least placeable building blocks in A—the Darboux skew-symmetric sub-pocket coupling over frozen cavity embeddings and the 4-block norm plus radial FFT atom descriptor (A page 4)—can only be placed broadly at the level of the geometric deep learning and physics-informed neural network subfield literatures (such as Hamiltonian or symplectic graph networks and spectral shape descriptors) rather than any specific prior SBVS paper. By contrast, Manuscript B breaks down into (1) a 3-layer ReLU MLP with sinusoidal time embeddings trained as a DDPM on four 2D toy datasets (circle, dino, line, moons) (B pages 6–7), which is placeable in Ho et al. (2020) and standard public toy-diffusion implementations, and (2) an auxiliary scalar output head supervised with an MSE loss against the polar angle angle(x_0) of the clean 2D sample (B pages 6–7). Even B's least placeable block—adding an auxiliary MSE regression term for a known geometric attribute alongside a generative loss—is standard textbook and tutorial material across multi-task generative modeling, making A's building blocks far less specifically placeable. Regarding Surprising, for A's task of SBVS on unbound (apo) or AlphaFold2-predicted structures, the obvious approach would be either to perform flexible pose sampling/docking or to train a standard dual-tower contrastive encoder with pocket-crop data augmentations; for B's task of making a low-dimensional diffusion model capture an interpretable geometric factor, the obvious approach would be to attach a supervised auxiliary prediction head and MSE penalty for a known ground-truth data attribute. B follows that obvious direction directly by regressing the polar angle of 2D points with an auxiliary MSE loss (B pages 6–7). In contrast, A departs meaningfully from the expected direction both architecturally and empirically: it combines fast cached-embedding contrastive retrieval with a differentiable coordinate-opening flow, skew-symmetric sub-pocket message passing, quaternionic-spectral matching, and Sinkhorn optimal transport without generating atomistic poses (A pages 3–5), and its ablation and zero-shot transfer analyses unexpectedly reveal that end-to-end tri-modal projection fine-tuning drives bulk DUD-E benchmark gains while the geometric modules specifically govern collapsed-pocket recovery and cross-detector invariance (A pages 7–10, 13). Regarding Useful, A's central mechanism is fully specified with explicit equations, hyperparameters, and runtime profiling (10,370 mol/s screening throughput and 8.05 s/epoch training; A pages 4–5, 15). Although A has theoretical tradeoffs—some of its mathematical physics terminology overstates simple algebraic heuristics, such as defining sub-pocket momentum as p_s = q_s - x_bar where the bilinear form simplifies to differences of centroid projections, or treating arbitrary 4-tuples of a 128-d MLP vector as quaternions (A page 4), and its geometric channels slightly lower naive max-pooled blind early enrichment unless paired with a volume-penalized aggregator (A pages 9–10, 14, Tables 4 and 7)—its empirical payoff is rigorously demonstrated and transparently scoped. Specifically, A includes a full 'No-Geometry' ablation showing that tri-modal projection fine-tuning lifts 5-setting DUD-E AUROC from 0.761 to 0.9403 while the geometric stack recovers severe apo conformational collapses (e.g., COMT AUROC from 0.393 to 0.933 and MAPK2 from 0.219 to 0.938; A pages 7, 9–10, 14) and prevents catastrophic collapse across alternative cavity detectors like PocketFinder, SURFNET, and LIGSITE (holding ~0.90 AUROC vs. ~0.30 for frozen DrugCLIP*; A page 13, Table 5), while honestly showing via zero-shot BayesBind and PLINDER evaluations where DUD-E decoy biases limit transfer (A pages 8–9, Table 2). Conversely, B's proposal is in need of repair: while B claims to learn a joint Markov reverse process p_theta(x_{t-1}, z_{t-1} | x_t, z_t) over an evolving latent variable (B page 6, Eq. 1), the actual MLP architecture only takes (x_t, t) as input without conditioning on z_t and merely regresses the static clean polar angle angle(x_0) via a non-periodic MSE loss (B pages 6–7, Eq. 3). Furthermore, angle(x_0) is already a trivial deterministic function of the observable 2D coordinates, adding the auxiliary loss worsens evaluation loss on three of the four datasets and degrades KL divergence on Dino and Line (B page 8, Table 1), the abstract's claimed Moons evaluation loss (0.6173, B page 1) contradicts the text and Table 1 (0.6200, B pages 2, 8), and the manuscript is incomplete, ending with the literal placeholder 'CONCLUSIONS HERE' in Section 7 (B page 9). Consequently, even accounting for the heuristic nature of some of A's geometric formulations, A's novel components, candid deconstructions, and supported empirical payoffs decisively outweigh B.

Regarding New, each manuscript can be decomposed into core building blocks. Manuscript A relies on: (1) an action-condensed partial-tree state space where actions select unreached destination terminals and connect them via multi-source Dijkstra shortest paths from the existing partial tree (A pages 2, 4–5), (2) a randomized greedy rollout sampling uniformly from the top-K closest unreached destinations (A page 5), and (3) Upper Confidence Bound for Trees (UCT) Monte Carlo Tree Search over terminal insertion sequences (A pages 4–5). Every block in A is readily placeable in standard combinatorial optimization works: growing a Steiner tree by iteratively adding the shortest path from the entire current partial tree to an unreached terminal is the classic Takahashi–Matsuyama (1980) Steiner tree heuristic, top-K candidate sampling is the standard Restricted Candidate List mechanism from Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedures (GRASP, Feo & Resende, 1995), and applying MCTS over constructive heuristic decisions is standard in the combinatorial routing subfield. Manuscript B relies on: (1) a neural network parameterizing a time-inhomogeneous Merton Jump Diffusion process with a truncated Poisson–Gaussian mixture density (B pages 3–4), placed directly in Neural MJD (Gao et al., 2025) and Merton (1976); (2) analytical median and mode inversion via vectorized Newton–Raphson root-finding on the mixture CDF and log-density (B page 4), placeable in numerical mixture-distribution root-finding (e.g., Carreira-Perpiñán, 2000) and statistical decision theory; (3) deterministic stratified quantile sampling via inverse-CDF evaluation at midpoint strata (B page 4), placeable in quasi-Monte Carlo and variance-reduction literature (e.g., Glasserman's Monte Carlo Methods in Financial Engineering); and (4) a Spectral Energy-Variance Conservation Loss coupled with an expectation-restart Euler–Maruyama scheme that regularizes predicted continuous-plus-jump variance against empirical context variance (B page 5). While the variance formula itself comes from moment matching for compound Poisson diffusions (e.g., Press, 1967; Ball & Torous, 1985), B's least placeable block—formulating instantaneous total jump-diffusion variance conservation against historical context variance as a multi-horizon neural training regularizer alongside periodic analytical-mean state resets (B page 5)—can only be placed at the broader subfield level of physics-informed/moment-regularized neural SDEs rather than a single prior formulation. Regarding Useful, Manuscript A's central proposal is an Action-Condensed MCTS solver that constructs low-cost directed Steiner trees for multi-cloud broadcast routing within a 2.0-second budget (A pages 2, 4–5). While the multi-source Dijkstra expansion and top-K rollout mechanisms are coherent, A suffers from severe internal contradictions and missing technical details that leave it in need of repair. First, the Abstract claims to propose a "hybrid neuro-symbolic solver that combines the global structural exploration of LLMs with an Action-Condensed Monte Carlo Tree Search" (A page 1), yet the Methodology contains no LLM or neural network component whatsoever (A pages 3–5), and Future Work later admits that building a hybrid neuro-symbolic architecture is actually uncompleted future work (A page 9). Second, Section 3.3.1 asserts that it modifies the UCT formula to minimize costs rather than maximize rewards, but omits the formula entirely (A page 5), and Section 3.1 introduces link throughput capacities th(u,v) (A page 4) that the Limitations section admits are ignored by the objective function (A page 9). Meanwhile, Table 2 shows two discarded heuristic variants achieving better scores (618.08 and 618.10 $/GB) than 627.10, which the text dismisses via unsupported assertions of overfitting across a five-graph benchmark (A page 8). In contrast, Manuscript B's central proposal (Neural-MMA) is fully worked out with explicit equations for Newton–Raphson mixture-CDF median inversion and second-order mode inversion (B page 4), stratified inverse-CDF quantile trajectory generation (B page 4), the energy-variance conservation loss (B page 5), and mathematical proofs for truncation tail decay and restart weak-error bounds (B pages 4–5, 11). A departs from naive edge-by-edge RL by elevating the MCTS action space to unreached terminal selection with exact shortest-path transitions (A pages 2, 4–5), which is a sensible framing relative to edge-by-edge search, though standard within classical Steiner tree heuristics. For B's task of improving probabilistic accuracy, candidate diversity, and long-horizon stability in neural jump-diffusion forecasting, the obvious approach would be redesigning the neural backbone, increasing the number of Monte Carlo trajectory samples, or adopting multi-step iterative diffusion/flow-matching samplers (B pages 1–2). Both manuscripts mainly reuse established machinery. A consists of UCT search, incremental shortest-path tree construction, and randomized restricted-candidate rollouts. Its least readily attributable substantive block—the tree-to-terminal attachment rule—has a close precedent in Takahashi–Matsuyama-style Steiner heuristics, although that does not establish guarantees for A’s directed implementation (A pages 4–5). B consists of Merton mixtures, absolute-loss-optimal medians, inverse-CDF stratification, and variance matching. Its least specifically attributable central block is the contextual variance regularizer, which I can place in moment-matching regularization but not identify with a particular earlier neural-jump paper (B pages 4–5). The variance identity and squared penalty themselves are standard. Neither paper deserves substantial novelty credit merely for assembling these ingredients. For A’s routing task, the obvious approach is a cost-aware Steiner heuristic or integer program; searching terminal order with MCTS changes search granularity but remains close to established graph optimization. For B’s inference task, the obvious approach is improved Monte Carlo estimation or direct predictive summaries; exploiting the existing mixture CDF is therefore also a natural direction. B’s central shift toward deterministic candidate coverage rather than additional simulation is useful but only moderately unexpected, just as A’s terminal-level action abstraction is a modest rather than radical departure. The decisive difference is how much practical payoff survives scrutiny. A specifies a coherent implementable heuristic: select a destination, attach its cheapest path from the existing tree, and evaluate completion through randomized greedy rollouts. However, exact shortest-path attachment does not establish optimal Steiner subtrees, and the advertised neural integration is not worked out. More importantly, the principal empirical result remains unresolved: A page 6 reports 627.10, while Table 1 on A page 7 reports 1090.78 for the proposed method. This directly affects whether its central competitive-performance claim holds. A page 9 also acknowledges that throughput constraints and dynamic-network evaluation are absent, limiting the broader deployment claims. B provides explicit computational mechanisms and more discriminating evidence for a narrower benefit. Its fixed-checkpoint estimator swaps and additive/removal ablations distinguish point-estimation improvements from candidate-generation improvements (B page 7), while matched-environment results cover both financial and synthetic data (B page 6). These support practical gains in finite-candidate coverage and modest improvements in point forecasting—not necessarily better calibrated stochastic dynamics. B nevertheless needs substantive theoretical repair: reusing the same quantile rank across time in Equation 7 imposes temporal dependence rather than faithfully sampling independent Merton increments (B page 4), and resetting a process to its mean cannot generally preserve weak accuracy for nonlinear observables, contrary to the restart argument (B pages 5 and 11). Its variance penalty also worsens the 14-step results despite improving the 28-step results (B page 12). Thus B’s strongest exactness and stability claims should not be accepted wholesale. Nevertheless, its defensible core—deterministic mixture-based readouts and candidate construction—has component-specific empirical support that A’s unreconciled headline result lacks. With both offering limited primitive novelty and moderate directional departures, that better-supported, explicitly bounded practical contribution makes B the stronger overall creative manuscript.

A offers the stronger overall contribution, although its defensible payoff is narrower than its claims. Its building blocks are a Merton mixture, loss-optimal point estimation, numerical CDF inversion, stratified inverse-transform sampling, variance matching, and conditional-mean restarting. Most are recognizable statistical or numerical methods. The least placeable assertion is that mean restarting supplies a horizon-independent weak-error guarantee (A pages 5 and 11): I cannot identify a specific prior result supporting that assertion, only the broader SDE-stabilization literature. B consists of UCT-style search, terminal-selection actions, shortest-path attachment to a growing tree, and randomized top-K greedy completion (B pages 4–5). The attachment mechanism closely resembles the Takahashi–Matsuyama shortest-path Steiner heuristic; its least specifically placeable ingredient, treating terminal attachment as a search macro-action, fits macro-action MCTS literature, but I cannot name a particular prior directed-Steiner implementation. Neither paper’s unusual assembly alone establishes new constituent mechanisms. For A’s forecasting task, the obvious approach would be to improve jump-process parameter estimation and generate Monte Carlo forecasts; for B’s routing task, it would be to construct or optimize a cost-aware Steiner tree using shortest-path heuristics or mathematical programming. A redirects attention from model architecture to deterministic, loss-aligned extraction of an already available predictive distribution. B redirects search from individual edges to destination-attachment order, letting Dijkstra construct each path. Both are meaningful but moderate departures: analytical quantiles are natural once the mixture is explicit, and B’s path-level construction remains close to established Steiner heuristics. B’s advertised neural-symbolic departure is not operationally demonstrated—the described solver is MCTS plus graph algorithms, without a specified LLM role. The distinction is in how much useful payoff survives scrutiny. A works out its inference transformations and regularization explicitly (A pages 4–5), and its fixed-checkpoint and component-removal experiments provide interpretable attribution: analytical inversion improves p-MAE from 14.9 to 14.2, while stratification reduces oracle minMAE from 4.86 to 2.79 (A page 7). These support practical improvements over the stated sampling pipeline, not proof of better-calibrated trajectory distributions. Indeed, reusing each quantile across time in equation 7 changes the joint increment dependence, and resetting trajectories to their mean destroys variance, invalidating the claimed general weak-error argument. The regularizer also worsens the 14-step results despite improving the 28-step results (A page 12). Thus A needs substantial qualification, particularly around ‘exact’ trajectory inference and universal stability, but its narrower inference benefit has direct experimental support. B’s core algorithm is implementable and sensibly exploits already-paid tree edges through multi-source shortest paths (B page 5). Exact attachment costs, however, do not imply optimal Steiner subtrees or global optimality. More importantly, its central empirical payoff is unresolved in the supplied text: B page 6 reports 627.10, whereas Table 1 on B page 7 lists 1090.78 for the proposed method against the same baselines. The caption on B page 8 introduces yet another, incompatible lowest-cost claim. Its ablations conflate rollout changes with state-abstraction changes, and the rejection of cheaper variants for instability lacks corresponding success-rate measurements (B pages 6 and 8). B also acknowledges that throughput constraints and dynamic-network evaluation are absent (B page 9). Consequently, A’s modest but more directly isolated practical correction outweighs B’s attractive search abstraction, whose claimed competitive and robust payoff cannot presently be reconciled with its reported evidence.

Evaluated relative to their respective fields and research tasks, Manuscript B demonstrates substantially stronger overall creative quality than Manuscript A when considering New, Useful, and Surprising jointly. Regarding the obvious approach for each task and how far each manuscript departs from it (Surprising): for A's task of low-latency, topology-aware Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) expert placement and replication, a competent approach would typically implement greedy Longest Processing Time (LPT) bin-packing and sequential replica allocation in a compiled C++/CUDA kernel or run an approximate solver asynchronously; A departs from this by reformulating placement entirely as loop-free PyTorch tensor operations, replacing stateful bin-packing with a static boustrophedon (snake) scatter (A pages 4-5) and casting sequential greedy replica assignment as a parallel D'Hondt quotient matrix with global top-k selection (A page 5). For B's task of attributing multi-token generated spans across long contexts and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning chains, the obvious approach would be to compute layer-local continuous vector similarities (or whitened norms) and recursively propagate attribution by weighting intermediate reasoning tokens by their first-hop relevance scores; B departs much more counterintuitively by collapsing the aggregated final-layer target representation into a single binary sign vector s_S in {-1, +1}^D, projecting intermediate-layer head value-output vectors across all depths onto this fixed final-layer sign vector (B pages 3-5), and using an unweighted target (w_j = 1) over intermediate reasoning tokens during recursive attribution because weighting by first-hop relevance scores actively distorts the orientation signal (B pages 5-6, 10). Regarding prior art for each paper's building blocks (New): A's components can be placed in specific known formulations—two-level node/GPU packing is standard in distributed MoE serving (A pages 3-4), boustrophedon assignment is a classic zig-zag scheduling heuristic (A page 4), and the D'Hondt quotient matrix is the textbook proportional apportionment algorithm directly vectorized via tensor broadcasting (A page 5). In contrast, while B builds on residual-stream L1 proximity (Ferrando et al., 2022) and multi-token recursive attribution (Pan et al., 2025) (B page 3), its least placeable building block—linearizing L1 proximity into a single final-layer binary sign vector applied across all intermediate Transformer layers alongside an unweighted sign-orientation CoT recursion (B pages 3-6)—cannot be placed in a specific prior work and is only placeable within the broader subfield literature of Transformer mechanistic and residual-stream interpretability. Finally, comparing whether the mechanisms work and deliver their claimed payoffs (Useful): A defines its snake scatter and D'Hondt quotient equations (A pages 4-5), but its empirical payoff fails to support its claims and exhibits internal inconsistencies. Specifically, A's proposed method achieves a Combined Score of 0.1287, which is orders of magnitude worse than even the naive Round-robin baseline floor of 19.0 as well as AdaEvolve (22.06) and MicroMoE (100.0) (A page 6, Table 1); its 3.05ms execution latency exceeds its stated 2ms budget (which A inaccurately refers to as a microsecond-level budget and O(1) complexity despite sorting) (A pages 1, 3-7); its own ablation table shows two alternative variants scoring higher (0.1461 and 0.1449) than the designated 'Final solution (best)' (0.1287) (A page 7, Table 2); and Section 3.4 claims the system executes asynchronously using step t-1 statistics (A pages 5-6) whereas Section 5 states that asynchronous execution is left for future research (A page 8). Conversely, B works out its mathematical mechanism completely (B pages 3-6, 13)—with only minor theoretical caveats, such as an O(L*H*M*N) scalar attention pre-aggregation term noted in the appendix (B page 13) and a strong sufficient condition for the Taylor expansion (B page 4) that is nevertheless directly validated by cross-layer alignment measurements (B page 7)—and delivers a well-supported payoff across 11 RULER tasks, MATH, MoreHopQA, HotpotQA, and Aider on Qwen-3 8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B-It, improving ground-truth recovery (0.695 vs. 0.635) and causal deletion faithfulness in 0.30s-0.40s per sample while validating every component through six ablations (B pages 7-10, 13-15). While A offers a compact systems heuristic for loop-free tensor apportionment, its unsupported empirical payoff and internal contradictions weigh heavily against it, whereas B combines a more novel and counterintuitive theoretical simplification with rigorous empirical validation.

B builds from the standard L1 sign derivative, value-aware attention scoring, cross-layer aggregation, and recursive attribution (B pages 3–6). Its hardest-to-place contribution is not the elementary Taylor identity, but the finding that an unweighted reasoning target preserves useful attribution better than relevance-weighted targets. I can place that claim only within recursive Transformer-attribution research, not in a specific earlier result. Thus B has a harder-to-place substantive finding, without needing to treat its assembly of familiar mathematical primitives as new. For A’s task, the obvious approach is topology-aware greedy packing with sequential replication of heavily loaded experts; for B’s task, it is attention/value or gradient-based attribution that propagates relevance-weighted scores through intermediate reasoning. A makes a conspicuous cross-domain departure by importing electoral apportionment and replacing adaptive packing with a fixed serpentine pattern. B instead challenges an intuitive premise within attribution: discarding target magnitudes and preliminary relevance weights can improve the trace. Both departures are central, but B tests its counterintuitive choice more directly rather than relying chiefly on the appeal of the reformulation. A provides implementable placement equations, but its supported payoff falls short of its stated latency and communication objectives. A constant number of tensor calls is not constant computational work: sorting and the expert-by-replica quotient matrix grow with problem size. Its approximately 3.05-ms runtime misses its own 2-ms budget, its reported composite score falls below round-robin, and the converted baseline scores do not establish a convincing practical advantage (A pages 6–7). Actual inter-node traffic reduction and end-to-end serving gains are not demonstrated. Asynchronous latency hiding is described as operational on pages 5–6 but remains a future direction on page 8. Reported evidence recovery rises from 0.635 to 0.695 on average (B page 7); more importantly, replacing relevance-weighted reasoning targets with unweighted targets reduces MATH deletion AUC from 0.355 to 0.282, while the recursion ablation supports the additional hop itself (B pages 10 and 14). B also needs significant qualification: some local-sign and ungated alternatives perform better on individual metrics, and its appendix explicitly includes O(LHMN) attention aggregation, contradicting target-length-independent complexity; cached attention additionally requires quadratic sequence-length memory (B pages 10, 13, and 15). Nevertheless, after discounting those overclaims, B retains a supported, counterintuitive methodological payoff. That makes its overall creative contribution stronger than A’s interesting transfer whose central systems advantage remains unestablished.

(2024) and distributed MoE load-balancing literature (B pages 3-4); (2) boustrophedon (snake-like) draft assignment on sorted weights, which is standard material in parallel task scheduling and partitioning heuristics (B pages 4-5); and (3) its least placeable block: computing dynamic MoE expert replica allocations in parallel via a D'Hondt apportionment quotient matrix Q_{i,j} = W_i / D_j - epsilon_j with global top-k selection (B page 5). Because the D'Hondt quotient matrix is a standard formulation in proportional resource allocation and closely matches standard vectorized Expert Parallelism Load Balancer (EPLB) heuristics, A's least placeable block is harder to place specifically than B's. Regarding Surprising, for A's task of attributing multi-token CoT outputs in anisotropic Transformer spaces, the obvious approach is to apply layer-wise normalization or local proximity metrics at each layer and weight intermediate reasoning tokens by their first-hop output relevance scores (w_j^{(0)}) when tracing back to the input context; for B's task of low-latency MoE expert replication and placement, the obvious approach is to execute iterative greedy Longest Processing Time (LPT) bin-packing and sequential highest-load replica assignment in a compiled low-level routine or fast solver. Paper B departs by reformulating sequential bin-packing and greedy replica allocation into loop-free PyTorch tensor operations (boustrophedon scatter and a parallel D'Hondt quotient matrix; B pages 2, 4-5). Paper A makes a more unexpected central departure in two ways: first, it discards target magnitudes across depth in favor of a single final-layer binary sign vector s_S projected across all intermediate layers, showing this global sign is more faithful than both exact L1 proximity and per-layer local sign vectors because it filters intermediate FFN/LayerNorm fluctuations (A pages 4, 7, 9-10); second, it shows that the intuitive approach of weighting intermediate CoT tokens by their preliminary relevance scores (w_j^{(0)}) actively distorts the target orientation signal (degrading MATH RISE from 0.282 to 0.355), whereas an unweighted target span (w_j = 1) cleanly propagates attribution to the source context (A pages 2, 5-6, 10). Even accounting for the tradeoff that B tackles strict real-time systems constraints without external solvers, B's failure to beat the naive round-robin baseline or meet its stated latency budget leaves it in need of repair, whereas A delivers a theoretically grounded, counterintuitive, and empirically validated advance.

A combines L1 sign linearization, value-aware attention scoring, depth weighting, and recursive span attribution. The sign derivative is standard calculus, and value-aware proximity has a concrete antecedent in ALTI. A’s least-placeable block is the decision to discard first-hop relevance weights when constructing the recursive reasoning target (A pages 5–6): I can situate that only within recursive Transformer attribution, not name a specific earlier prescription. B combines hierarchical placement, serpentine packing, D’Hondt quotient selection, and asynchronous scheduling (B pages 4–6). Its allocation primitives have direct standard formulations in serpentine allocation and D’Hondt’s highest-averages rule; its least specifically placeable block, node-local expert replication, belongs to topology-aware MoE scheduling, although I cannot confidently name an exact antecedent. The novelty distinction is therefore modest, but A’s particular unweighted-recursion prescription is less readily identifiable as a standard rule. Neither deserves novelty credit simply for assembling familiar components. For A’s attribution task, the obvious approach is to improve normalized proximity scoring and propagate relevance-weighted signals through intermediate reasoning. Using a single final-layer sign direction and deliberately ignoring those relevance weights is a central departure from that expectation. For B’s placement task, the obvious approach is topology-aware greedy/LPT packing or mathematical optimization. Recasting replication as electoral apportionment and replacing adaptive packing with a fixed snake pattern is also a genuine, central departure; its cross-domain assembly is interesting independently of whether it works. The stronger supported payoff favors A overall. Its mechanism is specified through attention-weighted positive projections, depth aggregation, and an additional reasoning-span attribution hop (A pages 4–6). Evidence recovery improves from 0.635 to 0.695 against its reported span-attribution baseline, while the targeted recursion ablation reduces MATH deletion AUC from 0.355 with relevance weighting to 0.282 without it (A pages 7 and 10). These results support the unusual simplification rather than merely the complete system. Nevertheless, the guarantees need repair: sign projection does not eliminate source-vector magnitude dependence, some ablations favor alternatives, and the appendix explicitly retains O(LHMN) attention aggregation despite claiming target-length-independent linear complexity (A pages 10 and 13). B likewise supplies an actionable outline, and its reported 0.6629 balancedness at approximately 3.05 ms shows that tensorized placement can execute (B page 7). More importantly, the measured runtime misses its stated 2 ms budget; the reported combined score does not demonstrate an advantage over even round-robin, and baseline latency/balancedness breakdowns are absent (B pages 6–7). Neither reduced inter-node traffic nor end-to-end inference improvement is demonstrated, while asynchronous latency hiding is asserted without corresponding measurements (B pages 5–8). Thus B’s inventive reformulation remains less convincingly connected to its promised systems benefit. Despite A’s overstated theory and scaling claims, its unexpected attribution simplification has substantially better mechanism-specific experimental support, making it the stronger overall creative contribution.

Regarding Useful, A's central proposal is Hybrid Semantic-Cartesian Positional Encodings (HSC-PE), which applies an EDT to binary HD map masks and dynamically gates the resulting embedding with Cartesian coordinates to improve strict 3D volumetric alignment (A pages 4-6). However, A's mechanism and claimed payoff are in need of repair due to severe internal contradictions and unsupported claims: Equation 1 (A page 4) formulates non-differentiable strict 3D IoU mAP as the optimization objective, whereas Section 3.4 (A page 6) reveals the model actually trains with standard CenterPoint focal and L1 losses; Figure 4 (A page 6) claims the ablation proves the EDT is critical for optimal performance, directly contradicting Table 2 and the text (A page 9), which show that removing the EDT and feeding raw binary masks improves the score (0.1766 vs. 0.1763) and renders the proposed transform unnecessary; the entire semantic map branch adds only +0.0017 mAP (A page 9, Table 2); and the paper admits it lacks any high-IoU or yaw/dimension error breakdown to verify volumetric alignment, compares only against internal search branches (five scoring 0.0000), and lacks verification artifacts for its self-reported logs (A pages 8-10). Conversely, B's central proposal—ST-FacRNN, combining static partial correlation with CKA-normalized multi-lag t-HSIC over cross-trial pooled minibatches (B pages 3-5)—is mathematically complete and rigorously validated across synthetic chaotic Lorenz-Thomas dynamics (B page 6, Table 1), macaque M1 reaching recordings under Gaussian and Poisson observation models (B pages 6-9, Tables 2-3; page 15, Table 8), and the standardized Neural Latents Benchmark '21 (B page 15, Tables 9-10). B's ablations directly verify every claimed mechanism: multi-step lags boost synthetic group recovery R2 from 0.822 to 0.904 and M1 alignment from 0.772 to 0.802 (B page 10, Table 4), cross-trial pooling improves accuracy while reducing epoch runtime from 6.41s to 4.24s and preventing collapse across five kernel types (B page 10, Table 5; page 14), and a 2D sensitivity sweep proves static PC and t-HSIC act synergistically (B page 10; page 13, Figure 5). Regarding Surprising, for A's task of incorporating HD maps into BEV 3D detection, the obvious approach is rasterizing map layers, encoding them alongside spatial coordinates, and fusing them into the BEV grid before a standard detection head; A follows this expected path directly, with its only unexpected finding being an empirical ablation showing raw binary masks beat its proposed distance transform (A page 9). For B's task of preventing temporal cross-talk between factorized recurrent sub-circuits, the obvious approach is adding a parametric latent transition prior or enforcing orthogonality on the decoder/recurrent weight subspaces. B explicitly tests those obvious structural regularizers (L_trans and L_orth) and shows they yield negligible gain (delta <= 0.005) because factorized rollouts already evolve on the sub-circuit manifolds (B page 4; page 9; page 13, Table 7); instead, B makes a central departure by reformulating the problem around non-parametric multi-lag CKA kernel independence pooled across short trials, which further leads to the unexpected discovery that disentangled sub-circuits automatically align with biological cardinal movement axes without supervision (+0.330 preference, B pages 7-8, Figure 3; page 13, Table 6) and automatically collapse surplus dimensions to <0.8% variance for label-free rank pruning (B pages 15-16, Table 11). While A tackles a large-scale multi-sensor engineering pipeline, its minor and internally contradicted feature-fusion tweaks cannot outweigh B's coherent theoretical mechanism, rigorous empirical validation, and non-obvious scientific payoff.

Preferred: SPATIO-TEMPORAL DISENTANGLED FACTORED RECURRENT NEURAL NETWORKS FOR NEURAL POPULATION DYNAMICS

Both manuscripts mainly reuse established ingredients, but B develops the more compelling research direction. A combines BEV fusion, coordinate embeddings, distance transforms, map priors, and sigmoid gating (A pages 5–6). Even its least routine substantive block—using HD-map geometry to improve object detection—has a specific precedent in HDNET: Exploiting HD Maps for 3D Object Detection. B combines low-rank factorization, latent-dependence regularization, normalized kernel alignment, temporal lags, and sample pooling (B pages 4–5). Its normalization is specifically recognizable as CKA from Kornblith et al.’s Similarity of Neural Network Representations Revisited; its least readily placeable block, cross-trial pooling of lagged pairs for dependence estimation, I can locate only in the broader kernel-based time-series estimation literature, not a particular antecedent. This supports only a narrow distinction in originality: neither deserves novelty credit simply for assembling familiar components. For A’s volumetric-detection task, the obvious approach is stronger sensor fusion and IoU-aware box regression; injecting environmental geometry through positional encodings is a modest departure. For B’s subcircuit-identification task, the obvious approach is static independence regularization or explicit structural decoupling; addressing lagged nonlinear dependence through estimator design is a central departure, although extending static penalties across time is itself predictable. B’s investigation of pooling rather than kernel choice as the source of stability is more consequential than A’s incidental finding that raw masks slightly outperform engineered distance fields (B page 14; A page 9). A provides an implementable gated-encoding mechanism, but its distinctive geometric payoff remains weakly established. Removing semantic encoding changes the reported score from 0.1763 to 0.1746, without repeated-run uncertainty, isolated yaw/dimension measurements, or map-misalignment tests (A page 9). Moreover, its stated TP/(TP+FP+FN) metric is not average precision, leaving an important discrepancy between the evaluation definition and claimed benchmark performance (A page 7). B more directly tests its proposed interventions: lagged versus instantaneous penalties improve reported M1 alignment from 0.772 to 0.802, and pooling versus per-trial estimation from 0.748 to 0.772 (B page 10). These are useful diagnostic comparisons, not proof of all its claims: one-step lags already match the proposed multiscale window, synthetic subcircuit recovery barely changes from 0.726 to 0.727, and Poisson-model results largely tie the static-factorized baseline (B pages 6, 10, and 15). There are also substantive mathematical problems: as printed, the one-index-shifted kernel need not be a symmetric positive-semidefinite Gram matrix suitable for standard HSIC, and factorizing W does not itself guarantee decoupled dynamics (B pages 4–5). Its independence guarantees therefore require repair or clarification. Nevertheless, B narrowly earns the overall choice for a more informative, intervention-tested empirical regularization proposal—not for established identifiability or universal performance superiority. A’s mechanism is simpler, but the specifically claimed map-driven geometric benefit is less directly demonstrated.

Preferred: SPATIO-TEMPORAL DISENTANGLED FACTORED RECURRENT NEURAL NETWORKS FOR NEURAL POPULATION DYNAMICS

Manuscript A demonstrates substantially stronger overall creative quality than Manuscript B when evaluated jointly across New, Useful, and Surprising relative to each paper's own field and task. Regarding New, Manuscript A decomposes into several building blocks: group-factorized low-rank recurrent connectivity W = AB = sum_g A_{:,g} B_{g,:} with an instantaneous aggregated-posterior partial correlation (PC) penalty in a VAE (placeable in a specific prior work, FacRNN by Li et al., 2025, and the low-rank RNN literature such as Mastrogiuseppe & Ostojic, 2017 and Valente et al., 2022; A pages 1-3); double-centered, Frobenius-norm-normalized Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) Gram matrices (placeable in Kornblith et al., 2019; A pages 3-5); and its least placeable building block, a cross-trial minibatch-pooled, multi-lag temporal Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (t-HSIC) regularizer paired with a label-free within-group PCA variance-collapse auto-pruning protocol for identifying neural sub-circuits on short trial sequences (A pages 4-5, 9, 15-16). While time-series HSIC and sequential disentanglement exist in the broader kernel independence testing and sequential VAE subfield literatures (e.g., Gretton et al. on kernel dependence and Yao et al., 2022 on temporal disentanglement), this specific cross-trial lagged Gram pooling and group-rank pruning mechanism for factorized recurrent sub-circuits can only be placed at the subfield level rather than a single prior paper. By contrast, Manuscript B breaks down into projecting LiDAR and camera features into a Bird's Eye View (BEV) grid with VoxelNet and a CenterPoint heatmap head (standard material in Yin et al., 2020 and Zhou & Tuzel, 2017; B pages 4-7), embedding 2D (x, y) grid coordinates via an MLP (standard formulation in coordinate-MLP and BEV detection works such as CoordConv and PETR; B page 5), applying a Euclidean distance transform or binary rasterization to HD map layers (standard material in map-aware BEV perception such as HDNET; B page 5), and combining embeddings via a sigmoid gate alpha = sigma(W_alpha [E_c; E_s] + b_alpha) (standard gated fusion across deep learning; B pages 5-6). Even B's least placeable block—gating a rasterized HD map embedding with a 2D Cartesian coordinate MLP in BEV—is standard material across multiple prior BEV perception works. Regarding Useful, Manuscript A's central mechanism—jointly optimizing the VAE ELBO, static aggregated-posterior PC, and cross-trial pooled multi-lag CKA-normalized t-HSIC—is mathematically worked out in full (A pages 3-5, Eqs. 1-8) and supported across synthetic Lorenz-Thomas dynamics (A page 6, Table 1), macaque M1 reaching recordings under both Gaussian and Poisson observation models (A page 7, Table 2; A page 15, Table 8), modern neural population baselines including CEBRA, LFADS, and PSID (A page 9, Table 3), and the standardized Neural Latents Benchmark '21 (A page 15, Tables 9-10). A key tradeoff in A is that on long, clean synthetic trajectories and Poisson NLB benchmarks, its quantitative gains over static FacRNN are small (e.g., connectivity R^2 of 0.783 vs. 0.771 in A page 6, Table 1, and matching co-bps in A page 15, Tables 8-9); however, A transparently explains and demonstrates through ablations that t-HSIC and cross-trial pooling specifically pay off on short, 14-bin biological trials by eliminating time-lagged cross-talk and lowering cross-group partial correlation (0.095 vs. 0.119 for FacRNN and 0.580 for CEBRA-Behavior at K=4; A page 9, Table 3; A page 10, Tables 4-5) while improving behavioral alignment (0.802 vs. 0.766; A page 7, Table 2) at no predictive cost. Conversely, Manuscript B's proposal is in need of repair due to internal contradictions and unsupported payoffs: B frames its objective as maximizing strict 3D IoU mAP (B page 4, Eq. 1) to fix the yaw and dimension errors of center-distance detectors, yet actually trains a standard CenterPoint center-heatmap focal loss and L1 regression head without any volumetric IoU loss (B page 6, Eq. 5). Furthermore, B contradicts itself on its core distance-transform mechanism—claiming in Figure 4 (B page 6) that the Euclidean distance transform is 'demonstrated by the ablation study to be critical for optimal performance,' while reporting in Table 2 (B page 9) and Section 5 (B page 10) that removing the distance transform and using raw binary map masks actually improves the score (0.1766 vs. 0.1763). Most importantly, removing the semantic map encoding altogether reduces B's score by only 0.0017 (0.1746 vs. 0.1763; B page 9, Table 2), B compares only against internal search branches (five scoring 0.0000; B page 8, Table 1) rather than external baselines, and B explicitly acknowledges missing granular high-IoU/yaw metrics and missing verification artifacts (B pages 9-10), leaving its claimed volumetric alignment payoff unsubstantiated. Regarding Surprising, for Manuscript A's task of disentangling temporal sub-circuits in low-rank RNNs, the obvious approach would be to impose an explicit factorized latent transition prior or orthogonalize the encoder/decoder subspaces, and compute independence per trial. A departs meaningfully from this expected direction: it proves empirically that transition-prior alignment and subspace orthogonality yield negligible effect (delta <= 0.005; A page 9; A page 13, Table 7) because closed-loop dynamics already evolve on decoupled sub-circuit manifolds (A page 4), and instead combines static PC with cross-trial pooled multi-lag HSIC. This central move leads to unexpected, domain-relevant payoffs: cross-trial pooling alone stabilizes arbitrary kernels on short trials without dataset-specific kernel switching (A page 14), temporal disentanglement causes unsupervised motor cortex latents to spontaneously align with physiological cardinal movement axes without behavioral labels (A page 8, Figure 3; A page 13, Table 6), and over-specified latent dimensions automatically collapse below 0.8% variance to enable label-free rank pruning (A pages 15-16, Table 11). For Manuscript B's task of incorporating HD maps into BEV 3D detection, the obvious approach is to rasterize map layers and 2D coordinates into BEV feature channels via MLPs and gated addition before a standard detection head; B follows this textbook direction directly (B pages 4-7), with its only unexpected observation being the incidental ablation result that raw binary masks slightly beat distance transforms (B page 9). Even accounting for A's modest margins on long continuous trajectories, A's rigorous mechanisms, verified empirical payoffs, and non-obvious insights into neural circuit identifiability clearly outweigh B.

A offers the stronger creative contribution, although its guarantees exceed its evidence. Its building blocks are low-rank recurrent factorization, posterior-independence regularization, kernel normalization, lagged dependence, and pooled estimation (A pages 3–5). The least specifically placeable block is its nonlinear cross-lag dependence statistic: I can locate that direction in kernel independence testing for time series, but cannot name a specific predecessor for the stated estimator. B’s components—BEV fusion, coordinate embeddings, distance transforms, and sigmoid convex gating—have more specific precedents (B pages 4–6): map geometry conditioning detection appears in HDNET: Exploiting HD Maps for 3D Object Detection, while its fusion operation follows the formulation in Gated Multimodal Units for Information Fusion. These precedents concern constituent mechanisms, not whether B’s particular assembly has appeared before. For A’s task, the obvious approach is static factor independence within a low-rank neural-dynamics model; its central departure is to constrain inter-group relationships across time and estimate them using multiple short trials. For B’s task, the obvious approach is improved BEV sensor fusion and box regression, incorporating map features when available; expressing those features as gated positional input is a narrower architectural departure. B’s finding that raw masks outperform engineered distance fields runs against its initial rationale, but changes preprocessing rather than the central approach (B page 9). A works out its training mechanism and provides relevant intervention evidence: lagged rather than instantaneous-only regularization improves M1 alignment from 0.772 to 0.802, while pooled rather than per-trial estimation improves it from 0.748 to 0.772 (A page 10). These support limited empirical benefits, not every claimed mechanism: one-step lags match the proposed multiscale configuration, and the Poisson results essentially tie FacRNN (A pages 10 and 15). Moreover, as written, the nonzero-lag cross-Gram is not the usual symmetric Gram construction underlying HSIC, so its independence interpretation needs justification; low-rank factorization alone also does not establish decoupled dynamics (A pages 4–5). B’s gate is implementable and its ablations suggest benefit, but removing map semantics costs only 0.0017 without reported repeat-run uncertainty. Its promised yaw/dimension improvements and robustness to map errors are explicitly untested (B page 9). The stated mAP formula is also TP/(TP+FP+FN), not average precision, requiring clarification of the evaluation definition and implementation (B page 7). The distinction is therefore qualified rather than overwhelming: A’s more distinctive temporal-dependence proposal has targeted experimental support for a narrower payoff than advertised, whereas B primarily supports a conventional fusion modification without isolating its central geometric-refinement explanation.
